lessons.title: SELECT, FROM, aliases, and reading a table
lessons.objective: Read any table, choose exactly the columns you need, compute new columns, and name every output column deliberately with AS.
lessons.context: Every analysis starts with 'what is actually in this table?'. The merchandising team wants quick lists — supplier directory, price sheet, order-line values — and each list must have clean, predictable column names so it can be pasted into a report or fed into a dashboard.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: read a table in 4 moves**

1. `FROM table` — decide *where* the rows come from (read this clause first, even though it is written second).
2. `SELECT col1, col2` — pick only the columns you need. `SELECT *` is for exploring, not for reports.
3. Compute: `quantity * unit_price`, `ROUND(x, 2)`, `a || ' ' || b` (string concat). Any expression works.
4. Name it: `expression AS clean_name`. Table aliases (`FROM products AS p`, then `p.list_price`) keep
   longer queries readable and become mandatory once you join tables.

```sql
SELECT p.product_name,
       ROUND(p.list_price * 0.9, 2) AS sale_price
FROM   products AS p;
```

**Logical order of evaluation:** `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`.
That's why an alias defined in SELECT can't be used in WHERE (later lessons), but can in ORDER BY.

**NULL preview:** any arithmetic or `||` with NULL yields NULL. You'll handle that properly in Lesson 3.

worked_example.question: Show each product's name, category and price, plus a 10%-off sale price.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT p.product_name,
       p.category,
       p.list_price,
       ROUND(p.list_price * 0.9, 2) AS sale_price
FROM products AS p
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: `p` is a table alias; `sale_price` is a column alias. `ROUND(..., 2)` keeps currency readable. Note `LIMIT 5` only trims the preview — remove it to see all 25 products.

common_mistakes: Leaving computed columns unnamed — you get a header like `quantity * unit_price` that breaks downstream tools.
Using `SELECT *` in a final report: it silently changes when the table changes.
Using double quotes for text. In standard SQL 'single quotes' are strings and "double quotes" are identifiers.
Assuming list_price is what the customer paid — always use order_items.unit_price for revenue.
Forgetting that NULL in arithmetic or concatenation makes the whole expression NULL.
recall: Write the logical evaluation order of a SELECT query.
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
What's the difference between a table alias and a column alias?
A table alias (FROM products AS p) names a table so you can write p.col; a column alias (expr AS name) names an output column.
Which quote style marks a string literal?
Single quotes: 'refund'.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 2 filters rows with WHERE. Before moving on, re-run exercise 1.3 and notice the NULL price_with_tax — you'll meet NULLs head-on in Lesson 3.

exercises.title: Supplier directory
exercises.question: Procurement wants the full supplier directory.
exercises.prompt: Return every supplier with columns supplier_id, supplier_name, country.
hints: All rows, three named columns — no filtering needed.
SELECT col_a, col_b, col_c FROM table;
SELECT supplier_id, supplier_name, country FROM suppliers;
exercises.why: Listing columns explicitly (instead of SELECT *) makes reports stable when someone adds a column to the table later.

recall.q: Which clause does the database logically evaluate first: SELECT or FROM?
recall.a: FROM — it first decides where rows come from, then SELECT shapes them.

exercises.solution:
SELECT supplier_id, supplier_name, country
FROM suppliers;

exercises.title: Customer contact sheet with clean column names
exercises.question: Customer success wants a contact sheet whose headers read customer_name and email_address.
exercises.prompt: Return all customers with columns customer_id, customer_name (from name) and email_address (from email). Keep NULL emails as they are.
hints: Rename columns with AS.
name AS customer_name
SELECT customer_id, name AS customer_name, email AS email_address FROM customers;
exercises.why: Downstream tools match on column names. Aliasing is how you control the contract between your query and whoever consumes it.

recall.q: Is the AS keyword required for a column alias in most SQL dialects?
recall.a: No — `name customer_name` also works — but writing AS is clearer and is the habit to keep.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       name  AS customer_name,
       email AS email_address
FROM customers;

exercises.title: Price sheet with tax
exercises.question: Finance needs each product's list price and the price including 8% sales tax.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, list_price and price_with_tax (list_price * 1.08 rounded to 2 decimals) for every product.
hints: A computed column is just an expression in the SELECT list.
ROUND(expression, 2) rounds to cents.
ROUND(list_price * 1.08, 2) AS price_with_tax
exercises.why: Derived columns are the bread and butter of analytics. Notice product 19 has a NULL list price, so its taxed price is NULL too — arithmetic with NULL is NULL.

recall.q: What is 100 * NULL in SQL?
recall.a: NULL. Any arithmetic with NULL yields NULL.

exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       list_price,
       ROUND(list_price * 1.08, 2) AS price_with_tax
FROM products;

exercises.title: Order line totals
exercises.question: What is the value of every order line?
exercises.prompt: Return order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price and line_total (quantity * unit_price) for all 150 order lines.
hints: Multiply two columns.
quantity * unit_price AS line_total
Select the five original columns plus the computed line_total.
exercises.why: Revenue in this warehouse is always quantity × unit_price at line level — the list price in products is NOT what the customer paid (discounts!).

recall.q: Why compute revenue from order_items.unit_price instead of products.list_price?
recall.a: Because unit_price is the price actually charged (after discounts); list_price is just the catalog price.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_item_id,
       order_id,
       product_id,
       quantity,
       unit_price,
       quantity * unit_price AS line_total
FROM order_items;

exercises.title: Table alias and a combined label
exercises.question: The CRM import needs one text label per customer like 'Alice Johnson (North)'.
exercises.prompt: Using the table alias c, return c.customer_id as customer_id and a column customer_label built as name || ' (' || region || ')'. (Customers with a NULL region will get a NULL label — that is expected here; Lesson 3 fixes it.)
hints: SQLite (and Snowflake) concatenate strings with ||.
FROM customers AS c lets you write c.name, c.region.
c.name || ' (' || c.region || ')' AS customer_label
exercises.why: Table aliases become essential with joins (Module 2). Seeing NULL poison a concatenation now will make COALESCE click in Lesson 3.

recall.q: What does 'abc' || NULL return?
recall.a: NULL. (Snowflake's CONCAT also returns NULL; use COALESCE or CONCAT_WS-style handling.)

exercises.title: Refund ledger with literal columns
exercises.question: Accounting wants refunds as negative ledger entries tagged with a transaction type.
exercises.prompt: Return return_id, return_date, a literal column transaction_type with the value 'refund', and signed_amount = the refund_amount as a negative number.
hints: You can SELECT a constant: 'refund' AS transaction_type.
Negate with a minus sign: -refund_amount (or refund_amount * -1).
SELECT return_id, return_date, 'refund' AS transaction_type, -refund_amount AS signed_amount FROM returns;
exercises.why: Literal columns are how you label rows before stacking datasets together with UNION ALL (Lesson 25).

recall.q: How do you add a constant column to every row of a result?
recall.a: Put the literal in the SELECT list with an alias, e.g. 'refund' AS transaction_type.

exercises.solution:
SELECT return_id,
       return_date,
       'refund'        AS transaction_type,
       -refund_amount  AS signed_amount
FROM returns;

lessons.title: Filtering with WHERE, AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE
lessons.objective: Keep only the rows you need by writing precise WHERE conditions, combining them safely with AND / OR / NOT and parentheses, and using IN, BETWEEN and LIKE as shorthands.
lessons.context: Stakeholders almost never want 'all rows'. Merchandising wants one category, operations wants the stuck orders, customer success wants every 'Smith'-like account before a merge. A filter that is slightly wrong (one missing parenthesis, one inclusive bound) silently returns the wrong list — and nobody notices until the numbers disagree.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: build a filter in 4 moves**

1. Write the condition for **one** requirement: `category = 'Electronics'`, `quantity >= 3`.
2. Combine requirements: `AND` = all must hold, `OR` = at least one holds, `NOT` flips a condition.
3. **Parenthesise every OR.** `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, so `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`.
4. Use the shorthands:
   - `col IN ('a', 'b', 'c')` — same as `col = 'a' OR col = 'b' OR col = 'c'`
   - `col BETWEEN 10 AND 20` — **inclusive** on both ends (`col >= 10 AND col <= 20`)
   - `col LIKE 'J%n Smith'` — `%` = any number of characters, `_` = exactly one character

```sql
SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status
FROM   orders
WHERE  order_status IN ('cancelled', 'pending')
  AND  order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31';
```

**Dates** here are ISO text (`'YYYY-MM-DD'`), so they compare correctly as strings.

**Case sensitivity:** in SQLite, `=` is case-sensitive but `LIKE` is case-*insensitive* for ASCII letters.
Snowflake is the opposite trap: `LIKE` is case-sensitive there; use `ILIKE` for case-insensitive matching.

**NULL preview:** a comparison with NULL is never true, so `WHERE category <> 'Books'` silently drops rows
whose category is NULL. Lesson 3 is all about this.

worked_example.question: Which Home or Apparel products cost less than $40?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT product_id, product_name, category, list_price
FROM products
WHERE category IN ('Home', 'Apparel')
  AND list_price < 40;
worked_example.explanation: `IN` replaces an `OR` chain, so there is no precedence trap. Written with OR you would need parentheses: `(category = 'Home' OR category = 'Apparel') AND list_price < 40`. Without them, every Home product would be returned regardless of price.

common_mistakes: Mixing AND and OR without parentheses — `a OR b AND c` is `a OR (b AND c)`.
Forgetting BETWEEN is inclusive (or using it on timestamps where '2025-12-31' means midnight only).
Using double quotes for strings: `"Electronics"` is an identifier in standard SQL, not text.
Assuming LIKE behaves the same everywhere: case-insensitive in SQLite, case-sensitive in Snowflake.
Forgetting that `<>`, `NOT IN` and `NOT LIKE` silently exclude NULLs.
recall: Which binds tighter, AND or OR?
AND. Always parenthesise OR groups to make intent explicit.
What does `price BETWEEN 30 AND 50` expand to?
price >= 30 AND price <= 50.
Write a LIKE pattern for 'emails at example.com'.
email LIKE '%@example.com'
Why can a filter on `category <> 'Books'` miss rows?
Rows with NULL category: NULL <> 'Books' is unknown, not true, so they are discarded.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 3 tackles NULLs head-on. Re-run exercise 2.7 and look for product 20 — understanding why it vanished is the key to the next lesson.

exercises.title: One category
exercises.question: Merchandising wants the electronics price list.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and list_price for every product whose category is exactly 'Electronics'.
hints: Filter rows with WHERE column = 'value'.
Text literals use single quotes: 'Electronics'.
SELECT product_id, product_name, list_price FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics';
exercises.why: Most report requests are a single filter on a dimension. Getting the literal exactly right (spelling, case, quotes) is the whole job.

recall.q: Which quote style do you use around 'Electronics' in a WHERE clause?
recall.a: Single quotes — they mark a string literal.

exercises.title: Mid-range price band
exercises.question: Marketing is planning a '$30–$50 gift ideas' email. Which products fit?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, category and list_price for products whose list_price is between 30 and 50, inclusive of both 30 and 50.
hints: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends.
list_price BETWEEN low AND high
SELECT product_id, product_name, category, list_price FROM products WHERE list_price BETWEEN 30 AND 50;
exercises.why: Price bands, age bands and date ranges are everywhere. Knowing BETWEEN includes both endpoints prevents off-by-one errors (the Yoga Mat at exactly $30 must appear).

recall.q: Is `x BETWEEN 30 AND 50` true when x = 50?
recall.a: Yes. BETWEEN is inclusive: it means x >= 30 AND x <= 50.

exercises.title: Stuck orders this year
exercises.question: Operations wants every 2025 order that was cancelled or is still pending.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, customer_id, order_date and order_status for orders whose order_status is 'cancelled' or 'pending' AND whose order_date is in 2025 (from '2025-01-01' to '2025-12-31' inclusive).
hints: Two requirements: a status list and a date range — combine them with AND.
order_status IN ('cancelled', 'pending') avoids an OR precedence trap.
WHERE order_status IN (...) AND order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
exercises.why: Writing `status = 'cancelled' OR status = 'pending' AND date ...` without parentheses would return 2024 cancellations too. IN makes the intent impossible to misread.

recall.q: How does SQL read `a OR b AND c`?
recall.a: As `a OR (b AND c)` — AND binds tighter than OR.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_status
FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('cancelled', 'pending')
  AND order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31';

exercises.title: Precedence trap: bulk headphone or monitor lines
exercises.question: Which order lines sold 2 or more units of product 4 (headphones) or product 5 (monitor)?
exercises.prompt: Return order_item_id, order_id, product_id and quantity for order lines where product_id is 4 or 5 AND quantity is at least 2. (The quantity condition applies to both products.)
hints: The quantity rule must apply to BOTH products — think about precedence.
Either use product_id IN (4, 5) or wrap the OR in parentheses.
WHERE (product_id = 4 OR product_id = 5) AND quantity >= 2
exercises.why: Try it without parentheses: you get every single-unit product-4 line too. This is the most common silent filter bug in real reporting code.

recall.q: Rewrite `product_id = 4 OR product_id = 5` with a shorthand.
recall.a: product_id IN (4, 5)

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity
FROM order_items
WHERE (product_id = 4 OR product_id = 5)
  AND quantity >= 2;

exercises.title: Smith-like accounts with LIKE
exercises.question: Customer success suspects duplicate accounts for 'John Smith' — including typo spellings like 'Jon Smith'. Find every candidate.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, email and signup_date for customers whose name starts with 'J', ends with 'n Smith', and has anything (or nothing) in between — i.e. name LIKE 'J%n Smith'.
hints: % matches any number of characters (including zero); _ matches exactly one.
The pattern is 'J' + anything + 'n Smith'.
WHERE name LIKE 'J%n Smith'
exercises.why: Pattern matching is how analysts hunt for dirty data: typo duplicates, test accounts ('%test%'), or email domains ('%@example.com'). Three accounts come back — two 'John Smith' with different emails and one 'Jon Smith'.

recall.q: What is the difference between % and _ in LIKE?
recall.a: % matches any number of characters (0 or more); _ matches exactly one character.

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake's LIKE is case-sensitive; use ILIKE 'j%n smith' for a case-insensitive match. SQLite's LIKE is already case-insensitive for ASCII.
exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, name, email, signup_date
FROM customers
WHERE name LIKE 'J%n Smith';

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake's LIKE is case-sensitive; use ILIKE 'j%n smith' for a case-insensitive
match. SQLite's LIKE is already case-insensitive for ASCII.
*/

exercises.title: NOT and NOT IN on a 2024 problem list
exercises.question: Finance is closing the 2024 books and wants every 2024 order that did NOT end as a plain completed sale.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, customer_id, order_date and order_status for orders placed in 2024 (order_date from '2024-01-01' to '2024-12-31' inclusive) whose order_status is NOT 'completed'.
hints: Two conditions joined with AND: a date range and a negated status.
Negation can be written NOT x = 'completed', x <> 'completed' or x != 'completed'.
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31' AND order_status <> 'completed'
exercises.why: Exception lists ('everything that isn't normal') drive month-end reconciliation. Only three 2024 orders qualify — a short list finance can check by hand.

recall.q: Name three ways to write 'status is not completed'.
recall.a: status <> 'completed', status != 'completed', NOT status = 'completed'.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_status
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
  AND NOT order_status = 'completed';

exercises.title: Cheap non-core products (and the NULL that vanishes)
exercises.question: Which products outside our two core categories (Electronics and Home) cost under $40?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, category and list_price for products whose category is NOT IN ('Electronics', 'Home') and whose list_price is below 40. Write it with NOT IN and do not add any NULL handling — products with a NULL category will (silently) not appear; Lesson 3 explains why.
hints: NOT IN is the negation of IN.
Combine NOT IN (...) with a price condition using AND.
WHERE category NOT IN ('Electronics', 'Home') AND list_price < 40
exercises.why: The 'Mystery Gift Box' (no category, $25) is arguably outside the core categories, yet NOT IN drops it because NULL NOT IN (...) is unknown, not true. Spotting what a filter silently removes is a core analyst skill.

recall.q: Does `NULL NOT IN ('Electronics', 'Home')` evaluate to true?
recall.a: No — it evaluates to NULL (unknown), so WHERE discards the row.

exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id, product_name, category, list_price
FROM products
WHERE category NOT IN ('Electronics', 'Home')
  AND list_price < 40;

lessons.title: Handling NULLs correctly
lessons.objective: Find missing values with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, replace them with COALESCE, avoid the NULL traps in <> and NOT IN, and know when COUNT(col) differs from COUNT(*).
lessons.context: Real warehouses are full of gaps: customers who never gave an email, products without a price or supplier, returns with no reason. NULL means 'unknown', and SQL treats unknown very differently from zero or empty text. Data-quality audits, contact lists and KPI denominators all go wrong if you treat NULL casually.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: handle NULL in 4 moves**

1. **Find it:** `WHERE email IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. Never `= NULL` — that is never true.
2. **Replace it for display:** `COALESCE(region, 'Unassigned')` returns the first non-NULL argument.
3. **Guard negative filters:** `col <> 'x'` and `col NOT IN (...)` drop NULL rows. If unknowns should
   be kept, say so: `WHERE col <> 'x' OR col IS NULL` (or compare `COALESCE(col, '?') <> 'x'`).
4. **Count deliberately:** `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` counts non-NULL values of col.
   Missing values = `COUNT(*) - COUNT(col)`.

```sql
SELECT customer_id,
       COALESCE(email, 'no email on file') AS contact_email
FROM   customers
WHERE  region IS NULL;
```

**Three-valued logic:** a condition is TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. `WHERE` keeps only TRUE.
`NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN; `NULL <> 'x'` is UNKNOWN; `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` is never TRUE.

**Aggregates skip NULLs** (`SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT(col)`) — Lesson 6 builds on this.
lessons.snowflake_notes: Snowflake has the same semantics plus helpers: `IFNULL(a, b)` / `NVL(a, b)` (two-argument COALESCE), `ZEROIFNULL(x)`, `NULLIF(a, b)`, and the NULL-safe comparison `a IS DISTINCT FROM b` / `EQUAL_NULL(a, b)`. SQLite also supports `IFNULL`, `NULLIF` and `IS` / `IS NOT` as NULL-safe equality (`region IS NOT 'North'`).

worked_example.question: Which customers have no region, and how should they appear in a regional report?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       name,
       region,
       COALESCE(region, 'Unassigned') AS region_label
FROM customers
WHERE region IS NULL;
worked_example.explanation: `IS NULL` finds the two customers (9 and 16). `region = NULL` would return zero rows. COALESCE gives them a readable label without changing the underlying data.

common_mistakes: Writing `= NULL` or `<> NULL` instead of `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.
Using `NOT IN` or `<>` and silently losing rows where the column is NULL.
Using `COUNT(col)` as a row count when the column can be NULL (or vice versa).
COALESCE-ing to 0 before averaging: `AVG(COALESCE(price, 0))` treats 'unknown' as 'free' and drags the average down.
Forgetting that `'text' || NULL` and `5 + NULL` are NULL.
recall: What are the three truth values in SQL logic?
TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only TRUE.
What does COALESCE do?
Returns its first non-NULL argument.
Why is `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` never true?
It expands to x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL, and x <> NULL is UNKNOWN.
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values of col.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 4 sorts results — and NULLs come back: where do they sort? Revisit exercise 3.5 and say out loud why product 22 disappears without the IS NULL clause.

exercises.title: Who has no email?
exercises.question: The CRM team needs to chase customers with no email on file.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and signup_date for customers whose email is NULL.
hints: `= NULL` never matches anything.
Use the IS NULL operator.
SELECT customer_id, name, signup_date FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL;
exercises.why: Missing contact data is a recurring data-quality KPI. `WHERE email = NULL` runs without an error and returns nothing — a classic silent bug.

recall.q: Why does `WHERE email = NULL` return no rows?
recall.a: Any comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows.

exercises.title: Mailing list with fallbacks
exercises.question: Marketing wants a full customer list where blanks are replaced by readable labels.
exercises.prompt: Return every customer with columns customer_id, name, contact_email (email, or the text 'no email on file' when email is NULL) and region_label (region, or 'Unassigned' when region is NULL).
hints: COALESCE(a, b) returns a unless a is NULL, otherwise b.
You need two COALESCE calls, each with an alias.
COALESCE(email, 'no email on file') AS contact_email, COALESCE(region, 'Unassigned') AS region_label
exercises.why: Dashboards show NULL as an empty cell that nobody can filter on. A labelled bucket ('Unassigned') is visible, countable and fixable.

recall.q: What does COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'x', 'y') return?
recall.a: 'x' — the first non-NULL argument.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       name,
       COALESCE(email, 'no email on file') AS contact_email,
       COALESCE(region, 'Unassigned') AS region_label
FROM customers;

exercises.title: COUNT(*) versus COUNT(email)
exercises.question: What share of our customer base can we actually email?
exercises.prompt: Return one row with columns total_customers (all customer rows), customers_with_email (customers whose email is not NULL) and customers_missing_email (customers whose email is NULL). Use COUNT(*) and COUNT(email) — no WHERE clause.
hints: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs in col.
The missing count is the difference of the two.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_customers, COUNT(email) AS customers_with_email, COUNT(*) - COUNT(email) AS customers_missing_email FROM customers;
exercises.why: Choosing COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) changes a denominator. 'Reachable customers: 17 of 20' is a different story from '20 of 20'.

recall.q: When do COUNT(*) and COUNT(email) differ?
recall.a: When some rows have a NULL email: COUNT(email) skips them, COUNT(*) doesn't.

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                AS total_customers,
       COUNT(email)            AS customers_with_email,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(email) AS customers_missing_email
FROM customers;

exercises.title: Product data-quality audit
exercises.question: Before the catalog migration, how many products are missing a category, a price or a supplier?
exercises.prompt: Return one row with columns total_products, missing_category, missing_price and missing_supplier, where each missing_* column is the number of products whose category / list_price / supplier_id is NULL.
hints: One query, one row — no WHERE needed.
missing = COUNT(*) - COUNT(column).
COUNT(*) - COUNT(category) AS missing_category, ... repeat for list_price and supplier_id
exercises.why: A one-row completeness audit is a standard first query on any new table. Note supplier_id 9 on product 21 is *not* NULL — it points to a supplier that doesn't exist, a different kind of problem you'll catch with joins in Module 2.

recall.q: How do you count NULLs in a column in a single expression?
recall.a: COUNT(*) - COUNT(col).

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                      AS total_products,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(category)    AS missing_category,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(list_price)  AS missing_price,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(supplier_id) AS missing_supplier
FROM products;

exercises.title: The NOT IN pitfall: suppliers other than 1 and 2
exercises.question: Procurement is consolidating suppliers 1 and 2. List every product NOT sourced from them — and products with no supplier on record definitely belong on that list.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and supplier_id for products whose supplier_id is not 1 and not 2, INCLUDING products whose supplier_id is NULL.
hints: Try `supplier_id NOT IN (1, 2)` alone and look for product 22 — it's missing.
NULL NOT IN (1, 2) is UNKNOWN, so you must ask for NULLs explicitly.
WHERE supplier_id NOT IN (1, 2) OR supplier_id IS NULL
exercises.why: Negative filters are where NULLs hide. The Phone Stand (no supplier) is exactly the product procurement most needs to see, and the naive query drops it.

recall.q: Fix `WHERE x NOT IN (1, 2)` so rows with NULL x are kept.
recall.a: WHERE x NOT IN (1, 2) OR x IS NULL

exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id, product_name, supplier_id
FROM products
WHERE supplier_id NOT IN (1, 2)
   OR supplier_id IS NULL;

exercises.title: Outside the North region, unknowns included
exercises.question: The South/East/West sales team will contact every emailable customer who is not assigned to North — customers with an unknown region should go to them too.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, email and region_label (region, or 'Unassigned' when NULL) for customers who have a non-NULL email AND whose region is not 'North' (customers with a NULL region count as 'not North').
hints: Two requirements: email present, region not North (NULL included).
region <> 'North' alone drops customers 9 and 16 — add OR region IS NULL, in parentheses.
WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND (region <> 'North' OR region IS NULL)
exercises.why: This combines both NULL skills: excluding missing values on purpose (email) and keeping them on purpose (region). Getting the parentheses wrong here would re-add customers without email.

recall.q: Give a NULL-safe way to write 'region is not North' in SQLite.
recall.a: region <> 'North' OR region IS NULL  — or  COALESCE(region, '') <> 'North'  — or  region IS NOT 'North'.

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake: WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND region IS DISTINCT FROM 'North'.
exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       name,
       email,
       COALESCE(region, 'Unassigned') AS region_label
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
  AND (region <> 'North' OR region IS NULL);

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake: WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND region IS DISTINCT FROM 'North'.
*/

lessons.title: Sorting and limiting results
lessons.objective: Sort by one or several columns in either direction, control where NULLs land, and use LIMIT / OFFSET for top-N lists and paging — with tie-breakers so results are reproducible.
lessons.context: 'Top 5', 'most recent', 'page 2 of the list' — ranked output is what executives actually read. A top-N list without a deterministic sort can change from one run to the next, which destroys trust in a report faster than anything.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: sort and cut in 4 moves**

1. `ORDER BY col` sorts ascending (default, `ASC`); add `DESC` for descending. Direction is **per column**.
2. Add more columns for ties: `ORDER BY region, name, customer_id` sorts by region, then name within region…
3. Decide where NULLs go. SQLite puts NULLs **first** in ASC and **last** in DESC. Override with
   `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST`.
4. Cut: `LIMIT n` keeps the first n rows; `LIMIT n OFFSET k` skips k rows first (page p of size n → `OFFSET (p-1)*n`).

```sql
SELECT product_id, product_name, list_price
FROM   products
ORDER  BY list_price DESC, product_id   -- tie-breaker!
LIMIT  5;
```

**Always finish with a unique tie-breaker** (usually the primary key) when order matters. Without it, rows with
equal sort values can come back in any order — and LIMIT may cut a different row each time.

ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so you may sort by a column alias (`ORDER BY line_total DESC`).
lessons.snowflake_notes: Snowflake puts NULLs **last** in ASC and **first** in DESC by default (the opposite of SQLite), so always write `NULLS FIRST/LAST` when it matters. Snowflake also supports `LIMIT n OFFSET k` and `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`; `TOP n` works in SELECT as well.

worked_example.question: What were the five most recent orders?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_status
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: Dates are ISO text, so they sort chronologically. order_id is a tie-breaker in case two orders share a date — harmless today, essential tomorrow.

common_mistakes: Relying on the 'natural' order of a table — without ORDER BY, row order is undefined.
Top-N with no tie-breaker, so LIMIT picks different rows on different runs.
Thinking `ORDER BY a, b DESC` sorts both columns descending (only b is).
Assuming NULLs sort the same way in every database (SQLite and Snowflake differ).
Paging with OFFSET over a non-unique sort key, causing duplicated or skipped rows between pages.
recall: Default sort direction?
ASC (ascending).
How do you get rows 21–30 of a sorted result?
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20.
What makes an ORDER BY deterministic?
Ending it with a column (or combination) that is unique, e.g. the primary key.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 5 removes duplicates with DISTINCT. Re-run exercise 4.2 and look at the two John Smiths and 'alice johnson' — are they duplicates or not? That's the next question.

exercises.title: Price sheet, most expensive first
exercises.question: Sales wants the catalog sorted from most to least expensive.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and list_price for all products, sorted by list_price descending, then product_id ascending for ties. Keep SQLite's default NULL placement (the product with a NULL price ends up last in a DESC sort).
hints: DESC goes after the column it applies to.
Add product_id as the second sort key so equal prices can never swap places.
ORDER BY list_price DESC, product_id
exercises.why: Every ranked list needs a tie-breaker. No two prices are equal today, but the moment one is, a sort without product_id could return them in either order between runs.

recall.q: In `ORDER BY a DESC, b`, which direction is b sorted?
recall.a: Ascending — direction is per column.

exercises.sf_note: Snowflake's default NULL placement is the opposite of SQLite's: NULLs sort LAST for ASC and FIRST for DESC. To keep the NULL price at the end of a DESC sort, write ORDER BY list_price DESC NULLS LAST explicitly.

exercises.title: Customer list by region, then name
exercises.question: Account managers want customers grouped visually by region, alphabetical within each.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and region for all customers, sorted by region ascending (NULL regions first, which is SQLite's default), then name ascending, then customer_id ascending.
hints: List several sort keys separated by commas.
Two customers are both 'John Smith' — customer_id breaks that tie.
ORDER BY region, name, customer_id
exercises.why: Multi-level sorting is how you make a long list scannable. Note 'alice johnson' (lower case) sorts after 'Priya Patel' in North: SQLite compares text by byte value, so uppercase letters come before lowercase ones.

recall.q: In SQLite, do NULLs come first or last in an ascending sort?
recall.a: First.

exercises.sf_note: Snowflake sorts NULLs LAST in an ascending sort (SQLite puts them first), so write ORDER BY region ASC NULLS FIRST to get NULL regions at the top.

exercises.title: Cheapest first, unknown prices last
exercises.question: Purchasing wants the cheapest products at the top, but the product with no price should be at the bottom where it won't be mistaken for 'free'.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and list_price for all products, sorted by list_price ascending with NULL prices LAST, then product_id ascending.
hints: SQLite's default puts NULLs first in an ascending sort — you need to override it.
Add NULLS LAST after the direction.
ORDER BY list_price ASC NULLS LAST, product_id
exercises.why: Default NULL placement differs between databases (SQLite vs Snowflake are opposite). Being explicit makes the query portable and the report honest.

recall.q: How do you force NULLs to the bottom of an ascending sort?
recall.a: ORDER BY col ASC NULLS LAST

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake already puts NULLs last in ASC, but writing NULLS LAST explicitly is still good practice.
exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id, product_name, list_price
FROM products
ORDER BY list_price ASC NULLS LAST, product_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake already puts NULLs last in ASC, but writing NULLS LAST explicitly is still
good practice.
*/
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake NULLS LAST is already the default for ASC (the opposite of SQLite), but writing ORDER BY list_price ASC NULLS LAST explicitly is still good practice.

exercises.title: Top 3 order lines by value
exercises.question: Which three individual order lines were worth the most?
exercises.prompt: Return order_item_id, order_id, product_id and line_total (quantity * unit_price) for the 3 order lines with the highest line_total. Sort by line_total descending, then order_item_id ascending.
hints: Compute line_total in SELECT; you can ORDER BY its alias.
Sort descending, add order_item_id as tie-breaker, then LIMIT 3.
ORDER BY line_total DESC, order_item_id LIMIT 3
exercises.why: Top-N is the most requested report shape. Four lines tie at 3 × 129 = 387 for third place, so without a tie-breaker LIMIT could pick a different line on each run.

recall.q: Why can you ORDER BY a SELECT alias but not filter on it in WHERE?
recall.a: ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT; WHERE is evaluated before it.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_item_id, order_id, product_id,
       quantity * unit_price AS line_total
FROM order_items
ORDER BY line_total DESC, order_item_id
LIMIT 3;

exercises.title: Paging through customers
exercises.question: The CRM screen shows 5 customers per page, oldest sign-ups first. What's on page 2?
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and signup_date for page 2 of the customer list when customers are sorted by signup_date ascending, then customer_id ascending, with 5 customers per page (i.e. rows 6–10).
hints: Page p of size n skips (p - 1) * n rows.
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5
ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5
exercises.why: OFFSET paging is how apps and APIs page through results. It only works if the sort is deterministic — otherwise a customer can appear on two pages, or on none.

recall.q: Which OFFSET gives page 4 with 20 rows per page?
recall.a: OFFSET 60 (skip 3 × 20 rows).

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, name, signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date, customer_id
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;

exercises.title: 2025 orders by status, newest first within status
exercises.question: Operations reviews 2025 orders status by status, latest first.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_status and order_date for orders with order_date on or after '2025-01-01', sorted by order_status ascending (alphabetical), then order_date descending, then order_id descending.
hints: WHERE filters first; ORDER BY then sorts what's left.
Mix directions: each sort key gets its own ASC/DESC.
ORDER BY order_status ASC, order_date DESC, order_id DESC
exercises.why: Mixed-direction sorts are common in operational queues ('group by state, newest first').

recall.q: Where does ORDER BY sit relative to WHERE in the written query?
recall.a: After WHERE (and after GROUP BY/HAVING); LIMIT comes last.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id, order_status, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY order_status ASC, order_date DESC, order_id DESC;

lessons.title: DISTINCT and removing duplicates
lessons.objective: Return unique values or unique combinations with DISTINCT, count distinct values, and recognise when rows only *look* duplicated (case, spelling) or truly are duplicated.
lessons.context: 'How many customers ordered?' and 'how many orders?' are different questions on the same table. Duplicates also creep in from data loads — this warehouse has two order lines that were loaded twice and customer names that differ only by capitalisation. Knowing what DISTINCT does (and doesn't) do protects every count you report.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: deduplicate deliberately in 4 moves**

1. `SELECT DISTINCT col` — one row per distinct value. NULL counts as one value here.
2. `SELECT DISTINCT a, b` — one row per distinct **combination** of a and b (DISTINCT applies to the whole row,
   not just the first column).
3. `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` — how many different non-NULL values. Compare with `COUNT(*)` to see repetition.
4. Normalise before deduplicating when 'the same' should ignore case or spacing:
   `COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(TRIM(name)))`.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                    AS order_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS ordering_customers
FROM   orders;
```

**DISTINCT is not a fix for bad data.** If identical rows exist (the duplicate order lines 149 and 150),
DISTINCT can hide them in one query — but the right move is to understand and report them.
lessons.snowflake_notes: Same syntax in Snowflake. For very large tables, `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(col)` (HyperLogLog) is much cheaper than `COUNT(DISTINCT col)`. Snowflake compares strings case-sensitively by default, like SQLite's `=`.

worked_example.question: Which order statuses exist?
worked_example.explanation: Sixty order rows collapse to five distinct statuses. This is the quickest way to learn a column's vocabulary before writing a filter on it.

common_mistakes: Thinking `DISTINCT a, b` deduplicates only a — it applies to the whole row.
Using DISTINCT to 'fix' a query whose duplicates come from a bad join (Module 2) instead of fixing the join.
Forgetting COUNT(DISTINCT col) ignores NULLs while SELECT DISTINCT shows NULL as a row.
Treating case/spelling variants as distinct people (or blindly merging people who share a name).
Including a surrogate key in the DISTINCT list, which makes every row unique.
recall: What does SELECT DISTINCT operate on?
The entire selected row (all listed columns together).
How do you count distinct values ignoring case?
COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(col)).
Does COUNT(DISTINCT region) count NULL as a region?
No — COUNT(DISTINCT ...) ignores NULLs.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 6 introduces SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. Keep the duplicate lines 149/150 in mind — they inflate any total computed over order_items.

exercises.title: Category vocabulary
exercises.question: Which product categories exist in the catalog (including 'no category')?
exercises.prompt: Return one column, category, with each distinct category value exactly once. The NULL category should appear as one row.
hints: DISTINCT goes right after SELECT.
DISTINCT treats all NULLs as one value.
SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products;
exercises.why: Before filtering on a column, look at its distinct values — that's how you discover the NULL category before it breaks a report.

recall.q: Does SELECT DISTINCT return NULL as a value?
recall.a: Yes, once — all NULLs are grouped together.

exercises.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT category
FROM products;

exercises.title: Which customer IDs have ordered?
exercises.question: Which customer IDs appear on at least one order (any status)?
exercises.prompt: Return one column, customer_id, listing each customer_id that appears in orders exactly once, sorted ascending.
hints: Customer 1 has nine orders but should appear once.
SELECT DISTINCT ... ORDER BY ...
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id;
exercises.why: Notice customer_id 99 — an order whose customer doesn't exist in the customers table. Distinct key lists are how you start hunting orphans (Module 2 finishes the job).

recall.q: Why does customer 1 appear only once?
recall.a: DISTINCT collapses identical rows (here identical customer_id values).

exercises.title: Status by year combinations
exercises.question: Which order statuses occurred in each year?
exercises.prompt: Return the distinct combinations of order_year (the first 4 characters of order_date, i.e. substr(order_date, 1, 4)) and order_status, sorted by order_year then order_status.
hints: DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row — here a (year, status) pair.
substr(order_date, 1, 4) AS order_year extracts the year from an ISO date.
SELECT DISTINCT substr(order_date, 1, 4) AS order_year, order_status FROM orders ORDER BY order_year, order_status;
exercises.why: DISTINCT over several columns shows which combinations exist — e.g. 'pending' only in 2025 — a quick sanity check before building a year-by-status report.

recall.q: Does `SELECT DISTINCT a, b` deduplicate a alone?
recall.a: No — it deduplicates the (a, b) combination.

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake: YEAR(order_date) or DATE_PART('year', order_date) instead of substr on text.
exercises.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT substr(order_date, 1, 4) AS order_year,
       order_status
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_year, order_status;

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake: YEAR(order_date) or DATE_PART('year', order_date) instead of substr on
text.
*/
exercises.sf_note: order_date is a real DATE in Snowflake. SUBSTR(order_date, 1, 4) only works through an implicit cast to text; the idiomatic way is TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY') (or YEAR(order_date) for a number).

exercises.title: Lines, products and orders in order_items
exercises.question: How many order lines do we have, and how many different products and orders do they cover?
exercises.prompt: Return one row with columns line_count (all rows in order_items), distinct_products (number of different product_id values) and distinct_orders (number of different order_id values).
hints: COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts different values.
Three counts in one SELECT.
COUNT(*) AS line_count, COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_products, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders
exercises.why: 22 of 25 products ever sold; 59 of 60 orders have lines (order 60 has none). Counting the right grain is the first defence against wrong KPIs.

recall.q: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on order_items?
recall.a: COUNT(*) counts lines; COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) counts orders that have lines.

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                   AS line_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_products,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)   AS distinct_orders
FROM order_items;

exercises.title: Duplicate-looking names
exercises.question: How many distinct customer names are there — and how many if we ignore capitalisation?
exercises.prompt: Return one row with columns customer_rows (all customers), distinct_names (number of distinct name values, case-sensitive) and distinct_names_ignoring_case (number of distinct LOWER(name) values).
hints: DISTINCT compares text exactly, so 'Alice Johnson' and 'alice johnson' are different.
Normalise inside the count: COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(name)).
COUNT(*) AS customer_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT name) AS distinct_names, COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(name)) AS distinct_names_ignoring_case
exercises.why: 20 rows, 19 names, 18 case-insensitive names. Each drop is a potential duplicate person — but the two John Smiths have different emails, so they may be two real people. Distinct counts raise questions; they don't answer them.

recall.q: How do you count distinct names ignoring case?
recall.a: COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(name))

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                     AS customer_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT name)         AS distinct_names,
       COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(name))  AS distinct_names_ignoring_case
FROM customers;

exercises.title: De-duplicated lines for two orders
exercises.question: Orders 9 and 38 were loaded with a duplicated line each. Show their distinct line contents.
exercises.prompt: For order_id 9 and 38 only, return the distinct combinations of order_id, product_id, quantity and unit_price (do NOT include order_item_id), sorted by order_id then product_id.
hints: Including order_item_id would make every row unique — leave it out.
Filter with WHERE order_id IN (9, 38), then DISTINCT the four content columns.
SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (9, 38) ORDER BY order_id, product_id;
exercises.why: A surrogate key (order_item_id) can hide true duplicates: the rows differ only by ID. Choosing which columns define 'the same' is the real decision in any dedup.

recall.q: Why must order_item_id be left out of the DISTINCT list here?
recall.a: It's unique per row, so every row would be distinct and nothing would be removed.

exercises.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id IN (9, 38)
ORDER BY order_id, product_id;

lessons.title: Aggregations: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
lessons.objective: Collapse a table (or a filtered part of it) into summary numbers with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, understand how each treats NULL, and compute conditional counts and ratios.
lessons.context: The CFO's first questions are always aggregates: how many orders, how much was sold, what's the average refund, when was the last order. These one-row answers feed KPI tiles, so every definition — which rows, which NULLs, how rounded — must be explicit.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: one-row summary in 4 moves**

1. Filter first with WHERE — the aggregate only sees rows that survive.
2. Pick the function: `COUNT(*)` rows, `COUNT(col)` non-NULL values, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`.
   All except `COUNT(*)` **ignore NULLs**.
3. Aggregate expressions, not just columns: `SUM(quantity * unit_price)`.
4. Conditional aggregates count/sum a subset without a WHERE:
   `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` (portable) — and make ratios with `100.0 * part / whole`.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)                                       AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled'
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                    AS cancelled_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2)                      AS avg_price
FROM   ...;
```

**Integer division:** `3 / 4` is `0` in SQLite (integer ÷ integer). Multiply by `100.0` or `1.0` first.

**Mixing:** without GROUP BY you can't put a plain column next to an aggregate in a meaningful way
(SQLite allows it but returns an arbitrary row's value; Snowflake raises an error). Lesson 7 adds GROUP BY.
lessons.snowflake_notes: Snowflake adds `COUNT_IF(cond)`, `IFF(cond, a, b)`, `DIV0(a, b)` (returns 0 instead of error on divide-by-zero), `MEDIAN(col)` and `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT`. In SQLite use `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` or `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)`.

worked_example.question: How many products are in the catalog, and what is the price range?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                  AS product_count,
       COUNT(list_price)         AS priced_products,
       MIN(list_price)           AS min_price,
       MAX(list_price)           AS max_price,
       ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products;
worked_example.explanation: 25 products, but only 24 have a price — AVG divides by 24, not 25, because AVG ignores the NULL. That's usually what you want: an unknown price isn't a $0 price.

common_mistakes: Replacing NULLs with 0 before AVG (`AVG(COALESCE(x, 0))`), which changes the denominator and the answer.
Integer division in ratios: `valid / total` → 0. Use 100.0 or 1.0.
Selecting a non-aggregated column next to aggregates without GROUP BY.
Calling a raw SUM over order_items 'revenue' without excluding cancelled/pending orders.
Averaging averages or using a simple average where a weighted one is meant.
recall: Which aggregates ignore NULLs?
All of them except COUNT(*): COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
Write a portable conditional count.
SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
What does SUM return over zero rows?
NULL (COUNT returns 0). Wrap with COALESCE(SUM(x), 0) when 0 is meant.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 7 splits these summaries per group with GROUP BY. Re-do exercise 6.5 and imagine it 'per year' — that's exactly what GROUP BY adds.

exercises.title: Electronics price spread
exercises.question: How wide is the price range in Electronics?
exercises.prompt: For products with category = 'Electronics', return one row with columns product_count, cheapest (MIN list_price), most_expensive (MAX list_price) and price_spread (most expensive minus cheapest).
hints: WHERE filters to Electronics before aggregating.
You can do arithmetic on aggregates: MAX(x) - MIN(x).
SELECT COUNT(*) AS product_count, MIN(list_price) AS cheapest, MAX(list_price) AS most_expensive, MAX(list_price) - MIN(list_price) AS price_spread FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics';
exercises.why: Range metrics give merchandisers a quick feel for a category's positioning.

recall.q: Does WHERE run before or after aggregation?
recall.a: Before — it decides which rows the aggregates see.

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                         AS product_count,
       MIN(list_price)                  AS cheapest,
       MAX(list_price)                  AS most_expensive,
       MAX(list_price) - MIN(list_price) AS price_spread
FROM products
WHERE category = 'Electronics';

exercises.title: 2025 order window
exercises.question: How many orders were placed in 2025, and what were the first and last order dates?
exercises.prompt: For orders with order_date from '2025-01-01' to '2025-12-31' inclusive (any status), return one row with columns order_count, first_order_date and last_order_date.
hints: MIN and MAX work on dates (and text) too.
Filter the year with BETWEEN, then aggregate.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count, MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date, MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date FROM orders WHERE ...
exercises.why: MIN/MAX of a date is how you describe a data window — and spot freshness problems (is the last order where you expect it?).

recall.q: Can MIN and MAX be used on text columns?
recall.a: Yes — they use the column's sort order (dates in ISO text sort chronologically).

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)        AS order_count,
       MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date,
       MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31';

exercises.title: Refund summary
exercises.question: Finance wants a one-line summary of all refunds.
exercises.prompt: Return one row with columns return_count (all returns), returns_with_reason (returns whose return_reason is not NULL), total_refunded (SUM of refund_amount, rounded to 2 decimals) and avg_refund (AVG of refund_amount, rounded to 2 decimals).
hints: COUNT(return_reason) skips the NULL reasons.
Wrap SUM and AVG in ROUND(..., 2).
COUNT(*) AS return_count, COUNT(return_reason) AS returns_with_reason, ROUND(SUM(refund_amount), 2) AS total_refunded, ROUND(AVG(refund_amount), 2) AS avg_refund
exercises.why: Two of ten returns have no reason recorded — a data-quality signal worth putting next to the money, so nobody over-reads the reason breakdown.

recall.q: Which aggregate is the only one that counts NULLs?
recall.a: COUNT(*).

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                      AS return_count,
       COUNT(return_reason)          AS returns_with_reason,
       ROUND(SUM(refund_amount), 2)  AS total_refunded,
       ROUND(AVG(refund_amount), 2)  AS avg_refund
FROM returns;

exercises.title: Units and line value across all lines
exercises.question: What's the raw volume in order_items: units, line value, and average line?
exercises.prompt: Over ALL rows of order_items (no status filter — status lives in orders, which you'll join in Module 2), return one row with columns total_units (SUM of quantity), total_line_value (SUM of quantity * unit_price, rounded to 2 decimals) and avg_line_value (AVG of quantity * unit_price, rounded to 2 decimals).
hints: Aggregate an expression: SUM(quantity * unit_price).
AVG of the same expression gives the average line value.
SELECT SUM(quantity) AS total_units, ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS total_line_value, ROUND(AVG(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS avg_line_value FROM order_items;
exercises.why: This is NOT revenue: it includes cancelled/pending orders and the two duplicate lines. Knowing exactly what a raw total contains is what separates a number from a metric.

recall.q: Why isn't SUM(quantity * unit_price) over all order_items equal to gross revenue?
recall.a: It includes cancelled/pending orders (and duplicate lines); revenue counts only valid orders.

exercises.solution:
SELECT SUM(quantity)                         AS total_units,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS total_line_value,
       ROUND(AVG(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS avg_line_value
FROM order_items;

exercises.title: Valid-order share (conditional counts)
exercises.question: What share of all orders are valid revenue orders?
exercises.prompt: Valid orders are those with order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned'). Return one row with columns total_orders, valid_orders, cancelled_orders (status = 'cancelled') and valid_pct (100 * valid_orders / total_orders, rounded to 1 decimal).
hints: SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts rows that meet a condition.
Multiply by 100.0 (not 100) to avoid integer division.
ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS valid_pct
exercises.why: Conditional aggregation computes several KPIs in one pass — the backbone of every summary dashboard. Forgetting the .0 would give valid_pct = 0 in SQLite.

recall.q: What is 53 / 60 in SQLite, and how do you fix it?
recall.a: 0 (integer division). Use 100.0 * 53 / 60 or 53 * 1.0 / 60.

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) AS valid_orders; Snowflake's / always returns a decimal, so the integer-division trap doesn't apply there.
exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS valid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / COUNT(*), 1) AS valid_pct
FROM orders;

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) AS
valid_orders; Snowflake's / always returns a decimal, so the integer-division trap
doesn't apply there.
*/
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake's / never does integer division (100 * 53 / 60 returns 88.333...), so the 100.0 trick is not needed there, though it does no harm.

exercises.title: Average price: simple versus unit-weighted
exercises.question: What's our average selling price — per line, or per unit actually sold?
exercises.prompt: Over all rows of order_items, return one row with columns avg_unit_price (simple AVG of unit_price), weighted_avg_unit_price (SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity)) and avg_quantity_per_line (AVG of quantity). Round all three to 2 decimals.
hints: A simple AVG gives every line equal weight regardless of quantity.
Weighted average = total value / total units.
ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity), 2) AS weighted_avg_unit_price
exercises.why: 'Average price' is ambiguous until you say what is being averaged. The two numbers differ because cheap items tend to be bought in larger quantities.

recall.q: Why can AVG(unit_price) differ from SUM(q * p) / SUM(q)?
recall.a: AVG weights every line equally; the weighted version weights each price by units sold.

exercises.solution:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2)                           AS avg_unit_price,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price) / SUM(quantity), 2) AS weighted_avg_unit_price,
       ROUND(AVG(quantity), 2)                             AS avg_quantity_per_line
FROM order_items;

lessons.title: GROUP BY
lessons.objective: Produce one summary row per group with GROUP BY, group by expressions and several columns, and get the grain of the result right.
lessons.context: Almost every business report is 'metric by dimension': orders by status, revenue by month, customers by region. GROUP BY is the machine that builds those tables — and the grain you choose (per order? per order and product?) decides what each number means.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: metric by dimension in 4 moves**

1. Decide the **grain**: one output row per … what? Those columns go in `GROUP BY`.
2. `SELECT` the grouping columns plus aggregates. Every non-aggregated SELECT column must be in GROUP BY.
3. Group by expressions when needed: `GROUP BY substr(order_date, 1, 7)` (month) or
   `COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')`. NULL forms its own group.
4. `WHERE` filters rows **before** grouping; `ORDER BY` sorts the groups (with a tie-breaker).

```sql
SELECT category,
       COUNT(*)                  AS product_count,
       ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2) AS avg_list_price
FROM   products
GROUP  BY category
ORDER  BY product_count DESC, category;
```

**Check the grain:** after writing a GROUP BY, ask 'is each row of my output unique on the GROUP BY columns?'
It always is — so if you expected one row per customer but grouped by customer *and* date, you get more rows.
lessons.snowflake_notes: Snowflake supports `GROUP BY ALL` (group by every non-aggregate SELECT column), `GROUP BY 1, 2` positional references, and `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` for months. SQLite supports positional GROUP BY too; use `substr(date, 1, 7)` or `strftime('%Y-%m', date)` for months.

worked_example.question: How many orders are in each status?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT order_status,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_status
ORDER BY order_count DESC, order_status;
worked_example.explanation: Sixty rows are bucketed by status, then each bucket is counted. The sum of order_count is 60 — a quick sanity check that no rows were lost.

common_mistakes: Selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated (SQLite returns an arbitrary value; Snowflake errors).
Grouping by too many columns (e.g. adding order_date when you wanted per-customer), changing the grain.
Forgetting that NULL forms its own group — or relabelling it in SELECT but not in GROUP BY.
Filtering valid orders after the fact instead of in WHERE, so the counts include cancelled orders.
Ordering grouped output without a tie-breaker.
recall: What must every non-aggregated SELECT column be?
Listed in GROUP BY.
What decides the number of output rows in a GROUP BY query?
The number of distinct combinations of the GROUP BY columns (after WHERE).
WHERE runs before or after GROUP BY?
Before — it filters rows that feed the groups.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 8 filters groups with HAVING. Look back at exercise 7.3: how would you list only products whose line_count exceeds their order_count? That's a HAVING question.

exercises.title: Products per category
exercises.question: How big is each category, and what's its average list price?
exercises.prompt: Return category, product_count (number of products) and avg_list_price (average list_price, rounded to 2 decimals) for each category. Keep the NULL category as its own group.
hints: One row per category → GROUP BY category.
COUNT(*) per group, ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2) per group.
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS product_count, ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2) AS avg_list_price FROM products GROUP BY category;
exercises.why: NULL forms its own group, so the uncategorised Mystery Gift Box shows up instead of vanishing. Sports' average ignores the unpriced dumbbells (3 prices, 4 products).

recall.q: Does GROUP BY put NULLs in a group?
recall.a: Yes — all NULLs form one group.

exercises.solution:
SELECT category,
       COUNT(*)                  AS product_count,
       ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2) AS avg_list_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category;

exercises.title: Customers per region, unknowns labelled
exercises.question: How are customers distributed across regions?
exercises.prompt: Return region_label (region, or 'Unknown' when NULL) and customer_count, one row per region_label, sorted by customer_count descending, then region_label ascending.
hints: You can GROUP BY an expression (or its alias in SQLite).
GROUP BY COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')
... GROUP BY COALESCE(region, 'Unknown') ORDER BY customer_count DESC, region_label;
exercises.why: Labelling the NULL group makes it visible on a chart. North/East and West/South tie on count, so the label tie-breaker keeps the order stable.

recall.q: Can you GROUP BY an expression instead of a plain column?
recall.a: Yes, e.g. GROUP BY COALESCE(region, 'Unknown').

exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(region, 'Unknown') AS region_label,
       COUNT(*)                   AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, region_label;

exercises.title: Times sold versus orders per product
exercises.question: For each product that has sold, how many units, lines and distinct orders?
exercises.prompt: Over all rows of order_items, return product_id, units_sold (SUM of quantity), line_count (number of order lines) and order_count (number of distinct order_id values), one row per product_id.
hints: Group by product_id.
line_count = COUNT(*), order_count = COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).
SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units_sold, COUNT(*) AS line_count, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id;
exercises.why: Products 5 and 9 have line_count > order_count — that's the duplicate lines showing up. Comparing COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT key) inside groups is a classic duplicate detector.

recall.q: Within a group, what does COUNT(*) > COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) tell you?
recall.a: Some order appears more than once in that group — repeated lines (possibly duplicates).

exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id,
       SUM(quantity)            AS units_sold,
       COUNT(*)                 AS line_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count
FROM order_items
GROUP BY product_id;

exercises.title: Top 5 orders by line value
exercises.question: Which five orders have the highest total line value?
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, line_count (number of lines) and order_value (SUM of quantity * unit_price, rounded to 2 decimals) for the 5 orders with the highest order_value, sorted by order_value descending, then order_id ascending. Use all order_items rows (no status filter).
hints: Group lines into orders, sum their value.
Then ORDER BY the alias and LIMIT 5.
GROUP BY order_id ORDER BY order_value DESC, order_id LIMIT 5
exercises.why: The #1 'order' is order 9 — which was cancelled and also carries a duplicated $279.99 line. A top-N list is only as good as the rows feeding it; Module 2 adds the status filter via a join.

recall.q: In which order are GROUP BY, ORDER BY and LIMIT applied?
recall.a: GROUP BY → (HAVING) → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id,
       COUNT(*)                             AS line_count,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS order_value
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id
ORDER BY order_value DESC, order_id
LIMIT 5;

exercises.title: Monthly order trend for 2025
exercises.question: How many orders — and how many valid ones — did we get each month of 2025?
exercises.prompt: For orders with order_date on or after '2025-01-01', return order_month (substr(order_date, 1, 7), e.g. '2025-03'), total_orders and valid_orders (orders with order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')), one row per month, sorted by order_month.
hints: Group by the month expression substr(order_date, 1, 7).
valid_orders is a conditional count: SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
SELECT substr(order_date, 1, 7) AS order_month, COUNT(*) AS total_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS valid_orders FROM orders WHERE ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY order_month;
exercises.why: Monthly trend tables with a conditional metric side-by-side are the bread and butter of business reviews. Note: a month with zero orders would simply be missing — filling such gaps (date spines) comes in a later module.

recall.q: How do you get 'YYYY-MM' from an ISO date in SQLite?
recall.a: substr(d, 1, 7) or strftime('%Y-%m', d).

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month, COUNT_IF(order_status IN (...)) AS valid_orders.
exercises.solution:
SELECT substr(order_date, 1, 7) AS order_month,
       COUNT(*)                AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS valid_orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY substr(order_date, 1, 7)
ORDER BY order_month;

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month, COUNT_IF(order_status IN
(...)) AS valid_orders.
*/
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') (or DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) for a date) instead of substr(order_date, 1, 7) on a DATE column.

exercises.title: Valid orders per customer per year
exercises.question: How many valid orders did each customer place in each year?
exercises.prompt: Using only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')), return customer_id, order_year (substr(order_date, 1, 4)) and order_count, one row per customer and year, sorted by customer_id then order_year.
hints: The grain is (customer, year): both go in GROUP BY.
Filter valid statuses in WHERE, before grouping.
WHERE order_status IN (...) GROUP BY customer_id, substr(order_date, 1, 4) ORDER BY customer_id, order_year
exercises.why: Two grouping columns = one row per combination. Customer 99 (the orphan order) shows up too — this table alone can't tell you it doesn't exist.

recall.q: If you GROUP BY customer_id, order_year, what is unique in the output?
recall.a: Each (customer_id, order_year) pair.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       substr(order_date, 1, 4) AS order_year,
       COUNT(*)                 AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY customer_id, substr(order_date, 1, 4)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_year;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use YEAR(order_date) or TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY') instead of substr(order_date, 1, 4) on a DATE column.

lessons.title: HAVING versus WHERE
lessons.objective: Filter rows before grouping with WHERE and filter groups after aggregation with HAVING — and combine both in one query without mixing them up.
lessons.context: 'Customers with at least 3 orders', 'categories averaging over $50', 'orders worth more than $500' — these are conditions on aggregates, which WHERE cannot see. Using the wrong clause either errors out or, worse, silently answers a different question.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: two filters, two moments**

1. **WHERE** — conditions on individual rows (status, date, category). Runs *before* GROUP BY.
2. **GROUP BY** — build the groups from the surviving rows.
3. **HAVING** — conditions on group aggregates (`COUNT(*) >= 3`, `SUM(...) > 500`). Runs *after* GROUP BY.
4. Then SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT as usual.

```sql
SELECT   customer_id, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders
FROM     orders
WHERE    order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')   -- row filter
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING   COUNT(*) >= 3                                          -- group filter
ORDER BY valid_orders DESC, customer_id;
```

**Rule of thumb:** if the condition mentions an aggregate → HAVING. Otherwise → WHERE (it's faster, because
fewer rows get grouped, and it's clearer). `WHERE COUNT(*) > 3` is an error.

**Order of evaluation:** `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`.
lessons.snowflake_notes: Identical in Snowflake. Snowflake additionally has `QUALIFY`, which filters on *window* functions after HAVING (covered with window functions later); it is not a substitute for HAVING on GROUP BY aggregates.

worked_example.question: Which customers placed at least 5 orders (any status)?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY order_count DESC, customer_id;
worked_example.explanation: COUNT(*) only exists after grouping, so the filter must be in HAVING. Notice customer 1's count includes a cancelled order — add a WHERE on status if only valid orders should count.

common_mistakes: Putting an aggregate in WHERE (`WHERE COUNT(*) > 3`) — an error.
Putting row conditions in HAVING (`HAVING order_status = 'completed'`) — works in SQLite only by accident, and filters on an arbitrary row of the group.
Forgetting the WHERE status filter, so cancelled orders count toward 'loyal customer' thresholds.
Filtering on the rounded alias and getting boundary cases wrong — compare the unrounded aggregate.
Confusing 'rows over X' (WHERE) with 'groups whose total is over X' (HAVING).
recall: Write the logical evaluation order including HAVING.
FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
Which clause filters groups?
HAVING.
Which is generally more efficient for a row condition, WHERE or HAVING?
WHERE — it removes rows before the grouping work is done.
lessons.review_next: That completes Module 1. Before joins, redo 8.2 and 8.6 from memory. Module 2 starts by joining orders to order_items so 'valid order' filters can finally apply to line-level revenue.

exercises.title: Repeat customers (any status)
exercises.question: Which customers have placed 4 or more orders of any status?
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id and order_count (number of orders, any status) for customers with at least 4 orders.
hints: The condition is on COUNT(*), an aggregate.
Aggregate conditions go in HAVING, after GROUP BY.
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4
exercises.why: Frequency thresholds define segments like 'loyal customers'. This is the simplest HAVING.

recall.q: Why can't you write WHERE COUNT(*) >= 4?
recall.a: WHERE runs before grouping, when COUNT(*) per customer doesn't exist yet.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;

exercises.title: Repeat customers on valid orders only
exercises.question: Same question, but only valid orders count toward loyalty.
exercises.prompt: Considering only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')), return customer_id and valid_orders (count of their valid orders) for customers with at least 4 valid orders, sorted by valid_orders descending, then customer_id ascending.
hints: Status is a row-level condition → WHERE. The count threshold → HAVING.
WHERE order_status IN (...) ... GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4
Add ORDER BY valid_orders DESC, customer_id.
exercises.why: Compare with 8.1: customers 11 and 14 drop out once their cancelled orders stop counting. WHERE and HAVING answer different questions — you usually need both.

recall.q: Status filter: WHERE or HAVING?
recall.a: WHERE — it's a condition on individual rows.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS valid_orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4
ORDER BY valid_orders DESC, customer_id;

exercises.title: Find the duplicate order lines
exercises.question: Data engineering suspects some order lines were loaded twice. Which ones?
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price, copies (number of rows with that exact combination) and last_order_item_id (the highest order_item_id among the copies), only for combinations that appear more than once.
hints: Group by every column that defines 'the same line' — not order_item_id.
Keep only groups with more than one row.
GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
exercises.why: GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 is THE standard duplicate check, run on every new table and every pipeline output. It finds lines 149 and 150.

recall.q: Write the skeleton of a duplicate check on columns a, b.
recall.a: SELECT a, b, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY a, b HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price,
       COUNT(*)           AS copies,
       MAX(order_item_id) AS last_order_item_id
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

exercises.title: Premium categories
exercises.question: Which categories have an average list price above $50?
exercises.prompt: Return category, product_count (number of products) and avg_list_price (average list_price, rounded to 2 decimals) for categories whose average list_price is greater than 50.
hints: The threshold is on AVG(list_price) — an aggregate.
Put the unrounded AVG in HAVING (or the alias, which SQLite also allows).
GROUP BY category HAVING AVG(list_price) > 50
exercises.why: Group-level thresholds drive segmentation ('premium' vs 'value' categories). Electronics, Apparel and Sports qualify.

recall.q: Can HAVING use an aggregate that isn't in the SELECT list?
recall.a: Yes — e.g. HAVING AVG(list_price) > 50 works even if avg isn't selected.

exercises.solution:
SELECT category,
       COUNT(*)                  AS product_count,
       ROUND(AVG(list_price), 2) AS avg_list_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING AVG(list_price) > 50;

exercises.title: Big orders
exercises.question: Which orders have a total line value of at least $500?
exercises.prompt: Over all order_items rows, return order_id and order_value (SUM of quantity * unit_price, rounded to 2 decimals) for orders whose total line value is at least 500, sorted by order_value descending, then order_id ascending.
hints: Sum per order, then keep groups over the threshold.
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) >= 500
GROUP BY order_id HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) >= 500 ORDER BY order_value DESC, order_id
exercises.why: 'Orders above X' is a threshold on an aggregate. Compare with 'lines above X' (a WHERE on quantity * unit_price) — a very different list.

recall.q: 'Lines worth over $500' vs 'orders worth over $500' — which uses HAVING?
recall.a: Orders: the order total is an aggregate of lines → HAVING. Lines: row-level → WHERE.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id,
       ROUND(SUM(quantity * unit_price), 2) AS order_value
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING SUM(quantity * unit_price) >= 500
ORDER BY order_value DESC, order_id;

exercises.title: Bulk-buy favourites
exercises.question: Which products are regularly bought in bulk (3 or more units on a line)?
exercises.prompt: Consider only order lines with quantity of at least 3. Return product_id, bulk_lines (number of such lines) and bulk_units (SUM of quantity on those lines) for products with at least 3 bulk lines, sorted by bulk_lines descending, then product_id ascending.
hints: 'quantity >= 3' is about one line → WHERE. 'at least 3 such lines' is about the group → HAVING.
WHERE quantity >= 3 GROUP BY product_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
Add ORDER BY bulk_lines DESC, product_id.
exercises.why: Two thresholds that sound alike ('3 units', '3 lines') live in different clauses. Getting this right is the whole point of WHERE vs HAVING.

recall.q: In one sentence: WHERE vs HAVING?
recall.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id,
       COUNT(*)      AS bulk_lines,
       SUM(quantity) AS bulk_units
FROM order_items
WHERE quantity >= 3
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY bulk_lines DESC, product_id;

exercises.title: Active 2025 customers with their window
exercises.question: Which customers placed at least 2 valid orders in 2025, and when were their first and last?
exercises.prompt: Considering only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')) with order_date from '2025-01-01' to '2025-12-31' inclusive, return customer_id, order_count, first_order_date and last_order_date for customers with at least 2 such orders, sorted by order_count descending, then customer_id ascending.
hints: Status and date are row conditions → WHERE. The 2-order threshold → HAVING.
MIN/MAX of order_date give the first and last order per customer.
WHERE order_status IN (...) AND order_date BETWEEN ... GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY order_count DESC, customer_id
exercises.why: This is a real retention-style query: a cohort filter (WHERE), a behavioural threshold (HAVING) and descriptive aggregates, all in one pass.

recall.q: Could the date filter go in HAVING instead of WHERE?
recall.a: Not as a row filter — HAVING sees groups. Row conditions belong in WHERE.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)        AS order_count,
       MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date,
       MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
  AND order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY order_count DESC, customer_id;

lessons.title: Keys and relationships
lessons.objective: Identify primary keys, foreign keys and the grain of each table, predict how many rows a join returns, and use joins to verify relationships (children per parent, orphan keys).
lessons.context: Before the analytics team trusts any joined report, the data-quality lead wants proof that the relationships in the warehouse hold: does every order point at a real customer? every product at a real supplier? how many lines does an order have? Joins are only as correct as your understanding of the keys underneath them.
lessons.recipe:
**Keys in this warehouse**

| table | primary key (one row per…) | foreign keys (points to…) |
|---|---|---|
| customers | customer_id (customer) | — |
| suppliers | supplier_id (supplier) | — |
| products | product_id (product) | supplier_id → suppliers |
