exercises.join_notes: The subquery runs once per customer (20 times) and always returns exactly one value, so the output is exactly 20 rows — customer 1's 9 orders collapse to one MAX. Customers 18, 19 and 20 have no orders → latest_order_date NULL. Orphan order 31 (customer 99) is never looked at, because the driving table is customers.
exercises.snowflake: Snowflake runs the correlated scalar subquery as written. Lateral form: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, lo.latest_order_date FROM customers c, LATERAL (SELECT MAX(order_date) AS latest_order_date FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) lo; — an aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row, so no customer is lost (Postgres: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) lo ON TRUE).
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT MAX(o.order_date)
        FROM orders AS o
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS latest_order_date
FROM customers AS c;

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake runs the correlated scalar subquery as written. Lateral form: SELECT
c.customer_id, c.name, lo.latest_order_date FROM customers c, LATERAL (SELECT
MAX(order_date) AS latest_order_date FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id =
c.customer_id) lo; — an aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row, so no
customer is lost (Postgres: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) lo ON TRUE).
*/

exercises.title: Latest order details (top-1 row per customer)
exercises.question: For each customer, show their latest order's id, date and status.
exercises.prompt: Return all 20 customers with columns customer_id, name, latest_order_id, latest_order_date and latest_order_status, taken from the customer's order with the latest order_date (ties broken by the higher order_id). NULLs for customers without orders.
hints: You need several columns from ONE row per customer. First find that row's order_id with a correlated subquery (ORDER BY … LIMIT 1).
Then join orders on order_id = (that subquery). Keep customers without orders.
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = (SELECT o2.order_id FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY o2.order_date DESC, o2.order_id DESC LIMIT 1)
exercises.why: 'Pick one row per parent, then show several of its columns' is the bread-and-butter LATERAL use case. In SQLite, the 'find the id, then join on it' trick is the equivalent.

recall.q: Why join on the id returned by the subquery instead of writing three scalar subqueries?
recall.a: One subquery picks the row once, guaranteeing all columns come from the same order (and it's less code).

exercises.join_notes: Because the ON condition compares order_id to a single id, each customer matches at most one order: 20 rows in, 20 out, despite 59 orders belonging to customers. Customers 18, 19, 20: subquery returns NULL, order_id = NULL matches nothing, the LEFT JOIN keeps them with three NULL columns. A plain inner join here would return 17 rows; joining on customer_id alone would return 62.
exercises.snowflake: Postgres: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC LIMIT 1) lo ON TRUE. Idiomatic Snowflake: LEFT JOIN (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders QUALIFY rn = 1) lo ON lo.customer_id = c.customer_id.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       o.order_id     AS latest_order_id,
       o.order_date   AS latest_order_date,
       o.order_status AS latest_order_status
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.order_id = (SELECT o2.order_id
                   FROM orders AS o2
                   WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id
                   ORDER BY o2.order_date DESC, o2.order_id DESC
                   LIMIT 1);

/* Snowflake notes:
Postgres: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC LIMIT 1)
lo ON TRUE. Idiomatic Snowflake: LEFT JOIN (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders QUALIFY rn = 1)
lo ON lo.customer_id = c.customer_id.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       lo.order_id     AS latest_order_id,
       lo.order_date   AS latest_order_date,
       lo.order_status AS latest_order_status
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_status
           FROM orders
           QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                      ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1) AS lo
       ON lo.customer_id = c.customer_id;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake can't evaluate a correlated subquery with ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1. Rank each customer's orders instead and keep the top one with QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1, then LEFT JOIN that.

exercises.title: Most expensive product each customer bought
exercises.question: Sales wants each paying customer's single most expensive purchase.
exercises.prompt: For customers with at least one valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), return customer_id, name, product_name and unit_price of the order line with the highest unit_price among their valid orders (ties broken by the lower order_item_id).
hints: Per customer, pick ONE order line: a correlated subquery over order_items JOIN orders, ordered by unit_price DESC, LIMIT 1.
Join order_items on order_item_id = (that subquery), then products for the name. Customers whose subquery finds nothing should disappear (inner).

FROM customers c JOIN order_items i ON i.order_item_id = (SELECT i2.order_item_id FROM order_items i2 JOIN orders o2 ON ... WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id AND <valid> ORDER BY i2.unit_price DESC, i2.order_item_id LIMIT 1) JOIN products p ON ...
exercises.why: Top-1-per-group with a join inside the per-row query is where LATERAL shines: the subquery can be as complex as needed and still returns one row per customer.

recall.q: CROSS JOIN LATERAL vs LEFT JOIN LATERAL — which drops customers with no valid order?
recall.a: CROSS (inner) LATERAL drops them; LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON TRUE keeps them with NULLs.

exercises.join_notes: 16 customers have a valid order; each gets exactly one line from the subquery, so the result is 16 rows even though they own 132 valid lines. Customers 16 (only a cancelled order), 18, 19 and 20 get NULL from the subquery and drop out of the inner join. Order 31's lines (customer 99) are never considered. Note several customers' top line is product 5 or 19 — and product 19 has a NULL list_price, which doesn't matter because we use the actual unit_price.
exercises.snowflake: FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT i.unit_price, i.product_id FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') ORDER BY i.unit_price DESC, i.order_item_id LIMIT 1) top JOIN products p ON p.product_id = top.product_id
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       p.product_name,
       i.unit_price
FROM customers AS c
JOIN order_items AS i
  ON i.order_item_id = (SELECT i2.order_item_id
                        FROM order_items AS i2
                        JOIN orders AS o2 ON o2.order_id = i2.order_id
                        WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id
                          AND o2.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
                        ORDER BY i2.unit_price DESC, i2.order_item_id
                        LIMIT 1)
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT i.unit_price, i.product_id FROM
order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = i.order_id WHERE o.customer_id =
c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') ORDER BY
i.unit_price DESC, i.order_item_id LIMIT 1) top JOIN products p ON p.product_id =
top.product_id
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       p.product_name,
       top.unit_price
FROM customers AS c
JOIN (SELECT o.customer_id, i.product_id, i.unit_price
      FROM order_items AS i
      JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id
                                 ORDER BY i.unit_price DESC, i.order_item_id) = 1) AS top
  ON top.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = top.product_id;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake can't evaluate a correlated ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 subquery. Pick the top line per customer with QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY unit_price DESC, order_item_id) = 1 and join to it.

exercises.title: Two most recent valid orders per customer (top-N)
exercises.question: The CRM card should show each customer's two most recent valid orders.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, order_id and order_date for each customer's (up to) 2 most recent valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); ties on order_date broken by the higher order_id. Customers without a valid order don't appear.
hints: A scalar subquery can't return 2 rows — but `IN (subquery … LIMIT 2)` can.
Correlate the subquery on the customer and filter it to valid orders.

JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_id IN (SELECT o2.order_id FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id AND <valid> ORDER BY o2.order_date DESC, o2.order_id DESC LIMIT 2)
exercises.why: Top-N per group ('last 3 tickets', 'top 5 products per store') is LATERAL's signature move. Window functions (Lesson 30) are the other standard solution.

recall.q: Why can't a scalar subquery in SELECT give you the top 2 orders?
recall.a: A scalar subquery must return a single value; top-N needs multiple rows per left row.

exercises.join_notes: Here the lateral side returns up to 2 rows per customer, so this join DOES multiply — but in a controlled way: 16 customers with valid orders → 30 rows (14 customers contribute 2 rows, 2 customers have only one valid order). Customers 16, 18, 19, 20 have no valid order and drop out; cancelled and pending orders never appear.
exercises.snowflake: FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN (...) ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC LIMIT 2) t
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_date
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND o.order_id IN (SELECT o2.order_id
                    FROM orders AS o2
                    WHERE o2.customer_id = c.customer_id
                      AND o2.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
                    ORDER BY o2.order_date DESC, o2.order_id DESC
                    LIMIT 2);

/* Snowflake notes:
FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders o WHERE
o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN (...) ORDER BY order_date DESC,
order_id DESC LIMIT 2) t
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_date
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id
                           ORDER BY o.order_date DESC, o.order_id DESC) <= 2;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake doesn't support a correlated IN (... ORDER BY ... LIMIT 2) subquery. For top-N per group use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) <= 2.

exercises.title: Explode the JSON order feed
exercises.question: The data team needs the raw order event feed flattened to one row per ordered item.
exercises.prompt: Using json_each on payload's '$.items' array, return one row per item with columns event_id, order_id (payload $.order_id), product_id, qty and price (fields of each item).
hints: json_each(json_text, '$.path') is a table-valued function: one row per array element, with the element in its `value` column.
Put it in FROM after the table, comma-separated, referencing r.payload — that's a lateral join.
FROM raw_order_events r, json_each(r.payload, '$.items') j, and select j.value ->> '$.product_id' etc.
exercises.why: Every event pipeline lands nested arrays. LATERAL FLATTEN (Snowflake) / json_each (SQLite) / UNNEST (Postgres, BigQuery) is how you turn them into relational rows.

recall.q: Why is json_each a lateral join?
recall.a: Its argument (r.payload) comes from the table to its left, so it's evaluated once per left row.

exercises.join_notes: 60 events fan out to 150 item rows — one per array element, matching the 150 order_items rows (order 9's payload even contains the duplicated product 5 item twice). Event 60 has an empty items array, so json_each yields no rows for it and the implicit (inner) lateral join drops it: only 59 events appear. There is no ON condition — the 'key' is that each json_each call reads its own row's payload.
exercises.snowflake: SELECT r.event_id, PARSE_JSON(r.payload):order_id::int AS order_id, f.value:product_id::int AS product_id, f.value:qty::int AS qty, f.value:price::number(10,2) AS price FROM raw_order_events r, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => PARSE_JSON(r.payload):items) f;
exercises.solution:
SELECT r.event_id,
       r.payload ->> '$.order_id' AS order_id,
       j.value   ->> '$.product_id' AS product_id,
       j.value   ->> '$.qty'        AS qty,
       j.value   ->> '$.price'      AS price
FROM raw_order_events AS r,
     json_each(r.payload, '$.items') AS j;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT r.event_id, PARSE_JSON(r.payload):order_id::int AS order_id,
f.value:product_id::int AS product_id, f.value:qty::int AS qty,
f.value:price::number(10,2) AS price FROM raw_order_events r, LATERAL FLATTEN(input =>
PARSE_JSON(r.payload):items) f;
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT r.event_id,
       r.payload:order_id::INT      AS order_id,
       f.value:product_id::INT      AS product_id,
       f.value:qty::INT             AS qty,
       f.value:price::NUMBER(10, 2) AS price
FROM raw_order_events AS r,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.payload:items) AS f;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no json_each or ->> '$.path'. payload is a VARIANT here: read fields with payload:order_id::INT and explode the array with LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.payload:items) f, then f.value:product_id::INT etc. (Use PARSE_JSON(payload) if it were stored as text.)

exercises.title: Item count per event, keeping empty orders
exercises.question: Data quality wants every event with its item count and payload value — including events whose items array is empty.
exercises.prompt: Return all 60 events with columns event_id, order_id (payload $.order_id), item_count (number of elements in $.items, 0 if empty) and payload_gross (SUM(qty * price) over the items, rounded to 2 decimals, 0 if no items). Use LEFT JOIN json_each(...) ON 1.
hints: The comma (inner) form drops event 60. Use LEFT JOIN json_each(r.payload, '$.items') j ON 1.
GROUP BY r.event_id; count a json_each column (COUNT(j.key)) so empty arrays give 0.

SELECT r.event_id, r.payload ->> '$.order_id' AS order_id, COUNT(j.key) AS item_count, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM((j.value->>'$.qty') * (j.value->>'$.price')), 0), 2) AS payload_gross FROM raw_order_events r LEFT JOIN json_each(r.payload, '$.items') j ON 1 GROUP BY r.event_id;
exercises.why: Inner FLATTEN silently drops parents with empty arrays — in Snowflake you add OUTER => TRUE. Counting parents before and after flattening catches it.

recall.q: How do you keep rows with an empty array when flattening in Snowflake?
recall.a: LATERAL FLATTEN(input => …, OUTER => TRUE) — the equivalent of LEFT JOIN LATERAL.

exercises.join_notes: LEFT JOIN json_each produces 151 rows: 150 item rows for 59 events plus 1 NULL-extended row for event 60 (order 60, empty items). GROUP BY brings it back to 60 rows. COUNT(j.key) ignores that NULL row → item_count 0; SUM over only NULLs is NULL → COALESCE to 0. COUNT(*) would have reported 1 item for order 60.
exercises.snowflake: FROM raw_order_events r, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => PARSE_JSON(r.payload):items, OUTER => TRUE) f GROUP BY r.event_id
exercises.solution:
SELECT r.event_id,
       r.payload ->> '$.order_id' AS order_id,
       COUNT(j.key) AS item_count,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM((j.value ->> '$.qty') * (j.value ->> '$.price')), 0), 2) AS payload_gross
FROM raw_order_events AS r
LEFT JOIN json_each(r.payload, '$.items') AS j ON 1
GROUP BY r.event_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
FROM raw_order_events r, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => PARSE_JSON(r.payload):items, OUTER
=> TRUE) f GROUP BY r.event_id
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT r.event_id,
       r.payload:order_id::INT AS order_id,
       COUNT(f.value) AS item_count,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(f.value:qty::INT * f.value:price::NUMBER(10, 2)), 0), 2) AS payload_gross
FROM raw_order_events AS r,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.payload:items, OUTER => TRUE) AS f
GROUP BY r.event_id, r.payload:order_id::INT;
exercises.sf_note: Instead of LEFT JOIN json_each(...) ON 1, Snowflake keeps events with an empty array via LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.payload:items, OUTER => TRUE); count f.value so empty arrays give 0. Read fields with payload:order_id::INT rather than ->> '$.order_id'.

exercises.title: Count orders per tag
exercises.question: Marketing tags some orders ('promo', 'gift', 'first_order') in the feed. How many orders carry each tag?
exercises.prompt: Explode payload's '$.tags' array with json_each and return tag and order_count (number of events carrying that tag), ordered by order_count descending, then tag.
hints: Same lateral pattern as before, on '$.tags'. Each tag element is a plain string in t.value.
Events without a tags key yield no json_each rows — fine here.
SELECT t.value AS tag, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM raw_order_events r, json_each(r.payload, '$.tags') t GROUP BY t.value ORDER BY order_count DESC, tag;
exercises.why: Optional arrays are common in event payloads. Knowing that an absent key simply produces zero lateral rows (not an error) tells you when you need the OUTER/LEFT form.

recall.q: What does json_each return when the path doesn't exist in the JSON?
recall.a: No rows — so that event disappears from an inner lateral join.

exercises.join_notes: 45 of the 60 events have no tags key at all; json_each returns zero rows for them, so they drop out. The 15 tagged events explode into 17 tag rows (events 20 and 44 carry two tags each, so they contribute two rows), grouped into 3 tags: promo 8, gift 6, first_order 3.
exercises.snowflake: SELECT f.value::string AS tag, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM raw_order_events r, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => PARSE_JSON(r.payload):tags) f GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC, 1;
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT f.value::STRING AS tag,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM raw_order_events AS r,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.payload:tags) AS f
GROUP BY f.value::STRING
ORDER BY order_count DESC, tag;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake explode the tags with LATERAL FLATTEN(input => r.payload:tags) f and cast the element with f.value::STRING (instead of json_each(r.payload, '$.tags')). Events without a tags key produce no rows, as with json_each.

lessons.title: CASE WHEN
lessons.objective: Turn raw values into business labels with CASE, count and sum conditionally with SUM(CASE ...), and write CASE expressions that handle NULL on purpose.
lessons.context: Merchandising wants price tiers, finance wants orders bucketed by size, and leadership wants a one-row-per-year scorecard with completed, cancelled and pending orders side by side. All of these are the same tool: a CASE expression placed in SELECT, inside an aggregate, in GROUP BY or in ORDER BY.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: label, then aggregate the label**

1. **Searched CASE** — the general form. Branches are tested top to bottom; the *first* true one wins:
   ```sql
   CASE WHEN list_price IS NULL THEN 'Unpriced'   -- handle NULL first, on purpose
        WHEN list_price < 30    THEN 'Budget'
        WHEN list_price < 100   THEN 'Mid'
        ELSE 'Premium'
   END AS price_tier
   ```
   Because branches are ordered, `< 100` already implies `>= 30` — no need for BETWEEN.
2. **Simple CASE** — compares one expression with values: `CASE order_status WHEN 'completed' THEN 1 ... END`.
   It uses `=`, so `WHEN NULL` never matches. Use a searched `WHEN col IS NULL` instead.
3. **No ELSE → NULL.** A row that matches nothing gets NULL. With an ELSE, NULL inputs silently fall into
   the ELSE bucket (a NULL price would be called 'Premium'!). Decide where NULL goes.
4. **Conditional aggregation** — put CASE *inside* the aggregate to pivot statuses/years into columns:
   ```sql
   SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                 AS cancelled_orders,
   SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2025' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS amount_2025
   ```
   `ELSE 0` gives 0 instead of NULL when nothing matches. (SQLite also has `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)`.)
5. **CASE anywhere an expression goes**: `GROUP BY` a bucket, or `ORDER BY CASE ... END` for a custom sort order.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- `CASE` is identical in Snowflake. Snowflake also has `IFF(cond, a, b)` (SQLite: `IIF(cond, a, b)`) for
  two-way choices, and `DECODE(expr, v1, r1, v2, r2, default)` — note that DECODE *does* treat NULL = NULL as a match.
- Conditional counts: `COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled')` is Snowflake shorthand for
  `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
- `DIV0(a, b)` / `DIV0NULL` avoid division-by-zero errors that you would otherwise guard with CASE.

worked_example.question: How many orders are in each lifecycle group, and how many of them count for revenue?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped') THEN 'fulfilled'
            WHEN order_status = 'returned'               THEN 'returned'
            ELSE 'not fulfilled'
       END                                          AS lifecycle_group,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                  AS revenue_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY lifecycle_group;
worked_example.explanation: The first CASE builds a label and GROUP BY groups on it (SQLite lets you reference the alias; Snowflake does too). The second CASE sits *inside* SUM: each row contributes 1 or 0, so the sum is a conditional count. 'not fulfilled' = 5 cancelled + 2 pending, and they contribute 0 revenue orders.

common_mistakes: Leaving NULL out of the plan: with an ELSE, NULL inputs fall into the ELSE bucket; without one, the label is NULL.
Writing `CASE col WHEN NULL THEN ...`. Simple CASE uses =, which never matches NULL. Use `CASE WHEN col IS NULL`.
Overlapping or out-of-order branches (`WHEN x < 300` before `WHEN x < 100`): the first true branch wins, so 'Small' is never reached.
Forgetting `ELSE 0` inside SUM(CASE ...) and getting NULL instead of 0 for empty buckets.
Filtering a LEFT JOIN's right table in WHERE, which turns it back into an inner join and drops the 'Inactive' customers.
recall: What's the difference between a simple CASE and a searched CASE?
Simple: CASE expr WHEN value THEN ... (equality only). Searched: CASE WHEN condition THEN ... (any predicate, including IS NULL).
What is conditional aggregation?
An aggregate whose input is a CASE, e.g. SUM(CASE WHEN status='cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), turning rows into pivoted columns.
Where can a CASE expression appear?
Anywhere an expression can: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, inside aggregates.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 21 puts a whole query inside WHERE. Conditional aggregation comes back in every scorecard you build in Lesson 27, so make sure you can write exercise 20.4 from memory.

exercises.title: Price tiers that don't lose NULLs
exercises.question: Merchandising wants every product tagged with a price tier for the catalog review.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, list_price and price_tier for all 25 products. price_tier is 'Unpriced' when list_price is NULL, 'Budget' when list_price < 30, 'Mid' when list_price is 30 up to (but not including) 100, otherwise 'Premium'.
hints: Branches are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, so put the NULL check first.
WHEN list_price < 100 only runs for rows that already failed < 30, so it means 30–99.99.
CASE WHEN list_price IS NULL THEN 'Unpriced' WHEN list_price < 30 THEN 'Budget' WHEN list_price < 100 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Premium' END AS price_tier
exercises.why: Product 19 has no price. Without the explicit NULL branch it falls through every comparison to ELSE and gets labelled 'Premium', which is a wrong label that nobody would notice.

recall.q: What does a CASE without ELSE return for a row that matches no WHEN?
recall.a: NULL.

exercises.snowflake: Same CASE syntax. For a two-way split you could write IFF(list_price < 30, 'Budget', 'Other').
exercises.solution:
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       list_price,
       CASE WHEN list_price IS NULL THEN 'Unpriced'
            WHEN list_price < 30    THEN 'Budget'
            WHEN list_price < 100   THEN 'Mid'
            ELSE 'Premium'
       END AS price_tier
FROM products;

/* Snowflake notes:
Same CASE syntax. For a two-way split you could write IFF(list_price < 30, 'Budget',
'Other').
*/

exercises.title: Revenue vs excluded orders
exercises.question: Finance wants a quick count of orders that count for revenue versus those that don't.
exercises.prompt: Return status_group and order_count. status_group is 'Revenue' for valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) and 'Excluded' for every other status. Count all orders in the table (including the orphan order 31).
hints: Build the label with CASE, then GROUP BY that label.
IN (...) works inside WHEN just like in WHERE.
SELECT CASE WHEN order_status IN (...) THEN 'Revenue' ELSE 'Excluded' END AS status_group, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY status_group;
exercises.why: Grouping by a derived label is how you collapse messy source codes into the handful of buckets a business actually reports on.

recall.q: Can you GROUP BY a CASE expression?
recall.a: Yes. Repeat the expression or (in SQLite/Snowflake) use its alias or position.

exercises.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') THEN 'Revenue'
            ELSE 'Excluded'
       END      AS status_group,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY status_group;

exercises.title: Bucket orders by size
exercises.question: The ops team wants each valid order labelled Small / Medium / Large by its value.
exercises.prompt: For each valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) return order_id, order_total = SUM(quantity * unit_price) rounded to 2 decimals, and size_bucket: 'Small' when the (unrounded) total is < 100, 'Medium' when < 300, otherwise 'Large'.
hints: Join orders to order_items, filter valid statuses, GROUP BY order_id.
A CASE can test an aggregate: WHEN SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) < 100 THEN ...
SELECT o.order_id, ROUND(SUM(...), 2) AS order_total, CASE WHEN SUM(...) < 100 THEN 'Small' WHEN SUM(...) < 300 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Large' END AS size_bucket FROM ... GROUP BY o.order_id;
exercises.why: Size buckets drive shipping rules, fraud review thresholds and marketing segments. CASE over an aggregate is evaluated per group, after GROUP BY.

recall.q: Can CASE wrap an aggregate like SUM(...)?
recall.a: Yes. In a grouped query, CASE WHEN SUM(x) < 100 ... is evaluated once per group.

exercises.solution:
SELECT o.order_id,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS order_total,
       CASE WHEN SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) < 100 THEN 'Small'
            WHEN SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) < 300 THEN 'Medium'
            ELSE 'Large'
       END AS size_bucket
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY o.order_id;

exercises.title: Yearly order scorecard (conditional aggregation)
exercises.question: Leadership wants one row per year showing how many orders were valid, cancelled and pending.
exercises.prompt: Return order_year (strftime('%Y', order_date)), total_orders (all orders), valid_orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), cancelled_orders and pending_orders. Use every row in orders.
hints: One GROUP BY year; each status becomes its own column.
SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts rows that meet a condition.
SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders — repeat for valid and pending.
exercises.why: Conditional aggregation is how a 'pivot' gets written in plain SQL. One pass over the table replaces three separate filtered queries.

recall.q: Name two ways to count only cancelled orders inside a grouped query.
recall.a: SUM(CASE WHEN order_status='cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), or COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE order_status='cancelled') (Snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status='cancelled')).

exercises.snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled_orders; YEAR(order_date) AS order_year.
exercises.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS order_year,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS valid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'pending'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_year;

/* Snowflake notes:
COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled_orders; YEAR(order_date) AS
order_year.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT YEAR(order_date) AS order_year,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       COUNT_IF(order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')) AS valid_orders,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled_orders,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'pending') AS pending_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_year;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): use YEAR(order_date) AS order_year. COUNT_IF(condition) is a shorter alternative to SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

exercises.title: Category revenue, 2024 vs 2025 side by side
exercises.question: The category managers want this year's and last year's revenue next to each other.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return category (NULL category shown as 'Uncategorized'), revenue_2024 and revenue_2025 (by order_date year), each rounded to 2 decimals and showing 0 rather than NULL if a category had no sales that year.
hints: Join orders → order_items → products and keep valid orders only.
Inside SUM, return the line value for the target year and 0 otherwise.
ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024' THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue_2024
exercises.why: Year-over-year columns are the most requested layout in business reviews. 'ELSE 0' vs no ELSE decides whether an empty year shows 0 or NULL, and dashboards treat those differently.

recall.q: In SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN x END) with no ELSE, what is the result if no row matches?
recall.a: NULL, because SUM over only NULLs is NULL. Add ELSE 0 to get 0.

exercises.snowflake: Snowflake also offers PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR order_year IN ('2024','2025')), but conditional aggregation is portable and easier to control.
exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024'
                      THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue_2024,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2025'
                      THEN i.quantity * i.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue_2025
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products    AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized');

/* Snowflake notes:
Snowflake also offers PIVOT (SUM(amount) FOR order_year IN ('2024','2025')), but
conditional aggregation is portable and easier to control.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
       ROUND(SUM(IFF(YEAR(o.order_date) = 2024, i.quantity * i.unit_price, 0)), 2) AS revenue_2024,
       ROUND(SUM(IFF(YEAR(o.order_date) = 2025, i.quantity * i.unit_price, 0)), 2) AS revenue_2025
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products    AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized');
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): test the year with YEAR(o.order_date) = 2024. IFF(cond, a, b) is a compact CASE WHEN for two outcomes.

exercises.title: Customer loyalty segments (including non-buyers)
exercises.question: CRM wants every customer, including ones who never bought, placed in a loyalty segment.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, valid_order_count (number of valid orders: valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and segment for all 20 customers: 'Inactive' for 0 valid orders, 'One-time' for 1, 'Repeat' for 2–4, 'Loyal' for 5 or more.
hints: Customers without orders must survive, so this needs a LEFT JOIN from customers.
Put the status filter in the ON clause (a WHERE would drop the non-buyers), and COUNT(o.order_id) so missing matches count 0.
... LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name — then CASE on COUNT(o.order_id).
exercises.why: Segments that silently drop non-buyers under-count your reactivation audience. Customer 16 (only a cancelled order) is 'Inactive', not missing.

recall.q: Why COUNT(o.order_id) instead of COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN?
recall.a: COUNT(*) counts the NULL-extended row as 1; COUNT(o.order_id) ignores NULLs and gives 0.

exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS valid_order_count,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(o.order_id) = 0 THEN 'Inactive'
            WHEN COUNT(o.order_id) = 1 THEN 'One-time'
            WHEN COUNT(o.order_id) <= 4 THEN 'Repeat'
            ELSE 'Loyal'
       END AS segment
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;

exercises.title: Status counts in lifecycle order
exercises.question: The ops dashboard lists statuses in lifecycle order, not alphabetically.
exercises.prompt: Return order_status and order_count (all orders), sorted in lifecycle order: pending, shipped, completed, returned, cancelled.
hints: ORDER BY can sort by any expression, including a CASE that maps statuses to numbers.
A simple CASE fits: CASE order_status WHEN 'pending' THEN 1 WHEN 'shipped' THEN 2 ... END
GROUP BY order_status ORDER BY CASE order_status WHEN 'pending' THEN 1 ... WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 5 END;
exercises.why: Business orderings (funnel stages, size tiers, weekdays) are rarely alphabetical. A CASE sort key keeps the sort in the query instead of in someone's spreadsheet.

recall.q: How do you sort rows in a custom, non-alphabetical order?
recall.a: ORDER BY a CASE expression that maps each value to its rank.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_status,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_status
ORDER BY CASE order_status
              WHEN 'pending'   THEN 1
              WHEN 'shipped'   THEN 2
              WHEN 'completed' THEN 3
              WHEN 'returned'  THEN 4
              WHEN 'cancelled' THEN 5
         END;

lessons.title: Subqueries in WHERE
lessons.objective: Filter rows using the result of another query: membership with IN / NOT IN and comparisons against a single computed value such as an average. Avoid the NOT IN + NULL trap.
lessons.context: Many questions are really two questions: 'which products cost more than *the average*?', 'which customers are *among those who bought books*?'. A subquery lets you answer the inner question first and filter on it, without building a join.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: answer the inner question, then filter on it**

1. Write the inner question as its own query and run it alone. Check it returns what you think.
2. **One value (scalar subquery)** → compare with `=`, `>`, `<`:
   ```sql
   WHERE list_price > (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products)
   ```
   It must return exactly one row and one column (zero rows becomes NULL).
3. **A list of values** → `IN (subquery)` / `NOT IN (subquery)`; the subquery returns one column:
   ```sql
   WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders
                         WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'))
   ```
4. **The NOT IN trap.** `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` is never TRUE (it is `x<>1 AND x<>2 AND x<>NULL` → NULL).
   If the subquery column can contain NULL, add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` inside it, or use NOT EXISTS (Lesson 24).
5. Subqueries can nest: IN inside IN walks a chain of tables without joining them (and without fan-out duplicates).
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- Subqueries in WHERE work the same way in Snowflake, including the NOT IN + NULL behaviour.
- Snowflake raises an error if a scalar subquery returns more than one row ("Single-row subquery returns
  more than one row"). SQLite quietly takes the first row, which hides the bug, so make sure your scalar subqueries really are scalar.

worked_example.question: Which order lines were sold for more than the average unit price across all lines?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT order_item_id, order_id, product_id, unit_price
FROM order_items
WHERE unit_price > (SELECT AVG(unit_price) FROM order_items)
ORDER BY unit_price DESC, order_item_id
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: The inner query runs once and produces one number (≈ 60.15). The outer query compares every line to it. You can't write `WHERE unit_price > AVG(unit_price)` because WHERE runs before aggregation. The subquery gets around that.

common_mistakes: Using NOT IN against a column that can be NULL. The result is silently empty.
A 'scalar' subquery that returns several rows: SQLite picks one arbitrarily, Snowflake errors.
Comparing against a benchmark computed over a different population (e.g. average including cancelled orders).
Trying `WHERE x > AVG(x)`. Aggregates aren't allowed in WHERE; use a subquery.
Returning more than one column from an IN subquery (`IN (SELECT id, name ...)`) is an error.
recall: What are the two main shapes of subquery in WHERE?
Scalar (one value, used with =, >, <) and list (one column, used with IN / NOT IN).
Why is `x NOT IN (SELECT col ...)` dangerous?
If col contains any NULL, the predicate is never TRUE and you get no rows.
Does an IN subquery cause row duplication like a join can?
No. It's a membership test; each outer row is kept or dropped once.
lessons.review_next: Lesson 22 moves subqueries into FROM so you can aggregate first and filter afterwards. Re-do exercise 21.4 until the NULL trap is a reflex. You'll see the NOT EXISTS fix in Lesson 24.

exercises.title: Products priced above the catalog average
exercises.question: Pricing wants the products whose list price is above the average list price.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, list_price for products whose list_price is greater than the average list_price of all products (AVG ignores the NULL price).
hints: First run SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products on its own.
Put that query in parentheses on the right side of >.
WHERE list_price > (SELECT AVG(list_price) FROM products)
exercises.why: 'Above average' is a very common filter. A scalar subquery keeps the threshold live: when prices change, the cut-off moves with them.

recall.q: Why can't you write WHERE list_price > AVG(list_price)?
recall.a: WHERE is evaluated before aggregation; aggregates aren't allowed there. Compute the average in a subquery.

exercises.title: Customers with at least one valid order
exercises.question: Marketing wants the list of customers who have actually bought something.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name of customers whose customer_id is IN the set of customer_ids having at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded). Each customer appears once.
hints: The inner question: which customer_ids have a valid order?
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE ...)
SELECT customer_id, name FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'));
exercises.why: Unlike a join, IN never duplicates the outer row. Customer 1 has 8 valid orders but appears once. Customer 16 (only a cancelled order) is correctly excluded.

recall.q: Can a customer appear twice in the result of WHERE customer_id IN (subquery)?
recall.a: No. IN is a yes/no test per outer row, so duplicates in the subquery don't multiply rows.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id
                      FROM orders
                      WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned'));

exercises.title: Products that have never been sold
exercises.question: Inventory wants to know which catalog items have never appeared on any order.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name for products whose product_id does NOT appear in order_items at all (any order status).
hints: NOT IN (subquery) keeps rows whose value is absent from the list.
order_items.product_id has no NULLs, so NOT IN is safe here (still, check it!).
WHERE product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items)
exercises.why: Dead stock ties up cash. Before trusting NOT IN, always check whether the subquery column can be NULL. Here it can't, but the next exercise shows what happens when it can.

recall.q: What must you check before using NOT IN (subquery)?
recall.a: That the subquery column cannot return NULL. Otherwise the result is empty.

exercises.title: The NOT IN NULL trap: suppliers with no products
exercises.question: Procurement asks: which suppliers currently supply none of our products?
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id, supplier_name for suppliers that have no product in products. Note: products.supplier_id is NULL for one product. Make sure your NOT IN still works (the correct answer is not empty).
hints: Try the naive NOT IN first. It returns zero rows. Why?
x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) evaluates to NULL (never TRUE) because x <> NULL is unknown.
Filter NULLs out inside the subquery: (SELECT supplier_id FROM products WHERE supplier_id IS NOT NULL).
exercises.why: This is one of the most common silent bugs in SQL: the query runs, returns nothing, and everyone concludes 'no such suppliers'. Supplier 5 (Andes Trading) is the real answer.

recall.q: Why does NOT IN return nothing when the subquery contains a NULL?
recall.a: NOT IN expands to a chain of <> comparisons ANDed together; the comparison with NULL is unknown, so the whole condition is never TRUE.

exercises.snowflake: Identical behaviour in Snowflake. NOT EXISTS (Lesson 24) avoids the trap by construction.
exercises.solution:
SELECT supplier_id, supplier_name
FROM suppliers
WHERE supplier_id NOT IN (SELECT supplier_id
                          FROM products
                          WHERE supplier_id IS NOT NULL);

/* Snowflake notes:
Identical behaviour in Snowflake. NOT EXISTS (Lesson 24) avoids the trap by
construction.
*/

exercises.title: Unusually large order lines
exercises.question: Finance wants to review order lines worth more than the average line in valid orders.
exercises.prompt: Consider only lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded). Return order_item_id, order_id and line_total (quantity * unit_price) for lines whose line_total is greater than the average line_total over all lines of valid orders.
hints: Two conditions: the line belongs to a valid order, and its value beats the average.
Both the outer rows and the average must use the same population (valid orders only).
WHERE i.order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE <valid>) AND i.quantity * i.unit_price > (SELECT AVG(i2.quantity * i2.unit_price) FROM order_items i2 JOIN orders o2 ... WHERE <valid>)
exercises.why: A benchmark is only fair if it's computed over the same population you compare against. Including cancelled orders in the average would move the threshold.

recall.q: How many rows and columns must a scalar subquery return?
recall.a: Exactly one row and one column (zero rows → NULL).

exercises.solution:
SELECT i.order_item_id,
       i.order_id,
       i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total
FROM order_items AS i
WHERE i.order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders
                     WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned'))
  AND i.quantity * i.unit_price >
      (SELECT AVG(i2.quantity * i2.unit_price)
       FROM order_items AS i2
       JOIN orders AS o2 ON o2.order_id = i2.order_id
       WHERE o2.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned'));

exercises.title: Orders that contain a returned item
exercises.question: Customer service wants every order that had at least one item returned, whatever its status.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_date, order_status for orders that contain at least one order_item_id present in returns. Use nested IN subqueries.
hints: Work outward: returned order_item_ids → their order_ids → those orders.
SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE order_item_id IN (SELECT order_item_id FROM returns)
SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders WHERE order_id IN (<the query above>);
exercises.why: Only 3 orders have status 'returned', but 10 orders had items refunded. order_status is not a reliable source for return analysis; the returns table is.

recall.q: Why might nested IN be preferable to joining orders → order_items → returns here?
recall.a: IN never duplicates outer rows, so an order with two returned lines still appears once.

exercises.solution:
SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status
FROM orders
WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id
                   FROM order_items
                   WHERE order_item_id IN (SELECT order_item_id FROM returns));

exercises.title: Who buys books?
exercises.question: The Books category manager wants to email customers who bought a book in a valid order.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, email of customers who have at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) containing a product whose category is 'Books'. Use subqueries in WHERE (no joins in the outer query). Each customer once.
hints: Chain of questions: Book product_ids → order_ids containing them → valid orders' customer_ids.
Innermost: SELECT product_id FROM products WHERE category = 'Books'.
customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE <valid> AND order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE product_id IN (<Books products>)))
exercises.why: Building audience lists is a daily task for analysts in marketing. Nested IN reads like the business sentence and cannot create duplicate emails.

recall.q: In a nested IN chain, which subquery should you write and test first?
recall.a: The innermost one. Then wrap each layer and re-run.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, name, email
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
        SELECT customer_id
        FROM orders
        WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
          AND order_id IN (
                SELECT order_id
                FROM order_items
                WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM products WHERE category = 'Books')));

lessons.title: Subqueries in FROM
lessons.objective: Use a subquery as a temporary table (derived table) to aggregate in stages, filter aggregated results, and pre-aggregate before joining so rows don't fan out.
lessons.context: 'What is our average order value?' is an average of *order totals*, which first have to be built from lines. Many metrics need two levels of aggregation, and many joins need pre-aggregation to avoid double counting. Derived tables do both.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: build a table, then query it**

1. Write the inner query that produces the grain you need (one row per order, per customer...). Run it.
2. Wrap it: `FROM ( inner query ) AS t` — the alias is mandatory in most databases.
3. Query `t` like any table: aggregate again, filter with plain WHERE, or join it.
   ```sql
   SELECT ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order_value
   FROM (SELECT o.order_id, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
         FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
         WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
         GROUP BY o.order_id) AS t;
   ```
4. **Avoid fan-out:** when two child tables (orders, web_events) both hang off customers, joining both
   multiplies rows (orders × events). Aggregate each child to one row per customer *first*, then join the
   small results.
5. Every computed column inside must have an alias, because the outer query refers to it by name.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- Derived tables work identically. Snowflake also has `LATERAL` (a FROM-subquery that can reference earlier
  tables) — SQLite has no LATERAL keyword; use a correlated subquery (Lesson 23) instead.
- In Snowflake you'd often write the same thing as a CTE (Lesson 26); the optimizer treats them the same.

worked_example.question: What does the fan-out bug look like? Count customer 3's orders and web events in one join.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT 'naive join' AS method,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS distinct_orders,
       COUNT(*)                   AS joined_rows
FROM orders o
JOIN web_events w ON w.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id = 3
UNION ALL
SELECT 'pre-aggregated',
       (SELECT order_count FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
                                 FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE customer_id = 3),
       (SELECT event_count FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS event_count
                                 FROM web_events GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE customer_id = 3);
worked_example.explanation: Customer 3 has 5 orders and 29 web events. Joining both tables produces 5 × 29 = 145 rows, so any COUNT(*) or SUM over that join is inflated. Aggregating each table separately (one row per customer) and joining the results gives the true 5 and 29.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the alias after the derived table: `FROM (SELECT ...) AS t` (required in most databases).
Averaging line values when the question asks for an average per order (wrong grain).
Joining two child tables at once and summing: fan-out inflates totals. Pre-aggregate each side.
Leaving a computed column unnamed inside the derived table, so the outer query can't reference it.
Integer division in percentages: use 100.0 * a / b.
recall: What is a derived table?
A subquery in FROM, given an alias, that the outer query treats like a table.
How do you avoid fan-out when combining two child tables?
Aggregate each child to the parent's grain first, then join the aggregates.
What's the first thing to decide before writing a two-level aggregation?
The grain of each level (e.g. lines → orders → regions).
lessons.review_next: Lesson 23 lets a subquery refer to the outer row (correlated subqueries). If exercise 22.3 felt tricky, re-run the worked example and compare the 145 joined rows with the true counts.

exercises.title: Average order value
exercises.question: The CFO asks: what is our average order value (AOV)?
exercises.prompt: Build one row per valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) with its gross total (SUM(quantity * unit_price)), then return order_count (number of such orders) and avg_order_value (average of those totals, rounded to 2 decimals). Orders without lines don't count.
hints: AOV is an average of per-order totals, not of per-line values.
Inner query: one row per order with SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_total.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count, ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order_value FROM (<inner>) AS t;
exercises.why: AVG(quantity * unit_price) over lines gives the average *line* value, which is a smaller, different number. Getting the grain right is the whole job.

recall.q: Why is AVG over order lines not the AOV?
recall.a: It averages lines, not orders. Orders with many lines would be weighted more heavily.

exercises.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*)                   AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM (SELECT o.order_id,
             SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      GROUP BY o.order_id) AS t;

exercises.title: Customers who spent $1,000+
exercises.question: The VIP program wants customers whose lifetime gross spend is at least $1,000.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), aggregate per orders.customer_id in a derived table, then filter it with WHERE. Return customer_id, order_count (number of valid orders), total_spend (rounded to 2 decimals) for customers with total_spend >= 1000.
hints: Inner query: one row per customer_id with order count and spend.
Joining to order_items repeats each order once per line, so count orders with COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id).
SELECT ... FROM (SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count, SUM(i.quantity*i.unit_price) AS total_spend FROM ... GROUP BY o.customer_id) AS spend WHERE total_spend >= 1000;
exercises.why: Aggregate-then-filter with a derived table is equivalent to HAVING, but it scales better: the derived table can then be joined, ranked or filtered further.

recall.q: Give two ways to filter on an aggregated value.
recall.a: HAVING in the same query, or WHERE on a derived table/CTE that computed it.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, order_count, ROUND(total_spend, 2) AS total_spend
FROM (SELECT o.customer_id,
             COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)     AS order_count,
             SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total_spend
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      GROUP BY o.customer_id) AS spend
WHERE total_spend >= 1000;

exercises.title: Orders and web events per customer, without fan-out
exercises.question: Growth wants, for every customer, how many orders they placed and how many site events they generated.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, order_count (all orders, any status) and event_count (rows in web_events) for all 20 customers, showing 0 (not NULL) when there are none. Pre-aggregate each table in its own derived table before joining.
hints: Joining customers → orders → web_events directly multiplies orders × events per customer.
Make two small tables first: one row per customer_id with COUNT(*) from orders; same for web_events.
customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) o ... LEFT JOIN (... web_events ...) w ..., then COALESCE(..., 0).
exercises.why: Fan-out is the #1 reason dashboards overstate numbers. Pre-aggregating each child table to the parent's grain is the standard fix.

recall.q: What is fan-out?
recall.a: Row multiplication when a parent joins to two (or more) independent child tables: rows = children₁ × children₂.

exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       COALESCE(o.order_count, 0) AS order_count,
       COALESCE(w.event_count, 0) AS event_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
           FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS event_count
           FROM web_events GROUP BY customer_id) AS w
       ON w.customer_id = c.customer_id;

exercises.title: Average basket size by region
exercises.question: Ops wants to know how many units a typical valid order contains, by customer region.
exercises.prompt: First build one row per valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) with units = SUM(quantity). Then join to customers (orders whose customer doesn't exist, i.e. order 31, drop out) and return region (NULL shown as 'Unknown'), order_count and avg_units_per_order rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: Two levels: lines → orders (SUM quantity), then orders → regions (AVG).
Keep customer_id in the inner query so you can join to customers afterwards.
SELECT COALESCE(c.region,'Unknown') AS region, COUNT(*) AS order_count, ROUND(AVG(t.units),2) AS avg_units_per_order FROM (<per-order units>) t JOIN customers c ... GROUP BY 1;
exercises.why: An 'average of a sum' cannot be done in one GROUP BY. Every 'average per X of a total per Y' metric needs two levels of aggregation.

recall.q: Why can't AVG(SUM(quantity)) be written in one SELECT?
recall.a: Aggregates can't be nested in one level; compute the inner SUM per order in a derived table, then AVG it.

exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown')  AS region,
       COUNT(*)                         AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(t.units), 2)           AS avg_units_per_order
FROM (SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.quantity) AS units
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id) AS t
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
GROUP BY COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown');

exercises.title: Category share of revenue
exercises.question: The board deck needs each category's share of total revenue.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return category (NULL → 'Uncategorized'), category_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) and pct_of_total = 100 * category revenue / total gross revenue, rounded to 1 decimal. Compute the total in its own derived table.
hints: Two derived tables: revenue per category (several rows) and total revenue (one row).
A one-row table can be attached to every row with CROSS JOIN.
FROM (<category revenue>) cr CROSS JOIN (<total revenue>) tot, then 100.0 * cr.revenue / tot.revenue.
exercises.why: Share-of-total is everywhere: mix reports, market share, contribution analysis. (Lesson 31's window functions offer SUM(...) OVER () as a shortcut.)

recall.q: Why multiply by 100.0 rather than 100 when computing a percentage?
recall.a: To force decimal arithmetic. Integer / integer truncates in SQLite (and many databases).

exercises.solution:
SELECT cr.category,
       ROUND(cr.revenue, 2)                     AS category_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * cr.revenue / tot.revenue, 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM (SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
             SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)        AS revenue
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      JOIN products    AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized')) AS cr
CROSS JOIN
     (SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')) AS tot;

exercises.title: Each customer's biggest order
exercises.question: Account managers want each customer's single largest valid order.
exercises.prompt: Using valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and order_total = SUM(quantity * unit_price), return customer_id (orders.customer_id, so the orphan 99 is included), order_id and order_total (rounded to 2 decimals) for the order with the highest total per customer. Join a derived table of order totals to a derived table of each customer's maximum.
hints: Step 1: order totals (one row per order). Step 2: max total per customer (built from step 1).
Join step 1 to step 2 on customer_id AND order_total = max_total.
FROM (<order totals>) t JOIN (SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_total) AS max_total FROM (<order totals>) GROUP BY customer_id) m ON m.customer_id = t.customer_id AND m.max_total = t.order_total
exercises.why: 'The row with the max per group' is a classic pattern. Notice the order-totals query is written twice. That repetition is exactly what CTEs (Lesson 26) and ROW_NUMBER (Lesson 30) remove.

recall.q: Why can't you just SELECT customer_id, order_id, MAX(order_total) ... GROUP BY customer_id?
recall.a: order_id is neither grouped nor aggregated. Standard SQL and Snowflake reject it. SQLite accepts it (taking order_id from the MAX row), but that is a non-portable quirk, and ties make it arbitrary.

exercises.snowflake: In Snowflake: SELECT ... FROM order_totals QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_total DESC) = 1.
exercises.solution:
SELECT t.customer_id,
       t.order_id,
       ROUND(t.order_total, 2) AS order_total
FROM (SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id) AS t
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_total) AS max_total
      FROM (SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
            FROM orders AS o
            JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
            WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
            GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id)
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS m
  ON m.customer_id = t.customer_id
 AND m.max_total   = t.order_total;

/* Snowflake notes:
In Snowflake: SELECT ... FROM order_totals QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY order_total DESC) = 1.
*/

lessons.title: Correlated subqueries
lessons.objective: Write subqueries that reference the current outer row, so you can compare each row with its own group (its category, its customer) or compute a per-row lookup.
lessons.context: 'Is this product expensive *for its category*?', 'When did *this* customer last order?', 'Which of *this* customer's orders was the latest?'. Each needs a calculation that depends on the row being looked at. Correlated subqueries express that directly.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: a subquery that 'looks back' at the outer row**

1. Alias the outer table (`FROM products AS p`) and the inner table differently (`products AS p2`).
2. Inside the subquery, tie it to the outer row: `WHERE p2.category = p.category`.
3. Conceptually the subquery is re-run for every outer row (optimizers often rewrite it as a join).
   ```sql
   SELECT p.product_id, p.list_price
   FROM products AS p
   WHERE p.list_price > (SELECT AVG(p2.list_price)
                         FROM products AS p2
                         WHERE p2.category = p.category);   -- ← correlation
   ```
4. Use it in **SELECT** as a per-row lookup (`(SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order_date`)
   or in **WHERE** as a per-row benchmark ("latest order per customer", "above its category average").
5. A correlated scalar subquery that finds nothing returns NULL. Wrap with COALESCE when 0 is meant.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- Snowflake supports correlated subqueries in WHERE and in SELECT, but it is stricter: correlated scalar
  subqueries in SELECT must be provably single-row (usually an aggregate), otherwise you get
  "Unsupported subquery type". Rewriting as a join to a pre-aggregated table (or a CTE) is the portable fix.
- "Latest row per group" is idiomatically `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1`.

worked_example.question: For each of the first few customers, how many orders (any status) have they placed?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM orders AS o
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS order_count
FROM customers AS c
WHERE c.customer_id IN (1, 2, 16, 18);
worked_example.explanation: For each customer row, the inner COUNT runs with c.customer_id plugged in. Customer 18 has no orders, and COUNT of nothing is 0 (whereas MAX or SUM of nothing would be NULL). No GROUP BY is needed and no rows are duplicated.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the correlation predicate, so the subquery computes a global value (same for every row).
Using the same alias inside and outside (`orders o` twice), so the correlation silently compares a column to itself.
Not handling 'no rows' → NULL for MAX/SUM lookups when 0 is intended.
Referencing a SELECT alias in WHERE of the same query; wrap it in a derived table instead.
Expecting a single 'latest' row when ties exist: the = MAX pattern returns all tied rows.
recall: What makes a subquery 'correlated'?
It references a column of the outer query, so its result depends on the current outer row.
Name two places a correlated subquery commonly appears.
In SELECT (a per-row lookup) and in WHERE (a per-row benchmark/filter).
What's a common performance-friendly rewrite of a correlated aggregate?
Pre-aggregate in a derived table/CTE and join it, or use a window function.
lessons.review_next: Lesson 24 covers EXISTS / NOT EXISTS, the correlated subquery that only asks 'is there at least one?'. Re-do 23.4 and think about how ROW_NUMBER (Lesson 30) would handle date ties.

exercises.title: Each customer's last order date
exercises.question: CRM wants every customer with the date of their most recent order.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and last_order_date (the latest order_date of any status) for all 20 customers, using a correlated subquery in SELECT. Customers without orders get NULL.
hints: The subquery goes in the SELECT list and needs a column alias.
Correlate with WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id.
(SELECT MAX(o.order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order_date
exercises.why: Per-row lookups like this feed recency metrics and churn flags. MAX over no rows returns NULL, which honestly says 'never ordered'.

recall.q: What does a correlated MAX(...) return for a customer with no orders?
recall.a: NULL.

exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       (SELECT MAX(o.order_date)
        FROM orders AS o
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order_date
FROM customers AS c;

exercises.title: Pricier than its category average
exercises.question: Pricing wants products whose list price is above the average of their own category.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name, category, list_price for products whose list_price is greater than the average list_price of products in the same category. (Product 20, with a NULL category, has no category to compare against, so it drops out.)
hints: Use two aliases of products: p (outer) and p2 (inner).
The inner AVG should only see rows WHERE p2.category = p.category.
WHERE p.list_price > (SELECT AVG(p2.list_price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category)
exercises.why: Global averages mislead: a $59 knife is expensive for Home but cheap for Electronics. Comparing within the group is the fair benchmark.

recall.q: Why does product 20 (NULL category) never appear?
recall.a: p2.category = NULL is never true, so its category average is NULL and the comparison is NULL.

exercises.solution:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category, p.list_price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.list_price > (SELECT AVG(p2.list_price)
                      FROM products AS p2
                      WHERE p2.category = p.category);

exercises.title: Lines sold below the product's typical price
exercises.question: Sales ops wants order lines where the product sold below its own average selling price.
exercises.prompt: Considering only lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return order_item_id, product_id, unit_price and avg_product_price (the average unit_price of that same product over all valid-order lines, rounded to 2 decimals) for lines whose unit_price is below that average.
hints: The benchmark depends on the row's product, so correlate on i2.product_id = i.product_id.
Compute the average in SELECT, then filter it in an outer query (or repeat it in WHERE). Compare against the unrounded average.

SELECT ... FROM (SELECT i.order_item_id, i.product_id, i.unit_price, (SELECT AVG(i2.unit_price) FROM order_items i2 JOIN orders o2 ... WHERE <valid> AND i2.product_id = i.product_id) AS avg ... FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ... WHERE <valid>) x WHERE x.unit_price < x.avg
exercises.why: Discount leakage analysis starts exactly like this: compare every transaction with its own product's norm, not with a global number.

recall.q: Can you reference a SELECT-list alias in the same query's WHERE?
recall.a: No. WHERE runs before SELECT. Wrap the query in a derived table (or repeat the expression).

exercises.solution:
SELECT x.order_item_id, x.product_id, x.unit_price, x.avg_product_price
FROM (SELECT i.order_item_id,
             i.product_id,
             i.unit_price,
             ROUND((SELECT AVG(i2.unit_price)
                    FROM order_items AS i2
                    JOIN orders AS o2 ON o2.order_id = i2.order_id
                    WHERE o2.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                      AND i2.product_id = i.product_id), 2) AS avg_product_price,
             (SELECT AVG(i2.unit_price)
              FROM order_items AS i2
              JOIN orders AS o2 ON o2.order_id = i2.order_id
              WHERE o2.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                AND i2.product_id = i.product_id) AS raw_avg
      FROM order_items AS i
      JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')) AS x
WHERE x.unit_price < x.raw_avg;
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT x.order_item_id, x.product_id, x.unit_price, ROUND(x.raw_avg, 2) AS avg_product_price
FROM (SELECT i.order_item_id,
             i.product_id,
             i.unit_price,
             AVG(i.unit_price) OVER (PARTITION BY i.product_id) AS raw_avg
      FROM order_items AS i
      JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')) AS x
WHERE x.unit_price < x.raw_avg;
exercises.sf_note: unit_price is an exact NUMBER(…,2) in Snowflake, so AVG is exact and an average of 40.075 rounds to 40.08, while SQLite's floating-point average (40.07499…) rounds to 40.07. The grader accepts either (one cent of rounding slack). A window AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) is the idiomatic replacement for the correlated subquery.

exercises.title: Latest order per customer
exercises.question: Support wants the full details of each customer's most recent order.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, order_id, order_date, order_status for each order whose order_date equals the latest order_date for that same customer_id (any status). Use orders only, so the orphan customer 99 appears too.
hints: Keep an order if no later order exists for the same customer, i.e. its date is the customer's max.
Inner: SELECT MAX(o2.order_date) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id.
WHERE o.order_date = (SELECT MAX(o2.order_date) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
exercises.why: Latest-record-per-entity is one of the most common queries in analytics (latest status, latest address, latest price). If two orders tied on date, both would be returned, so decide whether that's OK.

recall.q: What happens with this pattern if a customer has two orders on the same latest date?
recall.a: Both rows are returned. Add a tie-breaker (e.g. ROW_NUMBER with order_id) if exactly one is needed.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT * FROM orders QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;

exercises.title: Order sequence number per customer
exercises.question: Lifecycle marketing wants to know whether each valid order was the customer's 1st, 2nd, 3rd... purchase.
exercises.prompt: For each valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) return order_id, customer_id, order_date and order_seq = the number of valid orders by the same customer_id with an order_date on or before this one (so the first valid order is 1).
hints: Count the customer's valid orders that happened up to and including this order's date.
Both the outer query and the inner COUNT need the valid-status filter.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND <valid> AND o2.order_date <= o.order_date) AS order_seq
exercises.why: First-vs-repeat purchase flags drive retention reporting. This is a 'running count'. Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, Lesson 30) do it faster, but the logic is the same.

recall.q: What is the window-function equivalent of this correlated running count?
recall.a: ROW_NUMBER() (or COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date).

exercises.solution:
SELECT o.order_id,
       o.customer_id,
       o.order_date,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM orders AS o2
        WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
          AND o2.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
          AND o2.order_date <= o.order_date) AS order_seq
FROM orders AS o
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned');

exercises.title: Customers whose spend grew in 2025
exercises.question: The account team wants customers who spent more in 2025 than in 2024.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return customer_id, name, spend_2024 and spend_2025 (by order_date year, 0 when none, rounded to 2 decimals) for customers in the customers table whose spend_2025 is greater than spend_2024. Compute each year's spend with a correlated subquery.
hints: Two correlated SUM subqueries in SELECT, one per year. Each correlated on customer_id.
SUM over no rows is NULL, so wrap each in COALESCE(..., 0) or NULL > x fails silently.
Wrap the per-customer query as a derived table s, then WHERE spend_2025 > spend_2024.
exercises.why: Growth lists are core account-management inputs. Customers who only appeared in 2025 (e.g. 14, 15, 17) count as growth because their 2024 spend is 0, not NULL. That only works because of COALESCE.

recall.q: Why COALESCE the correlated SUMs before comparing them?
recall.a: SUM over no rows is NULL, and NULL > 0 is not TRUE, so new customers would vanish.

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, name, ROUND(spend_2024, 2) AS spend_2024, ROUND(spend_2025, 2) AS spend_2025
FROM (SELECT c.customer_id,
             c.name,
             COALESCE((SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)
                       FROM orders AS o
                       JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
                       WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                         AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                         AND strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024'), 0) AS spend_2024,
             COALESCE((SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)
                       FROM orders AS o
                       JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
                       WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                         AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                         AND strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2025'), 0) AS spend_2025
      FROM customers AS c) AS s
WHERE spend_2025 > spend_2024;
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT customer_id, name, ROUND(spend_2024, 2) AS spend_2024, ROUND(spend_2025, 2) AS spend_2025
FROM (SELECT c.customer_id,
             c.name,
             COALESCE((SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)
                       FROM orders AS o
                       JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
                       WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                         AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                         AND YEAR(o.order_date) = 2024), 0) AS spend_2024,
             COALESCE((SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)
                       FROM orders AS o
                       JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
                       WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                         AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                         AND YEAR(o.order_date) = 2025), 0) AS spend_2025
      FROM customers AS c) AS s
WHERE spend_2025 > spend_2024;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): filter the year with YEAR(o.order_date) = 2024.

lessons.title: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
lessons.objective: Test whether related rows exist (or don't) with EXISTS / NOT EXISTS. They are NULL-safe, duplicate-free and the standard tool for anti-joins and data-quality checks.
lessons.context: Data quality and lifecycle questions are existence questions: customers who never ordered, orders without items, orders pointing to missing customers, suppliers with no products. EXISTS answers them cleanly, without NOT IN's NULL trap or a LEFT JOIN's duplicates.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: 'is there at least one matching row?'**

1. Start from the entity you want to return: `SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers AS c`.
2. Add `WHERE [NOT] EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id [AND ...extra conditions])`.
3. The SELECT list inside doesn't matter (`SELECT 1` is the convention). Only whether a row exists matters.
   ```sql
   SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
   FROM customers AS c
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
   ```
4. **NULL-safe:** a NULL in the inner table just doesn't match, so NOT EXISTS never collapses to "no rows"
   the way NOT IN does.
5. **No duplicates:** each outer row is kept at most once, however many matches exist (unlike a JOIN).
6. Combine freely: `EXISTS (...) AND NOT EXISTS (...)` = "did X but never did Y".
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- EXISTS / NOT EXISTS are identical in Snowflake and are usually optimised into semi-joins / anti-joins.
