- Snowflake has no `LEFT ANTI JOIN` keyword (Spark does). Write NOT EXISTS, or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL.

worked_example.question: Which products have been sold in a cancelled order?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products AS p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_items AS i
              JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
              WHERE i.product_id = p.product_id
                AND o.order_status = 'cancelled')
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: The inner query can join and filter like any query. It is correlated on product_id. Each product appears once even if it was in several cancelled orders.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the correlation (`WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id`): EXISTS becomes true for every row (or false for all).
Using NOT IN when the inner column can be NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS.
Replacing EXISTS with a JOIN and getting duplicates of the outer rows.
Putting conditions (status, date) outside the subquery when they describe the inner rows.
Inner-joining orders to customers in a revenue report and silently losing orphan order 31.
recall: What's the difference between a semi-join and an anti-join?
Semi-join keeps outer rows WITH a match (EXISTS); anti-join keeps those WITHOUT (NOT EXISTS).
Why is EXISTS often preferred to IN for big tables?
It can stop at the first match, and NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe; optimizers handle both well.
Give two data-quality checks you can write with NOT EXISTS.
Orders without items; orders whose customer doesn't exist (orphans).
lessons.review_next: Lesson 25 combines whole result sets with UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT, which is another way to express 'in A but not B'. Compare 24.6 with an EXCEPT version.

exercises.title: Customers who have ordered
exercises.question: How many of our customers have placed any order at all, and who are they?
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name for customers with at least one order of any status, using EXISTS.
hints: The outer table is customers; the inner one is orders.
Correlate inside: WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id.
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
exercises.why: A semi-join keeps each customer once. A plain JOIN would return customer 1 nine times.

recall.q: Does the SELECT list inside EXISTS matter?
recall.a: No. Only whether at least one row exists. SELECT 1 is convention.

exercises.title: Customers who never ordered
exercises.question: Marketing wants a welcome-offer list of signed-up customers who have never ordered.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, signup_date for customers with no orders of any status, using NOT EXISTS.
hints: Same as the previous exercise, with NOT.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE ...)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.signup_date FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
exercises.why: Customers 18, 19 and 20 are the activation audience. Note that 19 ('alice johnson') may be a duplicate of customer 1, which is worth flagging before you email them.

recall.q: Name three ways to find customers with no orders.
recall.a: NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.order_id IS NULL, and NOT IN (with a NULL-free subquery).

exercises.title: Orders with no line items
exercises.question: Data engineering wants to catch order headers that have no lines.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, order_date, order_status for orders that have no rows in order_items.
hints: Outer: orders. Inner: order_items.
Correlate on order_id.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i WHERE i.order_id = o.order_id)
exercises.why: Header-without-lines rows inflate order counts while adding no revenue, which drags AOV down. Order 60 is pending, so it may simply be mid-checkout, but it should be monitored.

recall.q: Is an order with no items counted by COUNT(*) FROM orders?
recall.a: Yes, which is why such orphans distort per-order metrics.

exercises.title: Orphan orders (customer missing)
exercises.question: Finance found revenue that doesn't tie to any customer. Which orders point to a non-existent customer?
exercises.prompt: Return order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_status for orders whose customer_id has no matching row in customers.
hints: This time the outer table is orders and the inner one is customers.
Referential-integrity check: does a parent row exist for this child?
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
exercises.why: Order 31 (customer 99) is a completed order worth $363.30 that disappears from any report that inner-joins orders to customers. Orphan checks belong in every data-quality suite.

recall.q: Which report numbers change when orphan orders exist?
recall.a: Any revenue joined through customers (by region, by segment) is lower than the total from orders alone.

exercises.title: Suppliers with no products (NULL-safe)
exercises.question: Procurement asks again: which suppliers supply none of our products? This time, no traps.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id, supplier_name for suppliers with no product in products, using NOT EXISTS (products.supplier_id contains a NULL; NOT EXISTS is unaffected).
hints: Compare with exercise 21.4, where NOT IN returned nothing.
The NULL supplier_id row simply never matches p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id, so no harm done.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id)
exercises.why: This is the habit to keep: reach for NOT EXISTS for anti-joins and you never hit the NOT IN NULL bug.

recall.q: Why is NOT EXISTS NULL-safe while NOT IN is not?
recall.a: NOT EXISTS only asks whether a matching row exists; a NULL just fails to match. NOT IN compares against every value, and a comparison with NULL makes the whole test unknown.

exercises.title: First-time buyers in 2025
exercises.question: Growth wants customers whose first valid purchase happened in 2025, i.e. they bought in 2025 but never in 2024.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name for customers who have at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) dated in 2025 and no valid order dated in 2024. Customer 16, whose only order was cancelled, must not appear.
hints: Two existence tests on the same customer: EXISTS for 2025, NOT EXISTS for 2024.
Put the status and date filters inside each subquery.
WHERE EXISTS (... <valid> AND order_date in 2025) AND NOT EXISTS (... <valid> AND order_date in 2024)
exercises.why: 'Did X but never Y' is the shape of acquisition, churn and cross-sell lists. Customer 13 signed up in 2024 but first bought in 2025, so signup date is not first purchase.

recall.q: How do you express 'did A but never did B' in SQL?
recall.a: WHERE EXISTS (A-subquery) AND NOT EXISTS (B-subquery).

exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-01-01')
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                    AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
                    AND o.order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2025-01-01');

exercises.title: Buyers who never needed a refund
exercises.question: The reviews team wants to invite happy customers: those with valid orders and no refunded items, ever.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name for customers who have at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and for whom no order (any status) contains an order_item that appears in returns.
hints: The NOT EXISTS subquery has to walk orders → order_items → returns.
Correlate only on the customer: WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id.
... AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON ... JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
exercises.why: The inner query of EXISTS can be as complex as you need, with joins included. The outer result still never duplicates customers.

recall.q: Can the subquery inside EXISTS contain joins?
recall.a: Yes. Any query works; only 'at least one row?' is evaluated.

exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders AS o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                AND o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned'))
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM orders AS o
                  JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
                  JOIN returns     AS r ON r.order_item_id = i.order_item_id
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);

lessons.title: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
lessons.objective: Stack and compare whole result sets: UNION ALL to append, UNION to append and de-duplicate, INTERSECT for 'in both', EXCEPT for 'in the first but not the second'.
lessons.context: Ledgers combine sales and refunds; reconciliation compares two lists of IDs; reports need a TOTAL row under the detail. Set operators work on entire result sets, matching columns by position.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: line up the columns, then pick the operator**

1. Each SELECT must return the **same number of columns**, in the **same order**, with compatible types.
   Column **names come from the first SELECT**.
2. Choose:
   - `UNION ALL`: append everything (fast, keeps duplicates). **Default choice for stacking data.**
   - `UNION`: append, then remove duplicate rows (costs a sort; can silently drop legitimate duplicates).
   - `INTERSECT`: rows present in both. `EXCEPT`: rows in the first, not in the second (distinct).
3. Label the sources with a literal column so you can tell rows apart after stacking:
   ```sql
   SELECT 'sale'   AS activity_type, order_date  AS activity_date, ... FROM ...
   UNION ALL
   SELECT 'refund' AS activity_type, return_date AS activity_date, ... FROM returns;
   ```
4. `ORDER BY` goes once, at the very end, and refers to output columns. To aggregate or sort by a hidden key,
   wrap the whole compound query in a derived table: `SELECT ... FROM ( ... UNION ALL ... ) AS t GROUP BY ...`.
5. Set operators treat NULLs as equal to each other (unlike `=`), so a NULL row in both inputs INTERSECTs.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- Snowflake supports `UNION [ALL]`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT` and its synonym **`MINUS`**.
- Snowflake also has `UNION [ALL] BY NAME`, which matches columns by name instead of position.
  SQLite has no BY NAME, so always line columns up by position.
- For a TOTAL row, Snowflake can use `GROUP BY ROLLUP(region)` instead of a hand-made UNION ALL (SQLite has no ROLLUP).

worked_example.question: Reconcile customer IDs: which IDs appear in orders but not in customers, and vice versa?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT 'in orders, not customers' AS issue, customer_id
FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM orders EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM customers)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'in customers, not orders', customer_id
FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
ORDER BY issue, customer_id;
worked_example.explanation: Each EXCEPT returns distinct IDs from one side that are missing on the other. Wrapping them lets us add a label, and UNION ALL stacks the two findings. Order 31's customer 99 shows up on one side, and the three never-ordered customers on the other.

common_mistakes: Using UNION when you meant UNION ALL, which silently drops duplicate rows (and is slower).
Mismatched column order: SQL matches by position, not name, so 'amount' can land under 'year'.
Putting ORDER BY inside each branch; it belongs once, at the end (or wrap in a derived table).
Forgetting a label column, so you can't tell which source a stacked row came from.
Adding a varying column to INTERSECT/EXCEPT selects, which changes what counts as 'the same row'.
recall: Which set operator keeps duplicates?
UNION ALL (and only it).
What must be true of the SELECTs combined by a set operator?
Same number of columns, in compatible types, in the same order.
How do set operators treat NULLs?
As equal to each other (unlike =), so NULL rows can match in INTERSECT/EXCEPT/UNION de-duplication.
lessons.review_next: Lesson 26 introduces CTEs, which let you name the pieces you've been nesting. Look back at 22.6, where the order-totals query was written twice, and imagine naming it once.

exercises.title: Every customer ID we know about
exercises.question: Data governance wants the complete set of customer IDs referenced anywhere: the customer table or orders.
exercises.prompt: Return a single column customer_id with each distinct customer_id that appears in customers or in orders (each value once).
hints: You want distinct values from two sources, so UNION (not UNION ALL).
Both SELECTs return one column, customer_id.
SELECT customer_id FROM customers UNION SELECT customer_id FROM orders;
exercises.why: The result has 21 IDs. The extra one (99) is the orphan. Building a master key list with UNION is the first step of any reconciliation.

recall.q: What does UNION do that UNION ALL doesn't?
recall.a: It removes duplicate rows from the combined result (at the cost of a sort/hash).

exercises.title: Bought in both years
exercises.question: Retention wants the customers who made valid purchases in both 2024 and 2025.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id (from orders) for customers with at least one valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) dated in 2024 and at least one dated in 2025. Use INTERSECT.
hints: Two lists of customer_ids: 2024 buyers and 2025 buyers.
INTERSECT keeps values present in both lists (de-duplicated).
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE <valid> AND <2024> INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE <valid> AND <2025>;
exercises.why: Cross-period retention is a set intersection. INTERSECT states it directly, and it de-duplicates customers with several orders per year.

recall.q: Rewrite A INTERSECT B with EXISTS.
recall.a: SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM A WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.key = A.key).

exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
  AND strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2024'
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
  AND strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2025';
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
  AND YEAR(order_date) = 2024
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
  AND YEAR(order_date) = 2025;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): filter the year with YEAR(order_date) = 2024.

exercises.title: Catalog items with no valid sale
exercises.question: Which catalog products have never been part of a valid order?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id for products in the catalog EXCEPT those that appear on a line of a valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded).
hints: First set: all product_ids. Second set: product_ids sold in valid orders.
EXCEPT returns rows of the first set that are not in the second.
SELECT product_id FROM products EXCEPT SELECT i.product_id FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ... WHERE <valid>;
exercises.why: Unlike NOT IN, EXCEPT is NULL-safe (NULLs compare equal in set operations). It's a clean way to diff two ID lists.

recall.q: What is Snowflake's synonym for EXCEPT?
recall.a: MINUS.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT product_id FROM products MINUS SELECT ...;

exercises.title: Sales and refunds ledger by year
exercises.question: Accounting wants sales and refunds as separate ledger lines per calendar year.
exercises.prompt: Return activity_year, activity_type and amount. Stack (UNION ALL) two summaries: activity_type 'sale' with amount = gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), by year of order_date; and activity_type 'refund' with amount = -SUM(refund_amount) (negative), by year of return_date. Round amount to 2 decimals.
hints: Write the two grouped queries separately, each returning (year, label, amount).
Column names come from the first SELECT; the second just needs matching positions.

SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS activity_year, 'sale' AS activity_type, ROUND(SUM(...),2) AS amount ... GROUP BY ... UNION ALL SELECT strftime('%Y', r.return_date), 'refund', ROUND(-SUM(r.refund_amount),2) FROM returns r GROUP BY ...;
exercises.why: Ledgers, event logs and activity feeds are built by stacking differently shaped sources into one shape. The literal label column is what keeps them distinguishable.

recall.q: Where do the output column names of a UNION ALL come from?
recall.a: From the first SELECT.

exercises.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date)          AS activity_year,
       'sale'                                  AS activity_type,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS amount
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY strftime('%Y', o.order_date)
UNION ALL
SELECT strftime('%Y', r.return_date),
       'refund',
       ROUND(-SUM(r.refund_amount), 2)
FROM returns AS r
GROUP BY strftime('%Y', r.return_date);
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT YEAR(o.order_date)                     AS activity_year,
       'sale'                                  AS activity_type,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS amount
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
GROUP BY YEAR(o.order_date)
UNION ALL
SELECT YEAR(r.return_date),
       'refund',
       ROUND(-SUM(r.refund_amount), 2)
FROM returns AS r
GROUP BY YEAR(r.return_date);
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): use YEAR(order_date) / YEAR(return_date) (or TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY')) for the year.

exercises.title: Net cash by year
exercises.question: Now finance wants a single net number per year: sales minus refunds (cash basis).
exercises.prompt: Return activity_year and net_amount, where net_amount = gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) (by order_date year) minus refund_amount (by return_date year), rounded to 2 decimals. Stack line-level sales and negative refunds with UNION ALL inside a derived table, then GROUP BY year.
hints: Make one tall table of (year, signed amount), then aggregate it.
Use UNION ALL, not UNION: two identical line amounts in the same year must both count.
SELECT activity_year, ROUND(SUM(amount),2) AS net_amount FROM (<sales lines> UNION ALL SELECT strftime('%Y', return_date), -refund_amount FROM returns) AS ledger GROUP BY activity_year;
exercises.why: With UNION instead of UNION ALL, identical (year, amount) rows would be collapsed and revenue silently under-stated. Line 150 duplicates line 96 (same order, same 96.90), and several unrelated lines share amounts too.

recall.q: Why is UNION (without ALL) dangerous when stacking amounts?
recall.a: It removes duplicate rows, so legitimately equal amounts get dropped.

exercises.solution:
SELECT activity_year,
       ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS net_amount
FROM (SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS activity_year,
             i.quantity * i.unit_price    AS amount
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      UNION ALL
      SELECT strftime('%Y', return_date), -refund_amount
      FROM returns) AS ledger
GROUP BY activity_year;
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT activity_year,
       ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS net_amount
FROM (SELECT YEAR(o.order_date)         AS activity_year,
             i.quantity * i.unit_price  AS amount
      FROM orders AS o
      JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      UNION ALL
      SELECT YEAR(return_date), -refund_amount
      FROM returns) AS ledger
GROUP BY activity_year;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): use YEAR(order_date) / YEAR(return_date) for the year.

exercises.title: Region report with a TOTAL row
exercises.question: The regional summary should end with a TOTAL line, like the spreadsheet it replaces.
exercises.prompt: Return region and customer_count: one row per region (NULL region shown as 'Unknown') with its number of customers, plus a final row with region = 'TOTAL' and the count of all customers. Sort region rows alphabetically, with TOTAL last.
hints: Detail rows (GROUP BY region) UNION ALL one total row.
To sort by a hidden key (TOTAL last), wrap the compound query in a derived table.
SELECT region, customer_count FROM (<detail> UNION ALL SELECT 'TOTAL', COUNT(*) FROM customers) t ORDER BY CASE WHEN region = 'TOTAL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, region;
exercises.why: Subtotal/total rows are a staple of finance reports. In Snowflake you would use GROUP BY ROLLUP; in portable SQL, UNION ALL plus a sort key does the job.

recall.q: Where may ORDER BY appear in a compound (UNION) query?
recall.a: Only once, at the end, applying to the whole combined result.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT COALESCE(region, 'Unknown'), COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY ROLLUP (COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')); (the rollup row has a NULL region; label it with GROUPING()).
exercises.solution:
SELECT region, customer_count
FROM (SELECT COALESCE(region, 'Unknown') AS region, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
      FROM customers
      GROUP BY COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'TOTAL', COUNT(*)
      FROM customers) AS t
ORDER BY CASE WHEN region = 'TOTAL' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, region;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT COALESCE(region, 'Unknown'), COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY ROLLUP
(COALESCE(region, 'Unknown')); (the rollup row has a NULL region; label it with
GROUPING()).
*/

exercises.title: Products popular in both North and South
exercises.question: Merchandising wants products that sell in both the North and South regions to plan a joint promotion.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name for products that appear in a valid order (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) placed by a North-region customer AND in a valid order placed by a South-region customer. Use INTERSECT.
hints: Two queries with identical shape (product_id, product_name), differing only in region.
Each needs products → order_items → orders → customers joins.
<North query> INTERSECT <South query>; INTERSECT compares whole rows, so both columns must match.
exercises.why: INTERSECT compares entire rows. Selecting both id and name is fine because the name is a function of the id. Adding something that varies (like order_id) would break the logic.

recall.q: Does INTERSECT compare one column or the whole row?
recall.a: The whole row: every selected column must match.

exercises.solution:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products AS p
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders      AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
JOIN customers   AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') AND c.region = 'North'
INTERSECT
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products AS p
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders      AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
JOIN customers   AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned') AND c.region = 'South';

lessons.title: CTEs
lessons.objective: Name intermediate results with WITH ... AS (...) so queries read top to bottom, can reuse a step several times, and are easy to debug one step at a time.
lessons.context: As questions get bigger, nested subqueries become unreadable. Analytics teams (and dbt models) write almost every non-trivial query as a chain of CTEs: each step has a name, a grain and one job.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: name each step**

1. Start with `WITH step_name AS ( query )`. Separate more steps with commas. Later steps can reference earlier ones.
2. Finish with one main `SELECT` that uses the steps like tables.
   ```sql
   WITH valid_orders AS (
       SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date
       FROM orders
       WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
   ),
   order_totals AS (
       SELECT v.order_id, v.customer_id, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
       FROM valid_orders v JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = v.order_id
       GROUP BY v.order_id, v.customer_id
   )
   SELECT customer_id, ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order_value
   FROM order_totals
   GROUP BY customer_id;
   ```
3. A CTE can be referenced **more than once** (e.g. compare each row with an average of the same CTE).
4. **Debug by swapping the final SELECT** for `SELECT * FROM step_name` to inspect any step.
5. Name CTEs after what one row represents (`order_totals`, `customer_spend`) and keep one grain per CTE.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- CTE syntax is identical in Snowflake. Snowflake also lets the final SELECT use `QUALIFY` on a CTE,
  which often removes one CTE layer (filtering on ROW_NUMBER directly).
- dbt models are essentially CTE chains: `import` CTEs (`with orders as (select * from {{ ref('orders') }})`),
  logic CTEs, then `select * from final`.

worked_example.question: What is the average valid order value per year?
worked_example.sql:
WITH valid_orders AS (
    SELECT order_id, order_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT v.order_id,
           strftime('%Y', v.order_date)   AS order_year,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
    FROM valid_orders AS v
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = v.order_id
    GROUP BY v.order_id, order_year
)
SELECT order_year,
       COUNT(*)                   AS orders,
       ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM order_totals
GROUP BY order_year;
worked_example.explanation: Same logic as a derived table, but it reads in execution order: filter → per-order totals → per-year average. Each CTE can be run on its own while debugging.

common_mistakes: A comma after the last CTE, or a missing comma between CTEs.
Putting a semicolon after a CTE body: the WITH and the final SELECT are one statement.
Referencing a CTE defined *later* in the list (order matters, except in recursive CTEs).
Mixing grains in one CTE (lines and orders), then aggregating the wrong one.
Assuming a CTE is computed once and cached: some engines inline it each time it's referenced (fine for correctness, but matters for cost).
recall: Name two advantages of CTEs over nested derived tables.
Readability (top-to-bottom steps) and reuse (reference the same step multiple times); also easy debugging.
How do you debug a long CTE chain?
Replace the final SELECT with SELECT * FROM <some_cte> to inspect that step.
Does a CTE exist after the query finishes?
No. It's scoped to that single statement (unlike a view or temp table).
lessons.review_next: Lesson 27 chains 3–5 CTEs into full analytical pipelines (base → enrich → aggregate → final). Re-write exercise 22.6 with a CTE before moving on.

exercises.title: Valid orders per customer
exercises.question: Rewrite the classic: how many valid orders has each customer_id placed?
exercises.prompt: Define a CTE valid_orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), then return customer_id and valid_order_count for every customer_id that appears in it (orders.customer_id, so 99 is included).
hints: WITH valid_orders AS (SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE ...) then SELECT ... FROM valid_orders.
No comma after the last CTE, and no semicolon inside the WITH.
WITH valid_orders AS (SELECT order_id, customer_id FROM orders WHERE <valid>) SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS valid_order_count FROM valid_orders GROUP BY customer_id;
exercises.why: A 'valid_orders' CTE defines the business rule once, and every later step inherits it. That single definition stops revenue numbers drifting between reports.

recall.q: What keyword introduces a CTE?
recall.a: WITH name AS ( query ).

exercises.solution:
WITH valid_orders AS (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
)
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS valid_order_count
FROM valid_orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

exercises.title: Customer spend for every customer
exercises.question: CRM wants every customer (buyers or not) with lifetime gross spend.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), build a CTE customer_spend (one row per customer_id), then return customer_id, name, total_spend (rounded to 2 decimals, 0 when no valid orders) for all 20 customers.
hints: Aggregate in the CTE; join customers to it in the final SELECT.
LEFT JOIN from customers so non-buyers stay, then COALESCE(…, 0).
... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN customer_spend s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
exercises.why: Aggregate-then-join (via a CTE) avoids fan-out and keeps the customer grain exact: 20 rows in, 20 rows out.

recall.q: Why aggregate in a CTE before joining to customers instead of joining first?
recall.a: It keeps one row per customer and avoids multiplying rows; the join then can't inflate totals.

exercises.solution:
WITH customer_spend AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total_spend
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       ROUND(COALESCE(s.total_spend, 0), 2) AS total_spend
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN customer_spend AS s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id;

exercises.title: Products earning above-average revenue
exercises.question: Which products earn more than the average product revenue?
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), build a CTE product_revenue (product_id, revenue) over sold products, and return product_id, product_name, revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) for products whose revenue is greater than the average revenue across rows of product_revenue. Reference the CTE twice.
hints: The CTE is a table you can query twice: once for rows, once for the average.
WHERE pr.revenue > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM product_revenue)

WITH product_revenue AS (SELECT i.product_id, SUM(...) AS revenue ... GROUP BY i.product_id) SELECT ... FROM product_revenue pr JOIN products p ... WHERE pr.revenue > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM product_revenue);
exercises.why: Reuse is the big win over derived tables. Without a CTE you would paste the revenue query twice and hope they stay in sync.

recall.q: Can a CTE be referenced more than once in the same query?
recall.a: Yes. That's one of its main advantages over a derived table.

exercises.solution:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT i.product_id,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY i.product_id
)
SELECT pr.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       ROUND(pr.revenue, 2) AS revenue
FROM product_revenue AS pr
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = pr.product_id
WHERE pr.revenue > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM product_revenue);

exercises.title: Best month of each year
exercises.question: For the annual review: which month had the highest revenue in each year?
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), build a CTE monthly_revenue (order_year, order_month as 'YYYY-MM', revenue). Return order_year, best_month and revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) for the month with the highest revenue in each year.
hints: Step 1 (CTE): revenue per month, keeping the year as its own column.
Step 2: keep the month whose revenue equals the max for its year (a correlated subquery on the CTE).
... FROM monthly_revenue m WHERE m.revenue = (SELECT MAX(m2.revenue) FROM monthly_revenue m2 WHERE m2.order_year = m.order_year)
exercises.why: Combining a CTE with a correlated subquery is the portable 'top-1 per group'. In Snowflake you'd write QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY order_year ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1.

recall.q: Can a correlated subquery reference a CTE?
recall.a: Yes. Inside the WITH query, a CTE behaves like any table.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT order_year, order_month AS best_month, revenue FROM monthly_revenue QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY order_year ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1;
exercises.solution:
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date)    AS order_year,
           strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS order_month,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)  AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY order_year, order_month
)
SELECT m.order_year,
       m.order_month        AS best_month,
       ROUND(m.revenue, 2)  AS revenue
FROM monthly_revenue AS m
WHERE m.revenue = (SELECT MAX(m2.revenue)
                   FROM monthly_revenue AS m2
                   WHERE m2.order_year = m.order_year);

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT order_year, order_month AS best_month, revenue FROM monthly_revenue QUALIFY
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY order_year ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1;
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT YEAR(o.order_date)                 AS order_year,
           TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'YYYY-MM')   AS order_month,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)     AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY order_year, order_month
)
SELECT order_year,
       order_month         AS best_month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2)   AS revenue
FROM monthly_revenue
QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY order_year ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake build the month with TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') and the year with YEAR(order_date) instead of strftime. The best month per year is then simply QUALIFY RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY order_year ORDER BY revenue DESC) = 1.

exercises.title: Return rate by category
exercises.question: Quality wants to know which categories have the highest share of order lines returned.
exercises.prompt: Consider lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded). Build a CTE of those lines with their category (NULL → 'Uncategorized') and a flag for whether the order_item_id appears in returns. Return category, lines_sold (number of lines), lines_returned (lines that appear in returns) and return_rate_pct = 100 * lines_returned / lines_sold rounded to 1 decimal.
hints: CTE 1: valid lines with their category. CTE 2: add an is_returned 0/1 flag.
CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM returns r WHERE r.order_item_id = v.order_item_id) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
Final: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS lines_sold, SUM(is_returned) AS lines_returned, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(is_returned) / COUNT(*), 1) AS return_rate_pct FROM flagged GROUP BY category;
exercises.why: Flag-then-aggregate (a 0/1 column, then SUM and AVG) is the cleanest way to compute rates, and each CTE can be checked on its own.

recall.q: How do you compute a rate from a 0/1 flag?
recall.a: SUM(flag) / COUNT(*) (or AVG(flag)), times 100.0 for a percentage.

exercises.solution:
WITH valid_lines AS (
    SELECT i.order_item_id,
           COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category
    FROM order_items AS i
    JOIN orders   AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
flagged AS (
    SELECT v.category,
           CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM returns AS r WHERE r.order_item_id = v.order_item_id)
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_returned
    FROM valid_lines AS v
)
SELECT category,
       COUNT(*)          AS lines_sold,
       SUM(is_returned)  AS lines_returned,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(is_returned) / COUNT(*), 1) AS return_rate_pct
FROM flagged
GROUP BY category;

exercises.title: Region revenue vs the company average
exercises.question: Sales leadership wants each region's revenue and how far it is from the average region.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and only orders whose customer exists in customers, return region (NULL → 'Unknown'), revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) and diff_from_avg = region revenue minus the average of the region revenues (rounded to 2 decimals). Use one CTE for region revenue and another for the average.
hints: CTE 1: revenue per region. CTE 2 reads CTE 1 and produces one row: the average.
Attach the one-row CTE to every region row with CROSS JOIN.

WITH region_revenue AS (...), avg_region AS (SELECT AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue FROM region_revenue) SELECT r.region, ROUND(r.revenue,2) AS revenue, ROUND(r.revenue - a.avg_revenue,2) AS diff_from_avg FROM region_revenue r CROSS JOIN avg_region a;
exercises.why: A later CTE built on an earlier one is the core move of pipeline SQL, which Lesson 27 builds on. Notice orphan order 31 is excluded by the inner join to customers, as the prompt asks.

recall.q: Can a CTE reference a CTE defined before it?
recall.a: Yes. Later CTEs can read any earlier CTE in the same WITH.

exercises.solution:
WITH region_revenue AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown')  AS region,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers   AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown')
),
avg_region AS (
    SELECT AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue FROM region_revenue
)
SELECT r.region,
       ROUND(r.revenue, 2)                 AS revenue,
       ROUND(r.revenue - a.avg_revenue, 2) AS diff_from_avg
FROM region_revenue AS r
CROSS JOIN avg_region AS a;

lessons.title: Multi-CTE analytical queries
lessons.objective: Design analytical queries as pipelines of CTEs (base → enrich → aggregate → final), keeping each step's grain explicit, so complex business metrics stay correct and reviewable.
lessons.context: Real requests combine everything: 'net revenue per customer after refunds', 'margin by product', 'new vs returning revenue', 'a region scorecard'. The way to stay correct is to build the query as a pipeline where every step is small, named and checkable.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: base → enrich → aggregate → final**

1. **base**: the business rule applied once at the lowest grain, e.g. valid order lines
   (`order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')`, line_revenue = quantity × unit_price).
2. **enrich**: join lookups at the *same grain* (product category, unit cost, refund per line, customer region).
   Check the row count didn't change. If it did, you introduced fan-out.
3. **aggregate**: roll up to the reporting grain (per customer, per product, per region...). Pre-aggregate
   independent facts separately and join them afterwards.
4. **final**: join to the dimension you report on (LEFT JOIN to keep zero rows), add ratios, labels (CASE), rounding.
   ```sql
   WITH base AS (...lines of valid orders...),
        enriched AS (SELECT b.*, COALESCE(r.refund_amount, 0) AS refund FROM base b LEFT JOIN returns r ...),
        per_customer AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(line_revenue) AS gross, SUM(refund) AS refunds ... GROUP BY customer_id)
   SELECT c.customer_id, ..., gross - refunds AS net_revenue
   FROM customers c JOIN per_customer pc ON ...;
   ```
5. Round only in the final SELECT. Rounding early compounds errors.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- This structure is exactly how dbt models are written in Snowflake: staging (base) → intermediate (enrich)
  → marts (aggregate/final).
- Snowflake shortcuts you'd use inside such pipelines: `DATEDIFF('day', last_order, '2025-12-31')`
  (SQLite: `julianday(a) - julianday(b)`), `DIV0(a, b)` for safe ratios, `IFF` for flags, `QUALIFY` for top-N per group.

worked_example.question: What were gross revenue, refunds and net revenue for the whole business?
worked_example.sql:
WITH base AS (
    SELECT i.order_item_id,
           i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_revenue
    FROM order_items AS i
    JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
enriched AS (
    SELECT b.order_item_id,
           b.line_revenue,
           COALESCE(r.refund_amount, 0) AS refund
    FROM base AS b
    LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON r.order_item_id = b.order_item_id
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                        AS lines,
       ROUND(SUM(line_revenue), 2)                     AS gross_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(refund), 2)                           AS refunds,
       ROUND(SUM(line_revenue) - SUM(refund), 2)       AS net_revenue
FROM enriched;
worked_example.explanation: base fixes the revenue rule; enriched attaches at most one refund per line (returns is 1 row per returned line), so the line count is unchanged and nothing fans out. The final step aggregates and rounds once. Net = gross − refunds.

common_mistakes: Joining a lookup that isn't 1:1 at the base grain (e.g. returns per order instead of per line) and silently inflating revenue.
Rounding inside intermediate CTEs, then summing rounded values. Round once in the final SELECT.
Average of ratios instead of ratio of sums for margin % or rates.
Inner-joining the reporting dimension in the final step and losing zero rows (suppliers/regions with no sales).
Re-stating the valid-order filter differently in two CTEs. Define it once in base and reuse it.
recall: Name the four typical stages of an analytical CTE pipeline.
base → enrich → aggregate → final.
How can you detect fan-out in an 'enrich' step?
Compare its row count with the base CTE. It should be unchanged.
Where should ratios and rounding happen?
In the final step, from aggregated sums.
lessons.review_next: Lesson 28 adds recursion: CTEs that reference themselves to walk trees and generate date spines. Re-build 27.1 from memory; it's the template for most finance pipelines.

exercises.title: Net revenue per customer
exercises.question: Finance wants gross, refunds and net revenue for every customer who bought.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded); refunds = SUM(returns.refund_amount) for those same lines; net revenue = gross − refunds. Return customer_id, name, gross_revenue, refunds, net_revenue (all rounded to 2 decimals) for customers in the customers table that have valid order lines.
hints: base: valid lines with customer_id and line_revenue. enriched: LEFT JOIN returns on order_item_id.
LEFT JOIN, because most lines have no return. COALESCE the refund to 0.
per_customer: SUM(line_revenue), SUM(refund) GROUP BY customer_id; final: JOIN customers, net = gross − refunds.
exercises.why: Net revenue is what finance actually books. Refunds attach at line grain, so enriching at line level before aggregating guarantees no double counting.

recall.q: Why join returns at the line grain rather than after aggregating per customer?
recall.a: returns references order_item_id; joining at that grain is 1:0..1, so nothing multiplies.

exercises.solution:
WITH base AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id,
           i.order_item_id,
           i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
enriched AS (
    SELECT b.customer_id,
           b.line_revenue,
           COALESCE(r.refund_amount, 0) AS refund
    FROM base AS b
    LEFT JOIN returns AS r ON r.order_item_id = b.order_item_id
),
per_customer AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           SUM(line_revenue) AS gross_revenue,
           SUM(refund)       AS refunds
    FROM enriched
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.name,
       ROUND(pc.gross_revenue, 2)              AS gross_revenue,
       ROUND(pc.refunds, 2)                    AS refunds,
       ROUND(pc.gross_revenue - pc.refunds, 2) AS net_revenue
FROM per_customer AS pc
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = pc.customer_id;

exercises.title: Product margin
exercises.question: The CFO wants gross margin by product for everything we have sold.
exercises.prompt: For lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded): revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price), total_cost = SUM(quantity * product_costs.unit_cost), gross_margin = revenue − total_cost, margin_pct = 100 * gross_margin / revenue. Return product_id, product_name, units_sold (SUM quantity), revenue, total_cost, gross_margin (each rounded to 2 decimals) and margin_pct (rounded to 1 decimal) for each sold product.
hints: base = valid lines; enrich each line with its cost (quantity × unit_cost from product_costs).
Aggregate per product, then compute margin and margin_pct in the final SELECT (not per line).
margin_pct = ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - total_cost) / revenue, 1). Compute ratios from sums, never average the per-line ratios.
exercises.why: Margin percentages must be ratio-of-sums, not average-of-ratios. Doing the division only in the final step enforces that. Margins here range from about 24% to 48%. Ask why the low end is so low.

recall.q: Ratio of sums or average of ratios for a margin %?
recall.a: Ratio of sums: SUM(margin) / SUM(revenue). Averaging line ratios weights cheap lines too much.

exercises.solution:
WITH base AS (
    SELECT i.product_id,
           i.quantity,
           i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_revenue
    FROM order_items AS i
    JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
enriched AS (
    SELECT b.product_id,
           b.quantity,
           b.line_revenue,
           b.quantity * pc.unit_cost AS line_cost
    FROM base AS b
    JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = b.product_id
),
per_product AS (
    SELECT product_id,
           SUM(quantity)     AS units_sold,
           SUM(line_revenue) AS revenue,
           SUM(line_cost)    AS total_cost
    FROM enriched
    GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT pp.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       pp.units_sold,
       ROUND(pp.revenue, 2)                                    AS revenue,
       ROUND(pp.total_cost, 2)                                 AS total_cost,
       ROUND(pp.revenue - pp.total_cost, 2)                    AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * (pp.revenue - pp.total_cost) / pp.revenue, 1) AS margin_pct
FROM per_product AS pp
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = pp.product_id;

exercises.title: New vs returning revenue by year
exercises.question: The growth team asks how much of each year's revenue came from new customers versus returning ones.
exercises.prompt: Use valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and orders.customer_id as-is (99 included). A customer's first_year is the year of their earliest valid order. An order is 'new' if its year equals the customer's first_year, else 'returning'. Return order_year, customer_type, customers (distinct customer_ids), orders (distinct orders) and revenue (SUM(quantity * unit_price), rounded to 2 decimals).
hints: Steps: valid_orders → first_year per customer → order totals → classify each order → aggregate.
first_year = MIN(order_year) per customer over valid orders; classify with CASE.
Final: GROUP BY order_year, customer_type with COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), COUNT(*), SUM(order_total).
exercises.why: New-vs-returning revenue is a board-level metric. Note that all 2024 revenue is 'new' by construction (the data starts in 2024), so be careful how you present that.

recall.q: Why compute order totals before classifying instead of classifying lines?
recall.a: It keeps one row per order so COUNT(*) counts orders; the classification is an order attribute anyway.

exercises.solution:
WITH valid_orders AS (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, strftime('%Y', order_date) AS order_year
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
first_year AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_year) AS first_year
    FROM valid_orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT v.order_id, v.customer_id, v.order_year,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
    FROM valid_orders AS v
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = v.order_id
    GROUP BY v.order_id, v.customer_id, v.order_year
),
classified AS (
    SELECT t.*,
           CASE WHEN t.order_year = f.first_year THEN 'new' ELSE 'returning' END AS customer_type
    FROM order_totals AS t
    JOIN first_year AS f ON f.customer_id = t.customer_id
)
SELECT order_year,
       customer_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       COUNT(*)                    AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2)  AS revenue
FROM classified
GROUP BY order_year, customer_type;
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH valid_orders AS (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, YEAR(order_date) AS order_year
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
),
first_year AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_year) AS first_year
    FROM valid_orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT v.order_id, v.customer_id, v.order_year,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
    FROM valid_orders AS v
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = v.order_id
    GROUP BY v.order_id, v.customer_id, v.order_year
),
classified AS (
    SELECT t.*,
           IFF(t.order_year = f.first_year, 'new', 'returning') AS customer_type
    FROM order_totals AS t
    JOIN first_year AS f ON f.customer_id = t.customer_id
)
SELECT order_year,
       customer_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       COUNT(*)                    AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2)  AS revenue
FROM classified
GROUP BY order_year, customer_type;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no strftime(): use YEAR(order_date) for the order year.

exercises.title: Region scorecard
exercises.question: Sales leadership wants one scorecard row per region: customers, active customers, revenue and revenue per active customer.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return region (NULL → 'Unknown'), customers (all customers in that region), active_customers (customers with ≥1 valid order line), revenue (rounded to 2 decimals, 0 if none) and revenue_per_active (revenue / active_customers rounded to 2 decimals; NULL if no active customers). The orphan order 31 has no region and is excluded.
hints: Aggregate revenue per customer first; then LEFT JOIN from customers so inactive customers count in 'customers'.
COUNT(revenue) counts only customers with a non-NULL revenue, i.e. the active ones.
Guard the division with CASE WHEN active_customers > 0 THEN revenue / active_customers END.
exercises.why: Scorecards mix denominators (all customers vs active ones). Keeping them as separate, named columns in a per_region CTE makes each one auditable.

recall.q: What does COUNT(column) count, versus COUNT(*)?
recall.a: COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(*) counts rows.

exercises.snowflake: DIV0(revenue, active_customers) returns 0 instead of erroring on division by zero; DIV0NULL also returns 0 when the divisor is NULL.
exercises.solution:
WITH customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY o.customer_id
),
customer_enriched AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown') AS region,
           c.customer_id,
           cr.revenue
    FROM customers AS c
    LEFT JOIN customer_revenue AS cr ON cr.customer_id = c.customer_id
),
per_region AS (
    SELECT region,
           COUNT(*)                     AS customers,
           COUNT(revenue)               AS active_customers,
           COALESCE(SUM(revenue), 0)    AS revenue
    FROM customer_enriched
    GROUP BY region
)
SELECT region,
       customers,
       active_customers,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(CASE WHEN active_customers > 0 THEN revenue / active_customers END, 2) AS revenue_per_active
FROM per_region;

/* Snowflake notes:
DIV0(revenue, active_customers) returns 0 instead of erroring on division by zero;
DIV0NULL also returns 0 when the divisor is NULL.
*/

exercises.title: Supplier performance
exercises.question: Procurement wants every supplier, including ones with nothing sold, with how many distinct products sold and the revenue.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), return supplier_id, supplier_name, products_sold (distinct products with valid sales) and revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) for all 5 suppliers, showing 0 for both when a supplier sold nothing.
hints: Pipeline: revenue per product → roll up to supplier_id → LEFT JOIN from suppliers.
Because product_sales is one row per product, COUNT(*) per supplier = distinct products sold.
Final: suppliers s LEFT JOIN supplier_sales ss ... with COALESCE(..., 0).
exercises.why: Products 21 (supplier 9, which doesn't exist) and 22 (NULL supplier) have sales that don't land on any supplier row, so supplier revenue won't sum to total revenue. A good analyst reports that gap.

recall.q: Why might the sum of supplier revenue be less than total revenue?
recall.a: Some sold products have a NULL or non-existent supplier_id, so they don't join to any supplier.

exercises.solution:
WITH product_sales AS (
    SELECT i.product_id,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items AS i
    JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY i.product_id
),
supplier_sales AS (
    SELECT p.supplier_id,
           COUNT(*)       AS products_sold,
           SUM(ps.revenue) AS revenue
    FROM product_sales AS ps
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = ps.product_id
    GROUP BY p.supplier_id
)
SELECT s.supplier_id,
       s.supplier_name,
       COALESCE(ss.products_sold, 0)     AS products_sold,
       ROUND(COALESCE(ss.revenue, 0), 2) AS revenue
FROM suppliers AS s
LEFT JOIN supplier_sales AS ss ON ss.supplier_id = s.supplier_id;

exercises.title: RFM-lite customer segments
exercises.question: CRM wants a simple recency/frequency/monetary segmentation as of 2025-12-31.
exercises.prompt: Using gross revenue = SUM(order_items.quantity * order_items.unit_price) over the lines of valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded) and customers in the customers table with at least one valid order, return customer_id, days_since_last_order (integer days from the latest valid order_date to '2025-12-31'), order_count (valid orders), total_spend (rounded to 2 decimals) and segment: 'Champion' if days_since_last_order <= 90 and order_count >= 3; 'At risk' if days_since_last_order > 180 and total_spend >= 500; 'New' if order_count = 1; otherwise 'Regular' (test in that order).
hints: order_totals (one row per valid order) → rfm (one row per customer) → final CASE.
Days between dates in SQLite: julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(MAX(order_date)), CAST to INTEGER.
CASE WHEN days_since_last_order <= 90 AND order_count >= 3 THEN 'Champion' WHEN ... > 180 AND total_spend >= 500 THEN 'At risk' WHEN order_count = 1 THEN 'New' ELSE 'Regular' END AS segment
exercises.why: RFM is a classic CRM model, and it is CASE (Lesson 20) on top of a CTE pipeline. Always pin 'today' to the as-of date ('2025-12-31') so results are reproducible.

recall.q: Why use a fixed as-of date instead of date('now') for recency?
recall.a: So the result is reproducible and matches the data snapshot; 'now' changes every day.

exercises.snowflake: DATEDIFF('day', MAX(order_date), '2025-12-31'::date) AS days_since_last_order
exercises.solution:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date
),
rfm AS (
    SELECT t.customer_id,
           CAST(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(MAX(t.order_date)) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_last_order,
           COUNT(*)           AS order_count,
           SUM(t.order_total) AS total_spend
    FROM order_totals AS t
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
    GROUP BY t.customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id,
       days_since_last_order,
       order_count,
       ROUND(total_spend, 2) AS total_spend,
       CASE WHEN days_since_last_order <= 90 AND order_count >= 3 THEN 'Champion'
            WHEN days_since_last_order > 180 AND total_spend >= 500 THEN 'At risk'
            WHEN order_count = 1 THEN 'New'
            ELSE 'Regular'
       END AS segment
FROM rfm;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATEDIFF('day', MAX(order_date), '2025-12-31'::date) AS days_since_last_order
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS order_total
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
    GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date
),
rfm AS (
    SELECT t.customer_id,
           DATEDIFF('day', MAX(t.order_date), '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_last_order,
           COUNT(*)           AS order_count,
           SUM(t.order_total) AS total_spend
    FROM order_totals AS t
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
    GROUP BY t.customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id,
       days_since_last_order,
       order_count,
       ROUND(total_spend, 2) AS total_spend,
       CASE WHEN days_since_last_order <= 90 AND order_count >= 3 THEN 'Champion'
            WHEN days_since_last_order > 180 AND total_spend >= 500 THEN 'At risk'
            WHEN order_count = 1 THEN 'New'
            ELSE 'Regular'
       END AS segment
FROM rfm;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no julianday(). Days between dates: DATEDIFF('day', MAX(order_date), '2025-12-31'::DATE), which is already an integer.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.objective: Write WITH RECURSIVE queries to generate sequences (numbers, days, months) and walk hierarchies (category trees) to get depth, paths and all descendants.
lessons.context: Two everyday problems need recursion. First, reports must show every month, including months with zero revenue, so you need a calendar (a 'spine') to LEFT JOIN onto. Second, the category tree (All Products → Electronics → Audio) has unknown depth, so a fixed number of self-joins won't do.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: anchor + recursive step + stop condition**

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE seq(n) AS (
    SELECT 1                 -- 1. anchor: the starting row(s)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM seq    -- 2. recursive step: build the next row from the previous one
    WHERE n < 10             -- 3. stop condition: without it the query never ends
)
SELECT n FROM seq;
```

**Walking a tree (parent → children):**
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name, 0 AS depth, category_name AS path
    FROM categories WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL                  -- root(s)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, t.depth + 1, t.path || ' > ' || c.category_name
    FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id   -- children of rows found so far
)
SELECT * FROM tree;
```

**Date spine:** anchor `SELECT date('2024-01-01') AS month_start`, step `date(month_start, '+1 month')`,
stop `WHERE month_start < '2025-12-01'`. Then `spine LEFT JOIN facts` + `COALESCE(revenue, 0)`.

Rules: anchor and recursive parts are joined with `UNION ALL`; the recursive part references the CTE **once**;
always have a stop condition (or a depth limit to defend against cycles).
lessons.snowflake_notes:
- Snowflake accepts `WITH RECURSIVE` (the RECURSIVE keyword is optional there). It also has the Oracle-style
  `CONNECT BY PRIOR category_id = parent_category_id START WITH parent_category_id IS NULL`, with
  `SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(category_name, ' > ')` and `LEVEL`.
- For number/date spines Snowflake developers usually skip recursion:
  `SELECT DATEADD('month', SEQ4(), '2024-01-01'::date) AS month_start FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 24))`.
  (Note SEQ4 can have gaps in theory; `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1` is the safe version.)
- `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)` replaces SQLite's `date(order_date, 'start of month')`.

worked_example.question: List the direct and indirect sub-categories of 'Home', with their depth below Home.
worked_example.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name, 0 AS levels_below
    FROM categories
    WHERE category_name = 'Home'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, s.levels_below + 1
    FROM categories AS c
    JOIN sub AS s ON c.parent_category_id = s.category_id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
worked_example.explanation: The anchor finds Home. Each recursive pass finds the children of the rows found in the previous pass (Kitchen, Decor). When a pass finds no new rows, recursion stops on its own, because a finite tree is its own stop condition.

common_mistakes: Missing or wrong stop condition: infinite recursion (or a spine one month too long/short; check the endpoints).
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL in the recursive CTE. It is allowed in SQLite but slower, and hides cycle bugs.
Reversing the tree join (c.category_id = t.parent_category_id walks *up* the tree, not down).
Joining facts to the spine with a mismatched key format ('2024-01-01' vs '2024-01'). Format both sides the same way.
COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(fact_column) after a LEFT JOIN onto a spine: empty periods show 1 instead of 0.
recall: What are the three parts of a recursive CTE?
Anchor member, recursive member (referencing the CTE), and a stop condition; joined with UNION ALL.
How do you make empty months appear with 0 revenue?
Generate a month spine, LEFT JOIN the aggregated facts to it, COALESCE(revenue, 0).
How do you defend against cycles in hierarchical data?
Carry a depth (or path) column and stop at a maximum depth / when the id already appears in the path.
lessons.review_next: That completes Module 3. Module 4 (Lesson 29+) introduces window functions, which replace many correlated subqueries from Lesson 23. The month spine from 28.6 returns there for running totals and month-over-month growth.

exercises.title: Count from 1 to 12
exercises.question: You need a helper list of month numbers 1–12 for a report template.
exercises.prompt: Using a recursive CTE (no tables needed), return one column month_number with the integers 1 through 12.
hints: Anchor: SELECT 1. Recursive step: previous value + 1.
The stop condition goes in the recursive part's WHERE.
WITH RECURSIVE nums(month_number) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT month_number + 1 FROM nums WHERE month_number < 12) SELECT month_number FROM nums;
exercises.why: Number generators are the building block of every spine, bucket list and test-data generator.

recall.q: What happens if a recursive CTE has no stop condition?
recall.a: It recurses forever (or until the engine's recursion limit errors out).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) AS month_number FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 12));

exercises.title: Category depth
exercises.question: The site team needs each category's depth in the navigation tree.
exercises.prompt: Return category_id, category_name and depth for all 14 categories, where the root ('All Products', parent NULL) has depth 0, its children depth 1, and so on.
hints: Anchor: the root, WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL, with depth 0.
Recursive step: categories whose parent is a row already in the CTE; depth = parent's depth + 1.
... UNION ALL SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, t.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id
exercises.why: Depth drives indentation in menus and lets you report 'at level 1' consistently, however deep the tree grows. Strength Training sits at depth 3.

recall.q: In a parent→child tree walk, what does the recursive JOIN condition look like?
recall.a: child.parent_id = cte.id (find rows whose parent was found in the previous step).

exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name, 0 AS depth
    FROM categories
    WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name, t.depth + 1
    FROM categories AS c
    JOIN tree AS t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id
)
SELECT category_id, category_name, depth FROM tree;

exercises.title: Breadcrumb paths
exercises.question: The website needs breadcrumb text like 'All Products > Sports > Fitness'.
exercises.prompt: Return category_id and path for all 14 categories, where path is the chain of category names from the root down to that category joined with ' > ' (the root's path is just 'All Products'). Sort by path.
hints: Carry a text column through the recursion and extend it at each step.
Recursive part: t.path || ' > ' || c.category_name
Anchor: SELECT category_id, category_name AS path FROM categories WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL; finish with ORDER BY path.
exercises.why: Paths make hierarchies readable in flat reports, and sorting by path lists every category directly under its parent: a tree view for free.

recall.q: How do you build a path string in a recursive CTE?
recall.a: Carry it as a column: anchor = root name; step = parent_path || ' > ' || child_name.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT category_id, SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(category_name, ' > ') FROM categories START WITH parent_category_id IS NULL CONNECT BY PRIOR category_id = parent_category_id; (path starts with the separator).
exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name AS path
    FROM categories
    WHERE parent_category_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, t.path || ' > ' || c.category_name
    FROM categories AS c
    JOIN tree AS t ON c.parent_category_id = t.category_id
)
SELECT category_id, path
FROM tree
ORDER BY path;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT category_id, SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(category_name, ' > ') FROM categories START
WITH parent_category_id IS NULL CONNECT BY PRIOR category_id = parent_category_id;
(path starts with the separator).
*/
exercises.sf_note: || concatenates text in Snowflake too (a NULL operand makes the result NULL; CONCAT_WS or CONCAT behave the same way). Snowflake also offers CONNECT BY with SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(category_name, ' > ') for hierarchies, but that path starts with the separator.

rows: All Products > Sports > Fitness > Strength Training

exercises.title: Everything under Electronics
exercises.question: A promotion applies to 'Electronics and all its sub-categories'. Which categories are in scope?
exercises.prompt: Return category_id, category_name for 'Electronics' itself and all of its descendants (children, grandchildren, ...). Start the anchor from the name 'Electronics', not a hard-coded id.
hints: Same tree walk, but the anchor is the Electronics row instead of the root.
Anchor: WHERE category_name = 'Electronics'.

WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (SELECT ... WHERE category_name = 'Electronics' UNION ALL SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name FROM categories c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_category_id = s.category_id) SELECT ... FROM sub;
exercises.why: 'X and everything below it' is the standard question for org charts, product trees and geographies. Recursion keeps working when someone adds a sub-sub-category next quarter.

recall.q: How do you change a full-tree walk into a 'subtree of X' walk?
recall.a: Change the anchor to select X instead of the root.

exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT category_id, category_name
    FROM categories
    WHERE category_name = 'Electronics'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name
    FROM categories AS c
    JOIN sub AS s ON c.parent_category_id = s.category_id
)
SELECT category_id, category_name FROM sub;

exercises.title: Descendant counts for every category
exercises.question: Navigation design wants to know how many categories sit beneath each node (at any depth).
exercises.prompt: Return category_id, category_name and descendant_count (the number of categories strictly below it at any depth; 0 for leaves) for all 14 categories.
hints: Build (ancestor_id, descendant_id) pairs: anchor = every direct parent/child pair.
Recursive step: extend each pair one level down: join categories whose parent is the pair's descendant, keeping the ancestor.
Then LEFT JOIN categories to the pairs on ancestor_id and COUNT(descendant_id) (leaves get 0).
exercises.why: An ancestor/descendant 'closure table' answers every roll-up question about a hierarchy (counts, revenue under a node) with an ordinary join and GROUP BY.

recall.q: What is a closure table?
recall.a: A table of every (ancestor, descendant) pair in a hierarchy, at any distance.

exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE closure(ancestor_id, descendant_id) AS (
    SELECT parent_category_id, category_id
    FROM categories
    WHERE parent_category_id IS NOT NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT cl.ancestor_id, c.category_id
    FROM closure AS cl
    JOIN categories AS c ON c.parent_category_id = cl.descendant_id
)
SELECT cat.category_id,
       cat.category_name,
       COUNT(cl.descendant_id) AS descendant_count
FROM categories AS cat
LEFT JOIN closure AS cl ON cl.ancestor_id = cat.category_id
GROUP BY cat.category_id, cat.category_name;

exercises.title: Monthly Books revenue with zero months
exercises.question: The Books manager's chart skips months with no sales, which makes the trend look better than it is.
exercises.prompt: Generate every month from 2024-01 to 2025-12 with a recursive CTE, then return month ('YYYY-MM') and books_revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) for products with category 'Books' on valid orders (valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); cancelled and pending are excluded), rounded to 2 decimals, showing 0 for months without Books sales. Sort by month.
hints: Spine: anchor date('2024-01-01'), step date(month_start, '+1 month'), stop at '2025-12-01'.
Aggregate Books revenue per 'YYYY-MM' in a second CTE (you can list it after the recursive one).
FROM months m LEFT JOIN books_monthly b ON b.month = strftime('%Y-%m', m.month_start), COALESCE(b.revenue, 0), ORDER BY month.
exercises.why: Eight of the 24 months have no Books sales. Without a spine they vanish from the chart and any moving average or month-over-month calculation silently skips them.

recall.q: Why LEFT JOIN facts onto a date spine instead of grouping the facts alone?
recall.a: Grouping facts only produces months that have data; the spine guarantees every month appears (with 0).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT DATEADD('month', ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1, '2024-01-01'::date) AS month_start FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 24)); then LEFT JOIN on DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) = month_start.
exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE months(month_start) AS (
    SELECT date('2024-01-01')
    UNION ALL
    SELECT date(month_start, '+1 month') FROM months
    WHERE month_start < '2025-12-01'
),
books_monthly AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date)  AS month,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)   AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products    AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      AND p.category = 'Books'
    GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date)
)
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', m.month_start)    AS month,
       ROUND(COALESCE(b.revenue, 0), 2)    AS books_revenue
FROM months AS m
LEFT JOIN books_monthly AS b ON b.month = strftime('%Y-%m', m.month_start)
ORDER BY month;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT DATEADD('month', ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1, '2024-01-01'::date)
AS month_start FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 24)); then LEFT JOIN on
DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) = month_start.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH RECURSIVE months (month_start) AS (
    SELECT '2024-01-01'::DATE
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD('month', 1, month_start) FROM months
    WHERE month_start < '2025-12-01'::DATE
),
books_monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS month_start,
           SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price)    AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products    AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped', 'returned')
      AND p.category = 'Books'
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)
)
SELECT TO_CHAR(m.month_start, 'YYYY-MM')   AS month,
       ROUND(COALESCE(b.revenue, 0), 2)    AS books_revenue
FROM months AS m
LEFT JOIN books_monthly AS b ON b.month_start = m.month_start
ORDER BY month;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no date(x, '+1 month') or strftime(). Step the spine with DATEADD('month', 1, month_start), bucket orders with DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) and format with TO_CHAR(month_start, 'YYYY-MM'). A non-recursive alternative is TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 24)) with DATEADD('month', ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1, '2024-01-01'::DATE).

exercises.title: Daily orders in December 2025
exercises.question: Ops wants a day-by-day order count for December 2025, including the quiet days.
exercises.prompt: Generate every day from 2025-12-01 to 2025-12-31 and return order_day ('YYYY-MM-DD') and orders_placed (number of orders of any status with that order_date, 0 if none). Sort by order_day.
hints: Same spine pattern with '+1 day'.
LEFT JOIN orders on order_date = order_day and COUNT(o.order_id), not COUNT(*).

WITH RECURSIVE days(order_day) AS (SELECT date('2025-12-01') UNION ALL SELECT date(order_day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE order_day < '2025-12-31') SELECT d.order_day, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_placed FROM days d LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = d.order_day GROUP BY d.order_day ORDER BY d.order_day;
exercises.why: Only 3 of 31 days have orders. Daily spines are what make 'orders per day' averages honest (3/31, not 3/3).

recall.q: After a LEFT JOIN onto a spine, why COUNT(o.order_id) and not COUNT(*)?
recall.a: COUNT(*) would count the NULL-extended row on empty days as 1; COUNT(column) gives 0.

exercises.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(order_day) AS (
    SELECT date('2025-12-01')
    UNION ALL
    SELECT date(order_day, '+1 day') FROM days
    WHERE order_day < '2025-12-31'
)
SELECT d.order_day,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_placed
FROM days AS d
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_date = d.order_day
GROUP BY d.order_day
ORDER BY d.order_day;
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH days AS (
    SELECT DATEADD('day', ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1, '2025-12-01'::DATE) AS order_day
    FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 31))
)
SELECT d.order_day,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_placed
FROM days AS d
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_date = d.order_day
GROUP BY d.order_day
ORDER BY d.order_day;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no date(x, '+1 day'). Either recurse with DATEADD('day', 1, order_day) (WITH RECURSIVE days (order_day) AS (SELECT '2025-12-01'::DATE UNION ALL ...)) or generate the 31 days directly: DATEADD('day', ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SEQ4()) - 1, '2025-12-01'::DATE) FROM TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => 31)).

lessons.title: Date functions and time-based filtering
lessons.objective: Filter rows by date ranges, pull out date parts (year, month, quarter, weekday), do date arithmetic (add/subtract days, month ends) and measure the gap between two dates in days.
lessons.context: Almost every analytics question has a time window: 'last 90 days', 'Q1', 'how long until a customer's first purchase?'. Operations and finance want these answers relative to a fixed reporting date — in this course the as-of date is always '2025-12-31' (never date('now'), so results are reproducible).
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: work with dates in 5 moves**

Dates here are ISO text `'YYYY-MM-DD'`, which sorts and compares correctly as text.

1. **Filter a range with half-open bounds**: `order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-04-01'`.
   This is safe for dates *and* timestamps (`BETWEEN ... '2025-03-31'` silently drops '2025-03-31 14:00').
2. **Extract parts** with `strftime`: `'%Y'` year, `'%m'` month, `'%d'` day, `'%w'` weekday (0 = Sunday),
   `'%Y-%m'` month label. Results are TEXT — `CAST(strftime('%m', d) AS INTEGER)` for numbers.
3. **Shift dates** with modifiers: `date(d, '-90 days')`, `date(d, '+1 month')`,
   `date(d, 'start of month')`, `date(d, 'start of month', '+1 month', '-1 day')` (= month end).
4. **Difference in days**: `julianday(later) - julianday(earlier)` (a REAL; `CAST(... AS INTEGER)` for whole days).
5. **Anchor "today"** to the as-of date: `date('2025-12-31', '-90 days')`, never `date('now')`.

```sql
SELECT order_id,
       strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)                                  AS order_month,
       CAST(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_ago
FROM   orders
WHERE  order_date >= date('2025-12-31', '-90 days');
```
lessons.snowflake_notes:
Snowflake has real DATE/TIMESTAMP types and a richer function set:

| Idea | SQLite (this course) | Snowflake |
|---|---|---|
