recall.q: What's the difference between SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY c) and SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY c ORDER BY d)?
recall.a: Without ORDER BY you get the partition total on every row; with ORDER BY the default frame makes it a running total.

exercises.solution:
WITH order_values AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS order_value
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date
),
running AS (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_value,
           SUM(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id
                                  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_spend,
           SUM(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS lifetime_spend
    FROM order_values
)
SELECT order_id,
       customer_id,
       order_date,
       ROUND(order_value, 2) AS order_value,
       ROUND(cumulative_spend, 2) AS cumulative_spend,
       ROUND(100.0 * cumulative_spend / lifetime_spend, 1) AS pct_of_lifetime
FROM running;

exercises.title: Year-to-date revenue by month
exercises.question: Finance tracks revenue YTD: the running total must reset every January.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return month ('YYYY-MM'), revenue (rounded 2) and ytd_revenue (running total of revenue within the same calendar year up to and including this month, rounded 2), for all months 2024-01…2025-12. Order by month.
hints: The running total must restart each year: that's a PARTITION BY.
The year is substr(month, 1, 4) — you can partition by an expression.
SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY substr(month,1,4) ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
exercises.why: PARTITION BY resets the running total; that one clause turns 'cumulative since launch' into 'YTD'.

recall.q: Which clause makes a running total restart each year?
recall.a: PARTITION BY year — the window never crosses partition boundaries.

exercises.snowflake: SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY YEAR(month) ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), with month = DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date).
exercises.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY substr(month, 1, 4) ORDER BY month
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS ytd_revenue
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

/* Snowflake notes:
SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY YEAR(month) ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED
PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), with month = DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date).
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'YYYY-MM')  AS month,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)  AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY LEFT(month, 4) ORDER BY month
                                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS ytd_revenue
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') for the month; SUBSTR/LEFT(month, 4) for the year.

exercises.title: 3-month moving average
exercises.question: Monthly revenue is noisy (March 2025 was tiny). The growth team wants a trailing 3-month average.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return month ('YYYY-MM'), revenue (rounded 2), moving_avg_3m (average revenue of this month and the two previous months, rounded 2 — for the first two months average whatever months exist) and months_in_window (how many months that average used: 1, 2 or 3). Order by month.
hints: A sliding frame: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
COUNT(*) over the same frame tells you how many rows were really averaged.
AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg_3m, COUNT(*) OVER (same) AS months_in_window
exercises.why: Moving averages are how trends get shown to executives. months_in_window tells readers which early values are based on less data (many dashboards blank those out).

recall.q: What does ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW include?
recall.a: The current row plus up to two rows before it in the window order — at most 3 rows.

exercises.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3m,
       COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS months_in_window
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'YYYY-MM')  AS month,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)  AS revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3m,
       COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS months_in_window
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') instead of strftime('%Y-%m', order_date). Rounding caveat: SQLite computes AVG in binary floating point, so (630.85 + 655.0) / 2 = 642.925 is stored as 642.92499... and ROUND(..., 2) gives 642.92. Snowflake NUMBER arithmetic is exact and rounds the half up to 642.93. The grader accepts either value (it allows one cent of rounding difference), so write the natural exact-decimal version.

exercises.title: ROWS vs RANGE on tied dates
exercises.question: An analyst's running total 'jumps' several lines at once. Show Q4 2025 order lines with both frame types side by side.
exercises.prompt: Take order lines of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) with order_date between '2025-10-01' and '2025-12-31'. Return order_item_id, order_id, order_date, line_revenue (quantity * unit_price, rounded 2), running_rows (running SUM of line revenue ordered by order_date, order_item_id with a ROWS frame from the first row to the current row, rounded 2) and running_range (running SUM of line revenue ordered by order_date ONLY, using RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, rounded 2). Order by order_date, order_item_id.
hints: Same SUM, two different OVER clauses.
RANGE treats all rows with the same order_date as peers: they all get the total through the end of that date.
SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY o.order_date, oi.order_item_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) vs SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY o.order_date RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
exercises.why: The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE. If your ORDER BY has ties, a 'running total' silently includes future peer rows — compare the two columns on multi-line orders.

recall.q: Two rows tie on the ORDER BY value. Under RANGE ... CURRENT ROW, does the first one include the second in its frame?
recall.a: Yes — RANGE includes all peers of the current row; ROWS stops at the physical current row.

exercises.solution:
SELECT oi.order_item_id,
       o.order_id,
       o.order_date,
       ROUND(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price, 2) AS line_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) OVER (
                 ORDER BY o.order_date, oi.order_item_id
                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_rows,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) OVER (
                 ORDER BY o.order_date
                 RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_range
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
  AND o.order_date BETWEEN '2025-10-01' AND '2025-12-31'
ORDER BY o.order_date, oi.order_item_id;

exercises.title: First and latest order value (LAST_VALUE pitfall)
exercises.question: For every order, sales wants the customer's first-ever order value and their most recent order value side by side.
exercises.prompt: Order value = SUM(quantity * unit_price) of the order's lines, valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_value (rounded 2), first_order_value (order_value of the customer's earliest valid order) and latest_order_value (order_value of the customer's most recent valid order — the same value on all of that customer's rows). Order a customer's orders by order_date then order_id.
hints: FIRST_VALUE works with the default frame (it always starts at the first row). LAST_VALUE does not.
Default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so LAST_VALUE would return the current order. Extend it to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
LAST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
exercises.why: This is the single most common window-function bug in production dashboards. An alternative that dodges it: FIRST_VALUE(...) OVER (... ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC).

recall.q: Why does LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (PARTITION BY c ORDER BY d) usually return the current row's x?
recall.a: Because with ORDER BY the default frame ends at the current row, so the 'last' row of the frame is the current one.

exercises.snowflake: Same frame fix in Snowflake; or use FIRST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC).
exercises.solution:
WITH order_values AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS order_value
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_date
)
SELECT order_id,
       customer_id,
       order_date,
       order_value,
       FIRST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS first_order_value,
       LAST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id
                                     ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS latest_order_value
FROM order_values;

/* Snowflake notes:
Same frame fix in Snowflake; or use FIRST_VALUE(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC).
*/

lessons.title: Pivoting and unpivoting
lessons.objective: Turn rows into columns with conditional aggregation (pivot) and columns back into rows with UNION ALL (unpivot) — and know Snowflake's PIVOT/UNPIVOT equivalents.
lessons.context: Stakeholders think in spreadsheets: categories down the side, years or quarters across the top. Meanwhile BI tools and joins want long, tidy data. An analyst spends a surprising amount of time going back and forth between the two shapes.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: pivot with conditional aggregation**

1. Decide the **row key** (stays in GROUP BY), the **column key** (becomes column names) and the **value**.
2. One output column per column-key value: `SUM(CASE WHEN key = 'X' THEN value ELSE 0 END) AS x_col`.
   `ELSE 0` gives 0 for empty cells; omit it (→ NULL) when "no data" must differ from "zero".
3. `GROUP BY` the row key only.
4. Counts: `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` or `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)` (SQLite & Postgres).

```sql
SELECT category,
       SUM(CASE WHEN yr = '2024' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS revenue_2024,
       SUM(CASE WHEN yr = '2025' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS revenue_2025
FROM   base
GROUP  BY category;
```

**Recipe: unpivot with UNION ALL** — one SELECT per column, each emitting (key, 'column name', value):

```sql
SELECT category, '2024' AS yr, revenue_2024 AS revenue FROM wide
UNION ALL
SELECT category, '2025',       revenue_2025            FROM wide;
```

Use `UNION ALL`, not `UNION` — UNION would de-duplicate identical rows and silently drop data.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
Snowflake has native operators — handy, but the column list must be **static** (or use `ANY`):

```sql
-- PIVOT: rows → columns
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT COALESCE(p.category,'Uncategorized') AS category,
             YEAR(o.order_date)               AS yr,
             oi.quantity * oi.unit_price      AS revenue
      FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
                    JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
      WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'))
PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR yr IN (2024, 2025)) AS pv (category, revenue_2024, revenue_2025);
-- Newer Snowflake: FOR yr IN (ANY ORDER BY yr), and DEFAULT ON NULL (0) to turn empty cells into 0.

-- UNPIVOT: columns → rows (rows whose value is NULL are dropped unless INCLUDE NULLS)
SELECT product_id, price_type, amount
FROM prices UNPIVOT (amount FOR price_type IN (list_price, unit_cost));
```

- `IFF(cond, a, b)` is Snowflake's short CASE; `COUNT_IF(cond)` counts matching rows.
- Conditional aggregation (`SUM(CASE ...)`) works identically in Snowflake and is often clearer than PIVOT
  when you need several measures per cell or computed columns like growth %.
- Note PIVOT groups by **every** non-pivoted column of its input — select only what you need in the subquery.

worked_example.question: How many valid orders did we have per year and quarter, laid out as a year × quarter grid?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS order_year,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', order_date) BETWEEN '01' AND '03' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS q1_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', order_date) BETWEEN '04' AND '06' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS q2_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', order_date) BETWEEN '07' AND '09' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS q3_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', order_date) BETWEEN '10' AND '12' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS q4_orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY strftime('%Y', order_date)
ORDER BY order_year;
worked_example.explanation: Each CASE routes a row into exactly one quarter column; summing the 1s counts them. The row key (year) is the only GROUP BY column. strftime returns text, so the month comparison is a string comparison on zero-padded months — which works.

common_mistakes: Putting the column key in GROUP BY — you get one row per (row key, column key), i.e. nothing pivoted.
Forgetting ELSE 0 and then being surprised by NULL cells (or vice versa: showing 0 where 'no data' was meant).
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL when unpivoting, silently dropping duplicate rows.
Comparing strftime text to numbers: strftime('%Y', d) = 2024 is false in SQLite — compare to '2024'.
Expecting Snowflake PIVOT to discover new values automatically: the IN list is static unless you use ANY.
recall: Write the conditional-aggregation pattern for one pivot column.
SUM(CASE WHEN column_key = 'X' THEN value ELSE 0 END) AS x_col, with GROUP BY on the row key.
How do you unpivot three columns a, b, c in portable SQL?
Three SELECTs, each emitting key, a label literal and that column, combined with UNION ALL.
What does Snowflake's UNPIVOT do with NULL values by default?
It drops those rows (use INCLUDE NULLS to keep them).
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 38 combines pivots with date math to build cohort retention tables. Re-do 37.6 in your head as a Snowflake UNPIVOT.

exercises.title: Category × year revenue grid
exercises.question: Finance wants a simple grid: categories down the side, 2024 and 2025 revenue across the top.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return category ('Uncategorized' when NULL), revenue_2024, revenue_2025 (revenue of orders dated in that year; 0 when none) and total_revenue (both years), all rounded to 2 decimals. One row per category.
hints: Row key = category, column key = year, value = line revenue.
SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024' THEN oi.quantity*oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END)
Two CASE columns + a plain SUM for the total, GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category,'Uncategorized').
exercises.why: The 'crosstab' is the most requested report shape in business. Conditional aggregation works in every SQL dialect.

recall.q: In a pivot by conditional aggregation, what goes in GROUP BY?
recall.a: Only the row key(s); the column key lives inside the CASE expressions.

exercises.snowflake: PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR yr IN (2024, 2025)) — but total_revenue still needs a separate expression, e.g. revenue_2024 + revenue_2025 in the outer SELECT.
exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024'
                      THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue_2024,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2025'
                      THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue_2025,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized');

/* Snowflake notes:
PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR yr IN (2024, 2025)) — but total_revenue still needs a separate
expression, e.g. revenue_2024 + revenue_2025 in the outer SELECT.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
           YEAR(o.order_date)                    AS order_year,
           oi.quantity * oi.unit_price           AS line_revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
)
SELECT category,
       ROUND(rev_2024, 2)            AS revenue_2024,
       ROUND(rev_2025, 2)            AS revenue_2025,
       ROUND(rev_2024 + rev_2025, 2) AS total_revenue
FROM lines
PIVOT (SUM(line_revenue) FOR order_year IN (2024, 2025) DEFAULT ON NULL (0))
    AS pv (category, rev_2024, rev_2025);
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has a native PIVOT: FROM lines PIVOT (SUM(line_revenue) FOR order_year IN (2024, 2025) DEFAULT ON NULL (0)) AS pv (category, rev_2024, rev_2025). Use YEAR(order_date) instead of strftime('%Y', ...). The CASE WHEN conditional-aggregation version also works unchanged.

exercises.title: Order status mix by year
exercises.question: Ops wants to see how the order status mix changed between years.
exercises.prompt: Using ALL orders (every status), return order_year ('YYYY' text from order_date), completed, shipped, returned, cancelled, pending (number of orders with that status in that year; 0 when none) and total_orders. Order by order_year.
hints: Counting is summing 1s: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'x' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
Or in SQLite: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE order_status = 'completed').
Five CASE columns plus COUNT(*) AS total_orders, GROUP BY strftime('%Y', order_date) ORDER BY order_year.
exercises.why: A status-by-period matrix makes operational shifts (more cancellations, stuck pending orders) visible at a glance.

recall.q: Why does SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) give 0 rather than NULL for an empty cell?
recall.a: Because every row contributes a 0 when it doesn't match, so the sum over the group is 0 (not NULL).

exercises.snowflake: COUNT_IF(order_status = 'completed') AS completed, ... GROUP BY YEAR(order_date)
exercises.solution:
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS order_year,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'shipped'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'returned'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_status = 'pending'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pending,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY strftime('%Y', order_date)
ORDER BY order_year;

/* Snowflake notes:
COUNT_IF(order_status = 'completed') AS completed, ... GROUP BY YEAR(order_date)
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY')          AS order_year,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'completed') AS completed,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'returned')  AS returned,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       COUNT_IF(order_status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       COUNT(*)                             AS total_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_year
ORDER BY order_year;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has no aggregate FILTER (WHERE ...) clause; use COUNT_IF(order_status = 'completed') (or SUM(IFF(...,1,0))). Year text: TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY') instead of strftime('%Y', ...).

exercises.title: 2025 quarterly revenue by category
exercises.question: The category review needs 2025 revenue per quarter for each category.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Restrict to orders dated in 2025. Return category ('Uncategorized' when NULL), q1_revenue, q2_revenue, q3_revenue, q4_revenue (revenue of that calendar quarter, 0 when none, rounded to 2) — one row per category that had 2025 revenue. Order by category.
hints: Filter the year in WHERE; split quarters inside CASE.
Quarter from month: strftime('%m', d) BETWEEN '01' AND '03' (or (month+2)/3 = 1).
Four SUM(CASE WHEN month BETWEEN .. THEN qty*price ELSE 0 END) columns, GROUP BY category, ORDER BY category.
exercises.why: Filters that apply to every cell belong in WHERE; conditions that differ per column belong in CASE.

recall.q: Where should a filter common to all pivot columns go — WHERE or each CASE?
recall.a: WHERE: it's simpler, faster, and keeps rows that match no column out of the group entirely.

exercises.snowflake: PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR qtr IN (1, 2, 3, 4)) with qtr = QUARTER(order_date), filtered on YEAR(order_date) = 2025.
exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) BETWEEN '01' AND '03'
                      THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q1_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) BETWEEN '04' AND '06'
                      THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q2_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) BETWEEN '07' AND '09'
                      THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q3_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%m', o.order_date) BETWEEN '10' AND '12'
                      THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS q4_revenue
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
  AND o.order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized')
ORDER BY category;

/* Snowflake notes:
PIVOT (SUM(revenue) FOR qtr IN (1, 2, 3, 4)) with qtr = QUARTER(order_date), filtered
on YEAR(order_date) = 2025.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
           QUARTER(o.order_date)                 AS qtr,
           oi.quantity * oi.unit_price           AS line_revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
      AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-01-01'
)
SELECT category,
       ROUND(q1, 2) AS q1_revenue,
       ROUND(q2, 2) AS q2_revenue,
       ROUND(q3, 2) AS q3_revenue,
       ROUND(q4, 2) AS q4_revenue
FROM lines
PIVOT (SUM(line_revenue) FOR qtr IN (1, 2, 3, 4) DEFAULT ON NULL (0)) AS pv (category, q1, q2, q3, q4)
ORDER BY category;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: QUARTER(order_date) replaces the strftime('%m', ...) BETWEEN '01' AND '03' tests, and PIVOT (SUM(line_revenue) FOR qtr IN (1, 2, 3, 4) DEFAULT ON NULL (0)) builds the four columns. There is no FILTER (WHERE ...) clause on aggregates in Snowflake; use IFF/CASE or COUNT_IF.

exercises.title: Regional growth table
exercises.question: Sales leadership wants revenue by region for 2024 and 2025 with the growth rate.
exercises.prompt: Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Attribute revenue to the customer's region (INNER JOIN customers, so the orphan order 31 is excluded; label NULL regions 'Unknown'). Return region, revenue_2024, revenue_2025 (rounded 2, 0 when none) and growth_pct (100.0 * (revenue_2025 - revenue_2024) / revenue_2024 using unrounded sums, rounded to 1 decimal; NULL when revenue_2024 is 0). Order by region.
hints: Pivot in a CTE first, then compute growth from the pivoted columns.
NULLIF(rev_2024, 0) turns a zero denominator into NULL, so the division returns NULL instead of failing.

WITH pivoted AS (SELECT COALESCE(c.region,'Unknown') AS region, SUM(CASE ... '2024' ...) AS rev_2024, SUM(CASE ... '2025' ...) AS rev_2025 ... GROUP BY 1) SELECT region, ROUND(rev_2024,2), ROUND(rev_2025,2), ROUND(100.0*(rev_2025-rev_2024)/NULLIF(rev_2024,0),1) FROM pivoted ORDER BY region;
exercises.why: Pivot-then-compute is how growth tables, variance reports and budget-vs-actual sheets are built.

recall.q: How do you avoid divide-by-zero in a growth percentage?
recall.a: Divide by NULLIF(denominator, 0) (Snowflake also has DIV0 / DIV0NULL).

exercises.snowflake: DIV0NULL(rev_2025 - rev_2024, rev_2024) * 100 returns 0 instead of NULL for zero denominators; pick deliberately.
exercises.solution:
WITH pivoted AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown') AS region,
           SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2024'
                    THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END) AS rev_2024,
           SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y', o.order_date) = '2025'
                    THEN oi.quantity * oi.unit_price ELSE 0 END) AS rev_2025
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown')
)
SELECT region,
       ROUND(rev_2024, 2) AS revenue_2024,
       ROUND(rev_2025, 2) AS revenue_2025,
       ROUND(100.0 * (rev_2025 - rev_2024) / NULLIF(rev_2024, 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM pivoted
ORDER BY region;

/* Snowflake notes:
DIV0NULL(rev_2025 - rev_2024, rev_2024) * 100 returns 0 instead of NULL for zero
denominators; pick deliberately.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH pivoted AS (
    SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unknown') AS region,
           SUM(IFF(YEAR(o.order_date) = 2024, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price, 0)) AS rev_2024,
           SUM(IFF(YEAR(o.order_date) = 2025, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price, 0)) AS rev_2025
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT region,
       ROUND(rev_2024, 2) AS revenue_2024,
       ROUND(rev_2025, 2) AS revenue_2025,
       ROUND(100 * (rev_2025 - rev_2024) / NULLIF(rev_2024, 0), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM pivoted
ORDER BY region;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: YEAR(order_date) = 2024 instead of strftime('%Y', ...) = '2024'. Keep NULLIF for a NULL result; DIV0() would return 0 instead.

exercises.title: Unpivot price and cost
exercises.question: The pricing tool wants a long table: one row per product and price type.
exercises.prompt: For products 1 to 5, unpivot the two price columns into rows. Return product_id, price_type (the text 'list_price' or 'unit_cost') and amount (products.list_price or product_costs.unit_cost). That is 2 rows per product. Order by product_id, then price_type.
hints: Unpivot = one SELECT per column you turn into rows, stacked with UNION ALL.
Each SELECT emits the key, a literal label ('list_price') and the value.

SELECT product_id, 'list_price' AS price_type, list_price AS amount FROM products WHERE ... UNION ALL SELECT product_id, 'unit_cost', unit_cost FROM product_costs WHERE ... ORDER BY product_id, price_type;
exercises.why: Long ('tidy') data is what charting tools and joins want. ORDER BY on a UNION applies to the whole combined result.

recall.q: Why UNION ALL rather than UNION for an unpivot?
recall.a: UNION removes duplicate rows; two columns that happen to share a value for the same key would collapse into one row.

exercises.snowflake: WITH prices AS (SELECT p.product_id, p.list_price, pc.unit_cost FROM products p JOIN product_costs pc USING (product_id)) SELECT product_id, price_type, amount FROM prices UNPIVOT (amount FOR price_type IN (list_price, unit_cost)) — price_type comes back as upper-case 'LIST_PRICE'/'UNIT_COST'; also the two columns must share a data type.
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.product_id, 'list_price' AS price_type, p.list_price AS amount
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.product_id BETWEEN 1 AND 5
UNION ALL
SELECT pc.product_id, 'unit_cost' AS price_type, pc.unit_cost AS amount
FROM product_costs AS pc
WHERE pc.product_id BETWEEN 1 AND 5
ORDER BY product_id, price_type;

/* Snowflake notes:
WITH prices AS (SELECT p.product_id, p.list_price, pc.unit_cost FROM products p JOIN
product_costs pc USING (product_id)) SELECT product_id, price_type, amount FROM prices
UNPIVOT (amount FOR price_type IN (list_price, unit_cost)) — price_type comes back as
upper-case 'LIST_PRICE'/'UNIT_COST'; also the two columns must share a data type.
*/
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake also has a native UNPIVOT: SELECT product_id, LOWER(price_type) AS price_type, amount FROM (products joined to product_costs) UNPIVOT (amount FOR price_type IN (list_price, unit_cost)). Note UNPIVOT drops NULL values and returns the column names in upper case.

exercises.title: Budget vs actual (unpivot a wide sheet)
exercises.question: Finance pasted its 2025 quarterly budget as a wide sheet. Compare it with actual revenue, quarter by quarter.
exercises.prompt:
Start your query with this CTE (copy it):
WITH budget(category, q1, q2, q3, q4) AS (VALUES ('Electronics', 600, 600, 700, 800), ('Home', 300, 300, 300, 400), ('Books', 150, 150, 150, 200))
Unpivot it to (category, quarter, budget) with quarter = 1..4. Actual = 2025 revenue per category and calendar quarter (Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) from order_items, counting only valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')).); 0 when there was none. Return category, quarter (integer 1–4), budget, actual (rounded 2) and variance (actual - budget, rounded 2) for the 12 budget rows. Order by category, quarter.
hints: Three steps: unpivot the budget (UNION ALL of 4 SELECTs), aggregate actuals per category & quarter, join them.
Quarter number = (CAST(strftime('%m', order_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3. LEFT JOIN from the budget so a quarter without sales still appears.
budget_long: SELECT category, 1 AS quarter, q1 AS budget FROM budget UNION ALL SELECT category, 2, q2 ... ; then budget_long LEFT JOIN actuals ON category AND quarter, COALESCE(actual, 0).
exercises.why: Spreadsheets arrive wide; databases join long. Unpivoting is the step that makes the budget joinable to actuals.

recall.q: Why must the budget be unpivoted before joining to actuals?
recall.a: Actuals are one row per (category, quarter); the budget has quarters as columns. You can only join on matching keys, so both need the long shape.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT category, CAST(REPLACE(qtr, 'Q', '') AS INT) AS quarter, budget FROM budget UNPIVOT (budget FOR qtr IN (q1, q2, q3, q4)); actual quarter = QUARTER(order_date).
exercises.solution:
WITH budget(category, q1, q2, q3, q4) AS (
    VALUES ('Electronics', 600, 600, 700, 800),
           ('Home',        300, 300, 300, 400),
           ('Books',       150, 150, 150, 200)
),
budget_long AS (
    SELECT category, 1 AS quarter, q1 AS budget FROM budget
    UNION ALL SELECT category, 2, q2 FROM budget
    UNION ALL SELECT category, 3, q3 FROM budget
    UNION ALL SELECT category, 4, q4 FROM budget
),
actuals AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           (CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3 AS quarter,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS actual
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
      AND o.order_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
    GROUP BY p.category, (CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3
)
SELECT b.category,
       b.quarter,
       b.budget,
       ROUND(COALESCE(a.actual, 0), 2) AS actual,
       ROUND(COALESCE(a.actual, 0) - b.budget, 2) AS variance
FROM budget_long AS b
LEFT JOIN actuals AS a ON a.category = b.category AND a.quarter = b.quarter
ORDER BY b.category, b.quarter;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT category, CAST(REPLACE(qtr, 'Q', '') AS INT) AS quarter, budget FROM budget
UNPIVOT (budget FOR qtr IN (q1, q2, q3, q4)); actual quarter = QUARTER(order_date).
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH budget AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM VALUES ('Electronics', 600, 600, 700, 800),
                ('Home',        300, 300, 300, 400),
                ('Books',       150, 150, 150, 200)
         AS v (category, q1, q2, q3, q4)
),
budget_long AS (
    SELECT category,
           SUBSTR(quarter_col, 2)::INT AS quarter,
           budget
    FROM budget
    UNPIVOT (budget FOR quarter_col IN (q1, q2, q3, q4))
),
actuals AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           QUARTER(o.order_date)            AS quarter,
           SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS actual
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
      AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-01-01'
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT b.category,
       b.quarter,
       b.budget,
       ROUND(COALESCE(a.actual, 0), 2)            AS actual,
       ROUND(COALESCE(a.actual, 0) - b.budget, 2) AS variance
FROM budget_long AS b
LEFT JOIN actuals AS a ON a.category = b.category AND a.quarter = b.quarter
ORDER BY b.category, b.quarter;
exercises.sf_note: The given CTE does not parse in Snowflake: WITH name(cols) AS (VALUES ...) is SQLite syntax. Write it as WITH budget AS (SELECT * FROM VALUES ('Electronics', 600, 600, 700, 800), ... AS v (category, q1, q2, q3, q4)). Unpivot with UNPIVOT (budget FOR quarter_col IN (q1, q2, q3, q4)) — the label comes back as 'Q1'..'Q4', so SUBSTR(quarter_col, 2)::INT gives 1-4. Quarter of an order: QUARTER(order_date).

lessons.title: Cohort retention analysis
lessons.objective: Group customers into cohorts by when they started, measure how many come back in each later period, and present it as retention counts, rates and a cohort matrix.
lessons.context: The growth team wants to know whether customers acquired in 2025 stick around as well as the 2024 ones. Averages across all customers hide this; cohorts compare like with like — customers at the same age, regardless of calendar date.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: cohort retention in 5 moves**

1. **Activity table:** one row per customer per active period (here: valid orders of known customers,
   `order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')` joined to `customers`).
2. **Cohort:** each customer's first period — `MIN(order_date)` per customer (or `signup_date`).
3. **Period index:** periods since the cohort start. Month index trick in SQLite:
   `year*12 + month`; quarter index: `year*4 + (month-1)/3`. Subtract the cohort's index.
4. **Count:** `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` per (cohort, period_index).
5. **Rate:** divide by the cohort size (period 0 = 100%), optionally pivot periods into columns.

```sql
WITH activity AS (...),                          -- customer_id, order_date
first_order AS (SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date FROM activity GROUP BY customer_id),
idx AS (SELECT a.customer_id,
               strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_date) AS cohort_month,
               (CAST(strftime('%Y', a.order_date) AS INT)*12 + CAST(strftime('%m', a.order_date) AS INT))
             - (CAST(strftime('%Y', f.first_date) AS INT)*12 + CAST(strftime('%m', f.first_date) AS INT))
                 AS months_since_first
        FROM activity a JOIN first_order f USING (customer_id))
SELECT cohort_month, months_since_first, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers
FROM idx GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

**Right-censoring:** a cohort from 2025-Q4 *cannot* have "4 quarters later" data as of 2025-12-31.
Show those cells as NULL, not 0 — zero would look like everyone churned.
With only ~16 customers, quarterly cohorts are far more readable than monthly ones.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
Snowflake makes the date math much shorter:

```sql
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
cohorts AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           order_date,
           DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)) AS cohort_month
    FROM activity
)
SELECT cohort_month,
       DATEDIFF('month', cohort_month, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)) AS months_since_first,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS active_customers
FROM cohorts
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

- `DATEDIFF('month', a, b)` counts month *boundaries* crossed (Jan 31 → Feb 1 = 1), which is exactly the
  calendar-month index cohort tables want. Same for `DATEDIFF('quarter', ...)`.
- Pivot the retention matrix with `PIVOT (COUNT(DISTINCT ...) ...)`? Not allowed — PIVOT takes a simple aggregate
  over a column; pre-aggregate, then `PIVOT (MAX(retention_pct) FOR months_since_first IN (0,1,2,3))`.
- `DATEADD('day', 90, signup_date)` for "within 90 days" windows.

worked_example.question: When did each customer place their first valid order?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       MIN(o.order_date) AS first_order_date,
       strftime('%Y', MIN(o.order_date)) || '-Q'
         || ((CAST(strftime('%m', MIN(o.order_date)) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS cohort_quarter
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY o.customer_id
ORDER BY first_order_date
LIMIT 6;
worked_example.explanation: MIN(order_date) per customer is the cohort anchor. The INNER JOIN to customers drops the orphan order 31 (customer 99), and the status filter means customer 16 (only a cancelled order) is not a customer for this analysis at all.

common_mistakes: Counting orders instead of distinct customers in retention cells.
Defining the cohort from all orders (including cancelled) instead of valid ones.
Showing 0 for periods that haven't happened yet (right-censoring) instead of NULL.
Using day differences / 30 for month indexes instead of calendar-month arithmetic.
Using date('now') as the as-of date — results change every day; fix it ('2025-12-31').
Inner-joining signups to orders, which drops never-buyers from the denominator.
recall: Name the three columns of a long-format retention table.
cohort (start period), period index (periods since start), active customer count (or rate).
How do you compute a calendar-month index difference in SQLite? In Snowflake?
SQLite: (y2*12 + m2) - (y1*12 + m1) from strftime parts. Snowflake: DATEDIFF('month', d1, d2).
What's right-censoring in a cohort table?
Later periods of young cohorts aren't observable yet as of the as-of date; they must be NULL/blank, not 0.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 39 tracks customers through a web funnel. Revisit 38.6 and explain why 2025-Q3's q2_pct is NULL while 2024-Q4's q2_pct is 0.

exercises.title: Assign each customer a cohort month
exercises.question: Growth needs every customer tagged with their acquisition month.
exercises.prompt: Use valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) of known customers (INNER JOIN customers — the orphan order 31 is excluded). Return customer_id, first_order_date (their earliest valid order date) and cohort_month ('YYYY-MM' of first_order_date). One row per customer.
hints: The cohort is defined by each customer's FIRST valid order.
GROUP BY customer_id with MIN(order_date).
SELECT o.customer_id, MIN(o.order_date) AS first_order_date, strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(o.order_date)) AS cohort_month FROM orders o JOIN customers c ... WHERE ... GROUP BY o.customer_id;
exercises.why: Every cohort analysis starts with a stable, one-row-per-customer cohort assignment. Getting the 'what counts as an order' filter right here propagates everywhere.

recall.q: Why exclude cancelled orders when finding the first order?
recall.a: A cancelled order isn't a real purchase; counting it would put customers (e.g. #16) in a cohort they never truly joined.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(o.order_date)) AS cohort_month (a DATE, not text).
exercises.solution:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       MIN(o.order_date) AS first_order_date,
       strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(o.order_date)) AS cohort_month
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY o.customer_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(o.order_date)) AS cohort_month (a DATE, not text).
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT o.customer_id,
       MIN(o.order_date)                     AS first_order_date,
       TO_CHAR(MIN(o.order_date), 'YYYY-MM') AS cohort_month
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') (or DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) when you want a DATE) instead of strftime('%Y-%m', order_date).

exercises.title: Cohort sizes by quarter
exercises.question: How many new customers did we acquire each quarter?
exercises.prompt: Same customer/order definition as 38.1 (valid orders of known customers). Assign each customer the quarter of their first valid order as cohort_quarter (format 'YYYY-Qn', e.g. '2024-Q1'). Return cohort_quarter and new_customers (number of customers in that cohort). Order by cohort_quarter.
hints: Two levels of aggregation: first per customer (MIN), then per quarter (COUNT).
Quarter label: strftime('%Y', d) || '-Q' || ((CAST(strftime('%m', d) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3).
WITH first_order AS (... MIN(order_date) ... GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT <quarter label> AS cohort_quarter, COUNT(*) AS new_customers FROM first_order GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY cohort_quarter;
exercises.why: Cohort size is the denominator of every retention rate — and a growth KPI by itself (new customers per period).

recall.q: What is the denominator of a cohort retention rate?
recall.a: The cohort size: the number of customers whose first activity fell in that cohort period.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('quarter', first_date) AS cohort_quarter, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY 1
exercises.solution:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, MIN(o.order_date) AS first_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT strftime('%Y', first_date) || '-Q'
         || ((CAST(strftime('%m', first_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS cohort_quarter,
       COUNT(*) AS new_customers
FROM first_order
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY cohort_quarter;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATE_TRUNC('quarter', first_date) AS cohort_quarter, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY 1
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_date,
           TO_CHAR(MIN(order_date), 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_quarter
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT cohort_quarter,
       COUNT(*) AS new_customers
FROM first_order
GROUP BY cohort_quarter
ORDER BY cohort_quarter;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has QUARTER(d) (1-4), so the (month + 2) / 3 trick is unnecessary. Careful: in Snowflake '/' never does integer division (7 / 3 = 2.333333), so the SQLite formula would give fractions; if you need it, wrap it in FLOOR(). Label: TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(d).

exercises.title: Months since first order
exercises.question: For each customer, list the months they were active and how many months after their first order each was.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders of known customers (as in 38.1). Return one row per customer per active month: customer_id, cohort_month ('YYYY-MM' of their first valid order), order_month ('YYYY-MM' of a month with at least one valid order) and months_since_first (calendar-month difference: (year*12 + month) of order_month minus the same for cohort_month; 0 for the first month).
hints: Join each order back to the customer's first order date.
Month index = year*12 + month; the difference of two indexes is the calendar-month gap. Use DISTINCT so two orders in one month give one row.

SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id, strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_date), strftime('%Y-%m', a.order_date), (CAST(strftime('%Y',a.order_date) AS INTEGER)*12 + CAST(strftime('%m',a.order_date) AS INTEGER)) - (same for f.first_date) FROM activity a JOIN first_order f ...
exercises.why: The period index aligns customers by age, not calendar — month 3 means 'three months after joining' for everyone.

recall.q: Why not use (julianday(b) - julianday(a)) / 30 for months since first order?
recall.a: Day counts don't map cleanly onto calendar months; cohort tables count calendar-month boundaries (Jan 31 → Feb 1 is month 1).

exercises.snowflake: DATEDIFF('month', first_date, order_date) AS months_since_first — it counts month boundaries, exactly this index.
exercises.solution:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT DISTINCT
       a.customer_id,
       strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_date) AS cohort_month,
       strftime('%Y-%m', a.order_date) AS order_month,
       (CAST(strftime('%Y', a.order_date) AS INTEGER) * 12 + CAST(strftime('%m', a.order_date) AS INTEGER))
     - (CAST(strftime('%Y', f.first_date) AS INTEGER) * 12 + CAST(strftime('%m', f.first_date) AS INTEGER))
         AS months_since_first
FROM activity AS a
JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATEDIFF('month', first_date, order_date) AS months_since_first — it counts month
boundaries, exactly this index.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_date,
           TO_CHAR(MIN(order_date), 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_quarter
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT DISTINCT
       a.customer_id,
       TO_CHAR(f.first_date, 'YYYY-MM')               AS cohort_month,
       TO_CHAR(a.order_date, 'YYYY-MM')               AS order_month,
       DATEDIFF('month', f.first_date, a.order_date)  AS months_since_first
FROM activity AS a
JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: DATEDIFF('month', first_date, order_date) counts calendar-month boundaries, which is exactly the (year*12 + month) difference; TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY-MM') for the labels.

exercises.title: Quarterly retention counts
exercises.question: How many customers of each quarterly cohort were active 0, 1, 2… quarters after their first order?
exercises.prompt: Valid orders of known customers (as in 38.1). Quarter index of a date = year*4 + (month-1)/3 (integer division). Return cohort_quarter ('YYYY-Qn' of the first valid order), quarters_since_first (quarter index of an order minus quarter index of the first order) and active_customers (distinct customers with at least one valid order in that quarter). Order by cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first.
hints: Compute a quarter index once in the activity CTE; MIN of it per customer is the cohort's index.
COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) — a customer with two orders in one quarter counts once.
GROUP BY cohort_quarter, (q_idx - first_q_idx) and COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id).
exercises.why: This long table (cohort, period, count) is the canonical retention dataset — every chart and matrix is built from it.

recall.q: Why COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) rather than COUNT(*) in retention counts?
recall.a: Retention counts customers, not orders: a customer with three orders in a period is one retained customer.

exercises.snowflake: DATEDIFF('quarter', DATE_TRUNC('quarter', first_date), DATE_TRUNC('quarter', order_date)) AS quarters_since_first
exercises.solution:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           CAST(strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) * 4
             + (CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) - 1) / 3 AS q_idx
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date, MIN(q_idx) AS first_q_idx
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT strftime('%Y', f.first_date) || '-Q'
         || ((CAST(strftime('%m', f.first_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS cohort_quarter,
       a.q_idx - f.first_q_idx AS quarters_since_first,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id) AS active_customers
FROM activity AS a
JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATEDIFF('quarter', DATE_TRUNC('quarter', first_date), DATE_TRUNC('quarter',
order_date)) AS quarters_since_first
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_date,
           TO_CHAR(MIN(order_date), 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_quarter
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT f.cohort_quarter,
       DATEDIFF('quarter', f.first_date, a.order_date) AS quarters_since_first,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id)                   AS active_customers
FROM activity AS a
JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: DATEDIFF('quarter', first_date, order_date) equals the quarter-index difference, so no year*4 + (month-1)/3 arithmetic is needed. If you do write the index, note '/' is not integer division in Snowflake: use YEAR(d)*4 + QUARTER(d) - 1. Cohort label: TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(d).

exercises.title: Quarterly retention rates
exercises.question: Turn the counts into rates so cohorts of different sizes can be compared.
exercises.prompt: Extend 38.4: return cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first, cohort_size (customers in the cohort), active_customers and retention_pct (100.0 * active_customers / cohort_size, 0–100 scale, rounded to 1 decimal). Same definitions as 38.4. Order by cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first.
hints: Cohort size = active_customers at quarters_since_first = 0, or COUNT(*) of first_order per cohort.
Build counts and sizes as separate CTEs and join them on cohort_quarter.

... SELECT c.cohort_quarter, c.quarters_since_first, s.cohort_size, c.active_customers, ROUND(100.0 * c.active_customers / s.cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct FROM counts c JOIN sizes s USING (cohort_quarter) ORDER BY ...
exercises.why: Rates make a 4-customer cohort comparable to a 2-customer cohort. (With cohorts this small, one customer swings the rate by 25–50 points — always show cohort_size next to the rate.)

recall.q: What is retention_pct at quarters_since_first = 0, by construction?
recall.a: 100% — every customer is active in their own first quarter.

exercises.snowflake: Alternative for cohort_size: FIRST_VALUE(active_customers) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort_quarter ORDER BY quarters_since_first).
exercises.solution:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           CAST(strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) * 4
             + (CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) - 1) / 3 AS q_idx
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           strftime('%Y', MIN(order_date)) || '-Q'
             || ((CAST(strftime('%m', MIN(order_date)) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS cohort_quarter,
           MIN(q_idx) AS first_q_idx
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
counts AS (
    SELECT f.cohort_quarter,
           a.q_idx - f.first_q_idx AS quarters_since_first,
           COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id) AS active_customers
    FROM activity AS a
    JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
),
sizes AS (
    SELECT cohort_quarter, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size
    FROM first_order
    GROUP BY cohort_quarter
)
SELECT c.cohort_quarter,
       c.quarters_since_first,
       s.cohort_size,
       c.active_customers,
       ROUND(100.0 * c.active_customers / s.cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct
FROM counts AS c
JOIN sizes AS s ON s.cohort_quarter = c.cohort_quarter
ORDER BY c.cohort_quarter, c.quarters_since_first;

/* Snowflake notes:
Alternative for cohort_size: FIRST_VALUE(active_customers) OVER (PARTITION BY
cohort_quarter ORDER BY quarters_since_first).
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_date,
           TO_CHAR(MIN(order_date), 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_quarter
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
counts AS (
    SELECT f.cohort_quarter,
           DATEDIFF('quarter', f.first_date, a.order_date) AS quarters_since_first,
           COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id)                   AS active_customers
    FROM activity AS a
    JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT cohort_quarter,
       quarters_since_first,
       MAX(IFF(quarters_since_first = 0, active_customers, NULL)) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort_quarter) AS cohort_size,
       active_customers,
       ROUND(100 * active_customers / cohort_size, 1) AS retention_pct
FROM counts
ORDER BY cohort_quarter, quarters_since_first;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: DATEDIFF('quarter', first_date, order_date) gives quarters_since_first directly; QUARTER(d) builds the 'YYYY-Qn' label. '/' is decimal division in Snowflake, so the 100.0 is optional.

exercises.title: Retention matrix with censoring
exercises.question: The board deck wants the classic triangle: one row per cohort, columns for quarters 1–4 after acquisition.
exercises.prompt: Same definitions as 38.5 (valid orders of known customers; quarter index = year*4 + (month-1)/3). Return cohort_quarter, cohort_size, and q1_pct, q2_pct, q3_pct, q4_pct = percentage (0–100, rounded to 1 decimal) of the cohort active exactly 1, 2, 3, 4 quarters after their first quarter. Use 0 when that quarter is observable but nobody was active, and NULL when that quarter lies after 2025-Q4 (the as-of date is 2025-12-31). Order by cohort_quarter.
hints: Pivot the (cohort, k) counts with COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 1 THEN customer_id END) etc.
As-of quarter index = 2025*4 + 3 (2025-Q4). A cell is observable if first_q_idx + k <= that; otherwise CASE ... END yields NULL.

per_cohort CTE: cohort_quarter, MIN(first_q_idx), COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS cohort_size, a1..a4; final SELECT: CASE WHEN first_q_idx + 1 <= 2025*4+3 THEN ROUND(100.0*a1/cohort_size,1) END AS q1_pct, ...
exercises.why: Distinguishing 'nobody came back' (0) from 'too early to know' (NULL) is what makes a retention triangle honest. Never use date('now') — fix the as-of date so results are reproducible.

recall.q: Why show NULL rather than 0 for future cells of a young cohort?
recall.a: Because those periods haven't happened yet as of the as-of date; 0 would falsely claim everyone churned.

exercises.snowflake: Pre-aggregate retention_pct per (cohort, k), then PIVOT (MAX(retention_pct) FOR k IN (1,2,3,4)); censoring: IFF(DATEADD('quarter', k, cohort_quarter) <= '2025-10-01', pct, NULL).
exercises.solution:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date,
           CAST(strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) * 4
             + (CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) - 1) / 3 AS q_idx
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           strftime('%Y', MIN(order_date)) || '-Q'
             || ((CAST(strftime('%m', MIN(order_date)) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS cohort_quarter,
           MIN(q_idx) AS first_q_idx
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
cust_q AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT f.cohort_quarter, f.first_q_idx, a.customer_id, a.q_idx - f.first_q_idx AS k
    FROM activity AS a
    JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id
),
per_cohort AS (
    SELECT cohort_quarter,
           MIN(first_q_idx) AS first_q_idx,
           COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS cohort_size,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 1 THEN customer_id END) AS a1,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 2 THEN customer_id END) AS a2,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 3 THEN customer_id END) AS a3,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k = 4 THEN customer_id END) AS a4
    FROM cust_q
    GROUP BY cohort_quarter
)
SELECT cohort_quarter,
       cohort_size,
       CASE WHEN first_q_idx + 1 <= 2025 * 4 + 3 THEN ROUND(100.0 * a1 / cohort_size, 1) END AS q1_pct,
       CASE WHEN first_q_idx + 2 <= 2025 * 4 + 3 THEN ROUND(100.0 * a2 / cohort_size, 1) END AS q2_pct,
       CASE WHEN first_q_idx + 3 <= 2025 * 4 + 3 THEN ROUND(100.0 * a3 / cohort_size, 1) END AS q3_pct,
       CASE WHEN first_q_idx + 4 <= 2025 * 4 + 3 THEN ROUND(100.0 * a4 / cohort_size, 1) END AS q4_pct
FROM per_cohort
ORDER BY cohort_quarter;

/* Snowflake notes:
Pre-aggregate retention_pct per (cohort, k), then PIVOT (MAX(retention_pct) FOR k IN
(1,2,3,4)); censoring: IFF(DATEADD('quarter', k, cohort_quarter) <= '2025-10-01', pct,
NULL).
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           MIN(order_date) AS first_date,
           TO_CHAR(MIN(order_date), 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_quarter
    FROM activity
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
cust_q AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT f.cohort_quarter, f.first_date, a.customer_id,
           DATEDIFF('quarter', f.first_date, a.order_date) AS k
    FROM activity AS a
    JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = a.customer_id
),
per_cohort AS (
    SELECT cohort_quarter,
           DATEDIFF('quarter', MIN(first_date), '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS observable_quarters,
           COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)                    AS cohort_size,
           COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(k = 1, customer_id, NULL))  AS a1,
           COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(k = 2, customer_id, NULL))  AS a2,
           COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(k = 3, customer_id, NULL))  AS a3,
           COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(k = 4, customer_id, NULL))  AS a4
    FROM cust_q
    GROUP BY cohort_quarter
)
SELECT cohort_quarter,
       cohort_size,
       IFF(observable_quarters >= 1, ROUND(100 * a1 / cohort_size, 1), NULL) AS q1_pct,
       IFF(observable_quarters >= 2, ROUND(100 * a2 / cohort_size, 1), NULL) AS q2_pct,
       IFF(observable_quarters >= 3, ROUND(100 * a3 / cohort_size, 1), NULL) AS q3_pct,
       IFF(observable_quarters >= 4, ROUND(100 * a4 / cohort_size, 1), NULL) AS q4_pct
FROM per_cohort
ORDER BY cohort_quarter;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: DATEDIFF('quarter', first_date, '2025-12-31') is the number of quarters observable after the cohort quarter, replacing the year*4 + (month-1)/3 index arithmetic (and '/' is not integer division in Snowflake anyway).

exercises.title: Signup cohorts: converted within 90 days
exercises.question: Marketing measures acquisition by signup date. Of each quarter's signups, how many placed a valid order within 90 days?
exercises.prompt: Cohort = quarter of customers.signup_date (signup_quarter, 'YYYY-Qn'); include ALL customers, even those who never ordered. A customer converted if their first valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) is on or before signup_date + 90 days (julianday(first_order) - julianday(signup_date) <= 90). Return signup_quarter, signups, converted_90d and conversion_pct (100.0 * converted_90d / signups, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by signup_quarter.
hints: Start FROM customers and LEFT JOIN each customer's first valid order — non-buyers must stay in the denominator.
For non-buyers first_date is NULL, so the <= 90 comparison is NULL and the CASE falls to ELSE 0.

SELECT <signup quarter label>, COUNT(*) AS signups, SUM(CASE WHEN julianday(f.first_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) <= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converted_90d, ... FROM customers c LEFT JOIN first_order f ... GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY signup_quarter;
exercises.why: Signup cohorts answer 'is our onboarding converting?', while first-order cohorts answer 'do buyers come back?'. The LEFT JOIN is what keeps never-buyers (18, 19, 20) in the denominator.

recall.q: Why must this query start from customers with a LEFT JOIN?
recall.a: So customers who never ordered still count as signups; an inner join would inflate the conversion rate.

exercises.snowflake: COUNT_IF(f.first_date <= DATEADD('day', 90, c.signup_date)) AS converted_90d, grouped by DATE_TRUNC('quarter', c.signup_date).
exercises.solution:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT strftime('%Y', c.signup_date) || '-Q'
         || ((CAST(strftime('%m', c.signup_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3) AS signup_quarter,
       COUNT(*) AS signups,
       SUM(CASE WHEN julianday(f.first_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) <= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS converted_90d,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN julianday(f.first_date) - julianday(c.signup_date) <= 90 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / COUNT(*), 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY signup_quarter;

/* Snowflake notes:
COUNT_IF(f.first_date <= DATEADD('day', 90, c.signup_date)) AS converted_90d, grouped
by DATE_TRUNC('quarter', c.signup_date).
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT TO_CHAR(c.signup_date, 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(c.signup_date) AS signup_quarter,
       COUNT(*) AS signups,
       COUNT_IF(DATEDIFF('day', c.signup_date, f.first_date) <= 90) AS converted_90d,
       ROUND(100 * converted_90d / signups, 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN first_order AS f ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY signup_quarter;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: DATEDIFF('day', signup_date, first_date) <= 90 replaces the julianday difference, COUNT_IF(...) counts the converted customers (a NULL first_date is simply not counted), and TO_CHAR(d, 'YYYY') || '-Q' || QUARTER(d) builds the label.

lessons.title: Funnel analysis
lessons.objective: Measure how many sessions reach each step of the purchase funnel, compute step-to-step and overall conversion, and slice the funnel by month and visitor type.
lessons.context: The e-commerce team instrumented the website in 2025: every session logs visit → product_view → add_to_cart → checkout → purchase events in web_events. They want to know where shoppers drop off, whether it is getting better over the year, and whether logged-in customers convert better than anonymous visitors.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: session funnel in 4 moves**

1. **Grain = session.** Collapse events to one row per session with a 0/1 flag per stage:
   `MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted`.
2. **Reach per stage** = `SUM(flag)` (or `COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_type = ... THEN session_id END)`).
3. **Conversion:** step conversion = stage / previous stage; overall = stage / visits.
   Use a stage-number column so you can `ORDER BY` stages and use `LAG` to get the previous stage.
4. **Slice:** add a dimension (session month, anonymous vs known) to the session-level CTE and GROUP BY it.

```sql
WITH sessions AS (
    SELECT session_id,
           MAX(customer_id) IS NULL AS is_anonymous,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'visit'    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS visited,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased
    FROM web_events
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT SUM(visited) AS visits, SUM(purchased) AS purchases,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(purchased) / SUM(visited), 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM sessions;
```

**Data facts:** 80 sessions, all in 2025; each stage appears at most once per session and stages are never
skipped here — but real event data has duplicates and skipped steps, so always collapse with MAX/COUNT DISTINCT.
Session month = month of the session's `visit` event (`MIN(event_time)`); anonymous = `customer_id IS NULL`.
lessons.snowflake_notes:
Snowflake extras for funnels:

- `COUNT_IF(event_type = 'purchase')`, `MAX(IFF(event_type = 'purchase', 1, 0))`, `BOOLOR_AGG(event_type = 'purchase')`.
- `DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_time))` for the session month; `DATEDIFF('minute', visit_time, purchase_time)` for time-to-convert.
- Ordered funnels (step B must happen *after* step A) are elegantly expressed with `MATCH_RECOGNIZE`:

```sql
SELECT * FROM web_events
MATCH_RECOGNIZE (
    PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY event_time
    MEASURES MATCH_NUMBER() AS m
    PATTERN (v pv+ c)
    DEFINE v AS event_type = 'visit', pv AS event_type = 'product_view', c AS event_type = 'add_to_cart'
);
```

- Unpivot the one-row funnel into stage rows with `UNPIVOT (sessions FOR stage IN (visits, product_views, ...))`.
- `RATIO_TO_REPORT` doesn't help for step conversion — use `LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number)` as in SQLite.

worked_example.question: How many events of each type were logged, and in how many distinct sessions?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT event_type,
       COUNT(*) AS events,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
FROM web_events
GROUP BY event_type
ORDER BY sessions DESC;
worked_example.explanation: events = sessions for every type, confirming one event per stage per session in this data. Still, funnel queries should count DISTINCT sessions — a double-click on 'add to cart' must not count as two carts.

common_mistakes: Counting events instead of distinct sessions, so repeats inflate a stage.
Ordering stages alphabetically (add_to_cart, checkout, product_view, purchase, visit).
Dividing by the wrong base: step conversion uses the previous stage, overall conversion uses visits.
Classifying sessions (month, visitor type) at event level, splitting one session across groups.
Integer division: 100 * 20 / 80 is fine, but 20 / 80 * 100 is 0 in SQLite — always start with 100.0.
recall: What's the standard grain for a funnel, and how do you get to it from an event log?
One row per session: GROUP BY session_id with MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) flags.
How do you get the previous stage's count for step conversion?
LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number) on a stage-level result.
How do you list sessions that carted but didn't purchase?
An anti-join: add_to_cart events WHERE NOT EXISTS a purchase event with the same session_id.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 40 closes the module with revenue and margin analysis. Re-run 39.4 and say in one sentence which step loses the most sessions.

exercises.title: Sessions reaching each stage
exercises.question: How many sessions reached each step of the funnel?
exercises.prompt: Return stage_number (visit=1, product_view=2, add_to_cart=3, checkout=4, purchase=5), stage (the event_type text) and sessions (number of distinct sessions with that event). Order by stage_number.
hints: GROUP BY event_type and count distinct sessions.
Alphabetical order is wrong for a funnel — map each stage to a number with CASE.
SELECT CASE event_type WHEN 'visit' THEN 1 ... END AS stage_number, event_type AS stage, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions FROM web_events GROUP BY event_type ORDER BY stage_number;
exercises.why: A funnel is only readable in stage order. A stage-number column (or a small stage dimension table) is the standard fix.

recall.q: Why COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) and not COUNT(*) for funnel reach?
recall.a: Event logs contain repeats (refreshes, double-clicks); a funnel measures sessions, not clicks.

exercises.solution:
SELECT CASE event_type
           WHEN 'visit'        THEN 1
           WHEN 'product_view' THEN 2
           WHEN 'add_to_cart'  THEN 3
           WHEN 'checkout'     THEN 4
           WHEN 'purchase'     THEN 5
       END AS stage_number,
       event_type AS stage,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
FROM web_events
GROUP BY event_type
ORDER BY stage_number;

exercises.title: Furthest stage per session
exercises.question: For session-level analysis, tag every session with the furthest funnel stage it reached.
exercises.prompt: Return one row per session: session_id, session_month ('YYYY-MM' of the session's earliest event_time), visitor_type ('anonymous' if customer_id is NULL, else 'known') and furthest_stage (highest stage reached, as a number: visit=1, product_view=2, add_to_cart=3, checkout=4, purchase=5).
hints: GROUP BY session_id collapses events into sessions.
MAX over the stage number gives the furthest stage; MAX(customer_id) IS NULL means no event had a customer.

SELECT session_id, strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(event_time)), CASE WHEN MAX(customer_id) IS NULL THEN 'anonymous' ELSE 'known' END, MAX(CASE event_type WHEN 'visit' THEN 1 ... END) FROM web_events GROUP BY session_id;
exercises.why: The session-level table is the reusable building block: every funnel cut (by month, by visitor type, by device) starts from it.

recall.q: What grain should funnel analysis be built on?
recall.a: One row per session (or per user), with the stage flags/furthest stage as columns.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month; IFF(MAX(customer_id) IS NULL, 'anonymous', 'known').
exercises.solution:
SELECT session_id,
       strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month,
       CASE WHEN MAX(customer_id) IS NULL THEN 'anonymous' ELSE 'known' END AS visitor_type,
       MAX(CASE event_type
               WHEN 'visit'        THEN 1
               WHEN 'product_view' THEN 2
               WHEN 'add_to_cart'  THEN 3
               WHEN 'checkout'     THEN 4
               WHEN 'purchase'     THEN 5
           END) AS furthest_stage
FROM web_events
GROUP BY session_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month; IFF(MAX(customer_id) IS NULL,
'anonymous', 'known').
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT session_id,
       TO_CHAR(MIN(event_time), 'YYYY-MM')                  AS session_month,
       IFF(MAX(customer_id) IS NULL, 'anonymous', 'known')  AS visitor_type,
       MAX(DECODE(event_type, 'visit', 1, 'product_view', 2, 'add_to_cart', 3,
                              'checkout', 4, 'purchase', 5)) AS furthest_stage
FROM web_events
GROUP BY session_id;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: TO_CHAR(MIN(event_time), 'YYYY-MM') instead of strftime; IFF and DECODE are compact alternatives to the CASE expressions.

exercises.title: One-row funnel summary
exercises.question: The weekly email needs the whole funnel in one line.
exercises.prompt: Return a single row with visits, product_views, add_to_carts, checkouts, purchases (number of distinct sessions reaching each stage) and visit_to_purchase_pct (100.0 * purchases / visits, rounded to 1 decimal).
hints: Pivot event types into session-level 0/1 flags, then sum the flags.
MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) per session is 1 if the session ever checked out.
WITH s AS (SELECT session_id, MAX(CASE ...) AS visited, ... GROUP BY session_id) SELECT SUM(visited) AS visits, ..., ROUND(100.0*SUM(purchased)/SUM(visited),1) FROM s;
exercises.why: Flag-then-sum is a pivot (Lesson 37) applied to events; it makes every ratio a simple division of two columns.

recall.q: How do you turn many event rows into one 0/1 flag per session?
recall.a: GROUP BY session_id with MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'x' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

exercises.snowflake: COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(event_type = 'purchase', session_id, NULL)) AS purchases, or COUNT_IF on a session-level flag.
exercises.solution:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT session_id,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'visit'        THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS visited,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'product_view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS viewed,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'checkout'     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS checked_out,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase'     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased
    FROM web_events
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT SUM(visited)     AS visits,
       SUM(viewed)      AS product_views,
       SUM(carted)      AS add_to_carts,
       SUM(checked_out) AS checkouts,
       SUM(purchased)   AS purchases,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(purchased) / SUM(visited), 1) AS visit_to_purchase_pct
FROM s;

/* Snowflake notes:
COUNT(DISTINCT IFF(event_type = 'purchase', session_id, NULL)) AS purchases, or
COUNT_IF on a session-level flag.
*/

exercises.title: Step conversion and drop-off
exercises.question: Where is the biggest leak in the funnel?
exercises.prompt: Return stage_number (visit=1 … purchase=5), stage, sessions (distinct sessions reaching the stage), pct_of_previous (100.0 * sessions / sessions of the previous stage, rounded to 1 decimal; NULL for visit) and pct_of_visits (100.0 * sessions / visit sessions, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by stage_number.
hints: Start from the stage counts of 39.1 (as a CTE).
Previous stage = LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number); visits = FIRST_VALUE(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number).
ROUND(100.0 * sessions / LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number), 1) AS pct_of_previous, ROUND(100.0 * sessions / FIRST_VALUE(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number), 1) AS pct_of_visits
exercises.why: Step conversion pinpoints the leak (here: product page → cart); overall conversion tells you the size of the prize.

recall.q: What's the difference between step conversion and overall conversion?
recall.a: Step: stage ÷ previous stage (where people drop). Overall: stage ÷ first stage (cumulative yield).

exercises.snowflake: Identical windows work in Snowflake; DIV0(sessions, LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number)) avoids zero-division errors.
exercises.solution:
WITH stages AS (
    SELECT CASE event_type
               WHEN 'visit'        THEN 1
               WHEN 'product_view' THEN 2
               WHEN 'add_to_cart'  THEN 3
               WHEN 'checkout'     THEN 4
               WHEN 'purchase'     THEN 5
           END AS stage_number,
           event_type AS stage,
           COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
    FROM web_events
    GROUP BY event_type
)
SELECT stage_number,
       stage,
       sessions,
       ROUND(100.0 * sessions / LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number), 1) AS pct_of_previous,
       ROUND(100.0 * sessions / FIRST_VALUE(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY stage_number), 1) AS pct_of_visits
FROM stages
ORDER BY stage_number;

/* Snowflake notes:
Identical windows work in Snowflake; DIV0(sessions, LAG(sessions) OVER (ORDER BY
stage_number)) avoids zero-division errors.
*/

exercises.title: Monthly funnel trend
exercises.question: Is conversion improving over the year?
exercises.prompt: Session month = 'YYYY-MM' of the session's earliest event_time. For each month with sessions, return session_month, visits (sessions with a visit), add_to_carts, purchases (sessions reaching those stages), cart_rate_pct (100.0 * add_to_carts / visits) and purchase_rate_pct (100.0 * purchases / visits), both rounded to 1 decimal. Order by session_month.
hints: Add session_month to the session-level CTE, then GROUP BY it.
Assign the month per session (MIN(event_time)), not per event — otherwise a session crossing midnight on the last day of a month could be split.

WITH s AS (SELECT session_id, strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month, MAX(CASE ...) AS visited, ... GROUP BY session_id) SELECT session_month, SUM(...), ... GROUP BY session_month ORDER BY session_month;
exercises.why: Trend lines of conversion rates are how teams judge site changes. Note September has no sessions at all — a dashboard would need a month spine to show it as a gap rather than skip it.

recall.q: Why attribute a session to a month using the session's first event instead of each event's own month?
recall.a: So each session lands in exactly one month; events of one session can straddle a month boundary.

exercises.snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month ... GROUP BY session_month.
exercises.solution:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT session_id,
