           strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'visit'       THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS visited,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase'    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased
    FROM web_events
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT session_month,
       SUM(visited)   AS visits,
       SUM(carted)    AS add_to_carts,
       SUM(purchased) AS purchases,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(carted)    / SUM(visited), 1) AS cart_rate_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(purchased) / SUM(visited), 1) AS purchase_rate_pct
FROM s
GROUP BY session_month
ORDER BY session_month;

/* Snowflake notes:
DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(event_time)) AS session_month ... GROUP BY session_month.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT session_id,
           TO_CHAR(MIN(event_time), 'YYYY-MM') AS session_month,
           BOOLOR_AGG(event_type = 'visit')::INT       AS visited,
           BOOLOR_AGG(event_type = 'add_to_cart')::INT AS carted,
           BOOLOR_AGG(event_type = 'purchase')::INT    AS purchased
    FROM web_events
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT session_month,
       SUM(visited)   AS visits,
       SUM(carted)    AS add_to_carts,
       SUM(purchased) AS purchases,
       ROUND(100 * add_to_carts / visits, 1) AS cart_rate_pct,
       ROUND(100 * purchases / visits, 1)    AS purchase_rate_pct
FROM s
GROUP BY session_month
ORDER BY session_month;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake: TO_CHAR(MIN(event_time), 'YYYY-MM') instead of strftime. BOOLOR_AGG(event_type = 'purchase') is a neat per-session 'ever happened' flag (cast to INT to sum it).

exercises.title: Known vs anonymous visitors
exercises.question: Do logged-in customers convert better than anonymous visitors?
exercises.prompt: A session is 'anonymous' if none of its events has a customer_id, else 'known'. Return visitor_type, sessions (distinct sessions), product_view_sessions, add_to_cart_sessions, purchase_sessions (sessions reaching those stages) and purchase_rate_pct (100.0 * purchase_sessions / sessions, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by visitor_type.
hints: Decide visitor_type per session in the session CTE (MAX(customer_id) IS NULL).
Then GROUP BY visitor_type and sum the flags.

WITH s AS (SELECT session_id, CASE WHEN MAX(customer_id) IS NULL THEN 'anonymous' ELSE 'known' END AS visitor_type, MAX(CASE ...) ... GROUP BY session_id) SELECT visitor_type, COUNT(*), SUM(viewed), SUM(carted), SUM(purchased), ROUND(...) FROM s GROUP BY visitor_type ORDER BY visitor_type;
exercises.why: Segmenting a funnel often explains a conversion change (e.g. a traffic mix shift toward anonymous visitors). Watch sample sizes: 4 anonymous sessions is not a trend.

recall.q: Why classify visitor type at session level rather than event level?
recall.a: A session could log in midway; classifying per event would split one session across both groups.

exercises.snowflake: IFF(MAX(customer_id) IS NULL, 'anonymous', 'known') AS visitor_type; COUNT_IF(purchased = 1).
exercises.solution:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT session_id,
           CASE WHEN MAX(customer_id) IS NULL THEN 'anonymous' ELSE 'known' END AS visitor_type,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'product_view' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS viewed,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carted,
           MAX(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase'     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchased
    FROM web_events
    GROUP BY session_id
)
SELECT visitor_type,
       COUNT(*)       AS sessions,
       SUM(viewed)    AS product_view_sessions,
       SUM(carted)    AS add_to_cart_sessions,
       SUM(purchased) AS purchase_sessions,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(purchased) / COUNT(*), 1) AS purchase_rate_pct
FROM s
GROUP BY visitor_type
ORDER BY visitor_type;

/* Snowflake notes:
IFF(MAX(customer_id) IS NULL, 'anonymous', 'known') AS visitor_type;
COUNT_IF(purchased = 1).
*/

exercises.title: Abandoned carts to retarget
exercises.question: CRM wants a list of known customers who added to cart but never purchased in that session, to send a reminder.
exercises.prompt: Find sessions with an add_to_cart event but no purchase event, where the session has a known customer. Return session_id, customer_id, customer_name (customers.name), product_id (the product on the add_to_cart event) and cart_time (event_time of the add_to_cart event). Order by cart_time, session_id.
hints: Start from add_to_cart events; exclude sessions that have a purchase.
NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM web_events p WHERE p.session_id = e.session_id AND p.event_type = 'purchase')

SELECT e.session_id, e.customer_id, c.name AS customer_name, e.product_id, e.event_time AS cart_time FROM web_events e JOIN customers c ON ... WHERE e.event_type = 'add_to_cart' AND NOT EXISTS (...) ORDER BY cart_time, e.session_id;
exercises.why: Funnel analysis becomes action when the drop-off stage turns into a target list. The INNER JOIN to customers keeps only contactable, known customers.

recall.q: Which pattern finds 'did A but not B' within the same session?
recall.a: An anti-join: NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.key IS NULL) on the session key.

exercises.snowflake: Same NOT EXISTS; or GROUP BY session_id HAVING COUNT_IF(event_type = 'add_to_cart') > 0 AND COUNT_IF(event_type = 'purchase') = 0.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.session_id,
       e.customer_id,
       c.name AS customer_name,
       e.product_id,
       e.event_time AS cart_time
FROM web_events AS e
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = e.customer_id
WHERE e.event_type = 'add_to_cart'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM web_events AS p
                  WHERE p.session_id = e.session_id
                    AND p.event_type = 'purchase')
ORDER BY cart_time, e.session_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
Same NOT EXISTS; or GROUP BY session_id HAVING COUNT_IF(event_type = 'add_to_cart') >
0 AND COUNT_IF(event_type = 'purchase') = 0.
*/

lessons.title: Revenue, margin, and product-performance analysis
lessons.objective: Compute revenue, cost of goods, gross margin ($ and %) and refund-adjusted figures by product, category and year, find dead stock, and rank products by their contribution to total margin.
lessons.context: Revenue is vanity, margin is sanity. Finance has loaded unit costs (product_costs) and wants to know which products and categories actually make money after costs and refunds, which catalog items have never sold, and how concentrated margin is in a few hero products.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: margin analysis in 5 moves**

1. **Line-level facts** (valid orders only, `order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')`):
   revenue = `quantity * unit_price`; cost (COGS) = `quantity * unit_cost` from `product_costs`.
2. **Gross margin** = revenue − cost; **margin %** = 100.0 × margin / revenue (0–100 scale).
3. **Refunds** live in `returns` (one row per returned order line). Aggregate them separately and join on
   `order_item_id` — or pre-aggregate per product — so the join cannot multiply line rows.
   Net revenue = revenue − refunds.
4. **Roll up** with GROUP BY product / category / year. Compute percentages *from the sums*, never by
   averaging line-level percentages.
5. **Contribution:** share of total = `margin / SUM(margin) OVER ()`; Pareto curve = running sum of that
   share ordered by margin DESC.

```sql
SELECT p.category,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)                     AS revenue,
       SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost))    AS gross_margin
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items  oi ON oi.order_id   = o.order_id
JOIN products     p  ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id
JOIN product_costs pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY p.category;
```
lessons.snowflake_notes:
The SQL is the same in Snowflake; useful additions:

- `DIV0(margin, revenue)` returns 0 instead of an error when revenue is 0 (`DIV0NULL` also treats NULL as 0).
- `RATIO_TO_REPORT(gross_margin) OVER ()` for contribution share (0–1).
- `QUALIFY` for "top N products per category":

```sql
SELECT p.category, p.product_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost)) AS gross_margin
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi   ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p       ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
JOIN product_costs pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY 1, 2
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, p.product_name) <= 3;
```

- Use `NUMBER(38,2)` (fixed-point) for money in Snowflake tables; floating-point sums like 96.89999999 are
  a SQLite/FLOAT artifact — round at the end, not in the middle.

worked_example.question: What were total revenue, cost and gross margin across all valid orders?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2)                  AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost), 2)                    AS cogs,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost)), 2)  AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost))
             / SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 1)                 AS margin_pct
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned');
worked_example.explanation: Every product has a cost row, so the inner join to product_costs loses nothing. margin_pct is computed from the two sums — the revenue-weighted margin — not as an average of per-line percentages.

common_mistakes: Using products.list_price instead of order_items.unit_price for revenue.
Averaging line-level margin percentages instead of dividing summed margin by summed revenue.
Joining returns without pre-aggregation or with an INNER JOIN — losing or duplicating revenue.
Putting the valid-status filter in the WHERE of a LEFT JOIN anti-join, which silently turns it into an inner join.
Rounding intermediate values and then summing them; round only the final outputs.
Forgetting the NULL category (product 20) — it vanishes or shows as NULL unless you COALESCE it.
recall: Define gross margin and margin % as used in this lesson.
Gross margin = revenue − quantity × unit_cost; margin % = 100 × gross margin / revenue.
How do you compute each product's share of total margin in one pass?
gross_margin / SUM(gross_margin) OVER () (× 100), or RATIO_TO_REPORT in Snowflake.
Which products have never sold, and how do you find them?
Products 23, 24, 25 — via NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) against lines of valid orders.
lessons.review_next: Module 4 is complete. Before Module 5, rebuild 40.5 from memory and add a QUALIFY-style filter (CTE + WHERE) that keeps only products inside the first 80% of cumulative margin.

exercises.title: Product gross margin
exercises.question: Finance wants revenue, cost and margin for every product that sold.
exercises.prompt: Use lines of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price); cogs = SUM(quantity * unit_cost) with unit_cost from product_costs; gross_margin = revenue - cogs. Return product_id, product_name, units_sold (SUM(quantity)), revenue, cogs, gross_margin (each rounded to 2) and margin_pct (100.0 * gross_margin / revenue, 0–100 scale, rounded to 1 decimal). One row per product with sales.
hints: Join order lines to product_costs on product_id; cost is quantity * unit_cost.
Compute margin_pct from the summed revenue and summed margin — not as AVG of line percentages.

SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, SUM(oi.quantity), ROUND(SUM(qty*price),2), ROUND(SUM(qty*unit_cost),2), ROUND(SUM(qty*price) - SUM(qty*unit_cost),2), ROUND(100.0*(...)/SUM(qty*price),1) ... GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name;
exercises.why: The product P&L is the foundation of pricing and assortment decisions — high revenue with thin margin is a different problem from low revenue with fat margin.

recall.q: Why compute margin % as SUM(margin)/SUM(revenue) rather than AVG(line margin %)?
recall.a: AVG of ratios weights a $5 line the same as a $500 line; the ratio of sums is revenue-weighted, which is what finance means.

exercises.solution:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost), 2) AS cogs,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) - SUM(oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost), 2) AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * (SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) - SUM(oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost))
             / SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 1) AS margin_pct
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name;

exercises.title: Category performance
exercises.question: Which categories generate the most gross margin?
exercises.prompt: Same definitions as 40.1 (valid orders; gross_margin = revenue - quantity*unit_cost). Return category ('Uncategorized' when NULL), products_sold (distinct products with sales), revenue, gross_margin (rounded to 2) and margin_pct (100.0 * gross_margin / revenue, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by gross_margin descending, then category.
hints: Same joins as 40.1, but GROUP BY category.
Line margin = quantity * (unit_price - unit_cost); COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) for products_sold.
... GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, category;
exercises.why: Category managers are measured on margin dollars; margin % tells you whether growth there is healthy.

recall.q: Is quantity*(unit_price - unit_cost) summed the same as SUM(revenue) - SUM(cost)?
recall.a: Yes — summation distributes over subtraction, so both give the same margin.

exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized') AS category,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS products_sold,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost)), 2) AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost))
             / SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 1) AS margin_pct
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY COALESCE(p.category, 'Uncategorized')
ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, category;

exercises.title: Net of refunds
exercises.question: Returns eat into margin. Show each product's refunds and margin after refunds.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Per product with sales: revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price), refunds = SUM(returns.refund_amount) for that product's returned lines (0 if none), net_revenue = revenue - refunds, cogs = SUM(quantity * unit_cost), net_margin = net_revenue - cogs (we assume returned goods are written off, so cost stays). Return product_id, revenue, refunds, net_revenue, net_margin (all rounded to 2) for products that had at least one refund. Order by refunds descending, then product_id.
hints: Refunds attach to order lines (order_item_id). LEFT JOIN them so lines without a return keep their revenue.
Pre-aggregate returns per order_item_id so a line can never be duplicated by the join; COALESCE missing refunds to 0.
lines CTE (order_item_id, product_id, revenue, cogs) LEFT JOIN refunds CTE ON order_item_id, GROUP BY product_id HAVING SUM(COALESCE(refund,0)) > 0 ORDER BY refunds DESC, product_id;
exercises.why: A product with great gross margin can be a loser after returns. Pre-aggregating the 'many' side before joining is the habit that prevents fan-out double counting.

recall.q: Why LEFT JOIN returns rather than INNER JOIN when computing net revenue per product?
recall.a: An inner join would keep only returned lines and drop all the revenue from lines that weren't returned.

exercises.solution:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT oi.order_item_id,
           oi.product_id,
           oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS revenue,
           oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost  AS cogs
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
refunds AS (
    SELECT order_item_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS refund
    FROM returns
    GROUP BY order_item_id
)
SELECT l.product_id,
       ROUND(SUM(l.revenue), 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(COALESCE(r.refund, 0)), 2) AS refunds,
       ROUND(SUM(l.revenue) - SUM(COALESCE(r.refund, 0)), 2) AS net_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(l.revenue) - SUM(COALESCE(r.refund, 0)) - SUM(l.cogs), 2) AS net_margin
FROM lines AS l
LEFT JOIN refunds AS r ON r.order_item_id = l.order_item_id
GROUP BY l.product_id
HAVING SUM(COALESCE(r.refund, 0)) > 0
ORDER BY refunds DESC, l.product_id;

exercises.title: Products never sold
exercises.question: Merchandising wants the catalog items that have never sold, with the margin they would make at list price.
exercises.prompt: A product is 'never sold' if it appears on no line of a valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return product_id, product_name, category, list_price, unit_cost and potential_unit_margin (list_price - unit_cost, rounded to 2). Order by product_id.
hints: 'Never sold' is an anti-join: products with no matching valid sale.
Put the status filter INSIDE the NOT EXISTS subquery (join order_items to orders there).

SELECT ... FROM products p JOIN product_costs pc ... WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id AND o.order_status IN (...)) ORDER BY p.product_id;
exercises.why: Dead stock ties up cash and shelf space. Note the Smart Watch would carry the biggest unit margin of all — maybe it's a merchandising problem, not a product problem.

recall.q: If you use LEFT JOIN ... WHERE oi.order_item_id IS NULL for 'never sold', where must the status filter go?
recall.a: Into the ON clause (or a pre-filtered subquery) — in WHERE it would turn the anti-join back into an inner join.

exercises.solution:
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       p.category,
       p.list_price,
       pc.unit_cost,
       ROUND(p.list_price - pc.unit_cost, 2) AS potential_unit_margin
FROM products AS p
JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM order_items AS oi
                  JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
                  WHERE oi.product_id = p.product_id
                    AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'))
ORDER BY p.product_id;

exercises.title: Margin contribution (Pareto)
exercises.question: How concentrated is our margin? Do 20% of products make 80% of the margin?
exercises.prompt: Gross margin per product = SUM(quantity * (unit_price - unit_cost)) over lines of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Return product_id, product_name, gross_margin (rounded 2), pct_of_total_margin (product margin as a 0–100 percentage of total gross margin, rounded to 1) and cumulative_pct (running total of the percentage, products taken in order of gross_margin descending then product_id, computed from unrounded values and rounded to 1). Order by gross_margin descending, then product_id.
hints: Per-product margin in a CTE; then two windows: the grand total and a running total.
Grand total: SUM(gross_margin) OVER (). Running: SUM(gross_margin) OVER (ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, product_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
ROUND(100.0 * gross_margin / SUM(gross_margin) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total_margin, ROUND(100.0 * <running sum> / SUM(gross_margin) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
exercises.why: Pareto curves decide where to focus: protect the top contributors' availability and price, rationalise the long tail.

recall.q: Why compute cumulative_pct from unrounded values?
recall.a: Summing rounded percentages accumulates rounding error, so the curve may not end exactly at 100.

exercises.snowflake: RATIO_TO_REPORT(gross_margin) OVER () * 100 AS pct_of_total_margin; the running share uses the same SUM ... OVER (ORDER BY ... ROWS ...) frame.
exercises.solution:
WITH pm AS (
    SELECT p.product_id,
           p.product_name,
           SUM(oi.quantity * (oi.unit_price - pc.unit_cost)) AS gross_margin
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
)
SELECT product_id,
       product_name,
       ROUND(gross_margin, 2) AS gross_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * gross_margin / SUM(gross_margin) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(gross_margin) OVER (ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, product_id
                                             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
             / SUM(gross_margin) OVER (), 1) AS cumulative_pct
FROM pm
ORDER BY gross_margin DESC, product_id;

/* Snowflake notes:
RATIO_TO_REPORT(gross_margin) OVER () * 100 AS pct_of_total_margin; the running share
uses the same SUM ... OVER (ORDER BY ... ROWS ...) frame.
*/

exercises.title: Yearly P&L after refunds
exercises.question: The CFO wants a two-line P&L: 2024 vs 2025 revenue, refunds, cost and net margin.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders only (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); attribute everything to the year of the ORDER date (not the return date). Return order_year ('YYYY'), revenue (SUM(quantity * unit_price)), refunds (SUM(refund_amount) of returned lines, 0 if none), cogs (SUM(quantity * unit_cost)), net_margin (revenue - refunds - cogs), all rounded to 2, and net_margin_pct (100.0 * net_margin / (revenue - refunds), rounded to 1 decimal). Order by order_year.
hints: Line-level CTE with order_year, revenue and cogs; refunds pre-aggregated per order_item_id.
LEFT JOIN refunds to lines, GROUP BY order_year, then compute margin and % in an outer SELECT from the unrounded sums.
yearly CTE: SUM(revenue), SUM(COALESCE(refund,0)), SUM(cogs) GROUP BY order_year; final: ROUND(revenue - refunds - cogs, 2), ROUND(100.0*(revenue - refunds - cogs)/(revenue - refunds), 1).
exercises.why: Attribution choices (order date vs return date) change the numbers; stating them explicitly is part of the deliverable.

recall.q: Name two ways to attribute a refund to a period.
recall.a: By the original order date (cohort-style, used here) or by the return/refund date (cash/accounting view).

exercises.snowflake: YEAR(o.order_date) AS order_year; DIV0(net_margin, revenue - refunds) * 100 for the percentage.
exercises.solution:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y', o.order_date) AS order_year,
           oi.order_item_id,
           oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS revenue,
           oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost  AS cogs
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
refunds AS (
    SELECT order_item_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS refund
    FROM returns
    GROUP BY order_item_id
),
yearly AS (
    SELECT l.order_year,
           SUM(l.revenue) AS revenue,
           SUM(COALESCE(r.refund, 0)) AS refunds,
           SUM(l.cogs) AS cogs
    FROM lines AS l
    LEFT JOIN refunds AS r ON r.order_item_id = l.order_item_id
    GROUP BY l.order_year
)
SELECT order_year,
       ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(refunds, 2) AS refunds,
       ROUND(cogs, 2) AS cogs,
       ROUND(revenue - refunds - cogs, 2) AS net_margin,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - refunds - cogs) / (revenue - refunds), 1) AS net_margin_pct
FROM yearly
ORDER BY order_year;

/* Snowflake notes:
YEAR(o.order_date) AS order_year; DIV0(net_margin, revenue - refunds) * 100 for the
percentage.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT TO_CHAR(o.order_date, 'YYYY') AS order_year,
           oi.order_item_id,
           oi.quantity * oi.unit_price  AS revenue,
           oi.quantity * pc.unit_cost   AS cogs
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    JOIN product_costs AS pc ON pc.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
refunds AS (
    SELECT order_item_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS refund
    FROM returns
    GROUP BY order_item_id
),
yearly AS (
    SELECT l.order_year,
           SUM(l.revenue)             AS revenue,
           SUM(COALESCE(r.refund, 0)) AS refunds,
           SUM(l.cogs)                AS cogs
    FROM lines AS l
    LEFT JOIN refunds AS r ON r.order_item_id = l.order_item_id
    GROUP BY l.order_year
)
SELECT order_year,
       ROUND(revenue, 2)                  AS revenue,
       ROUND(refunds, 2)                  AS refunds,
       ROUND(cogs, 2)                     AS cogs,
       ROUND(revenue - refunds - cogs, 2) AS net_margin,
       ROUND(100 * DIV0(revenue - refunds - cogs, revenue - refunds), 1) AS net_margin_pct
FROM yearly
ORDER BY order_year;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use YEAR(order_date) (a number) or TO_CHAR(order_date, 'YYYY') (text) instead of strftime('%Y', order_date). DIV0(a, b) guards the division (returns 0 when b = 0).

lessons.title: Snowflake SQL differences and syntax awareness
lessons.objective: Read Snowflake-flavoured SQL fluently (QUALIFY, IFF, DATEADD/DATEDIFF/DATE_TRUNC, ILIKE, :: casts, NVL/ZEROIFNULL, TRY_ functions) and translate it into portable SQL that runs anywhere.
lessons.context: Your team is migrating its reporting from a SQLite prototype to Snowflake. Analysts on the Snowflake side keep pasting queries into Slack, and you need to reproduce their numbers in the prototype — and, the other way round, to know which Snowflake shortcut replaces each of your portable patterns. Being bilingual is what makes you useful on day one.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: translate Snowflake → portable SQL (and back) in 5 moves**

1. **Spot the dialect keywords.** `QUALIFY`, `IFF`, `NVL`, `ZEROIFNULL`, `ILIKE`, `DATEADD`, `DATEDIFF`,
   `DATE_TRUNC`, `::TYPE`, `TRY_TO_*` are the usual suspects.
2. **Map each one to its portable form:**

| Snowflake | Portable / SQLite equivalent |
|---|---|
| `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1` | compute `ROW_NUMBER()` in a CTE, then `WHERE rn = 1` |
| `IFF(cond, a, b)` | `CASE WHEN cond THEN a ELSE b END` (SQLite also has `IIF`) |
| `NVL(x, y)` / `ZEROIFNULL(x)` | `COALESCE(x, y)` / `COALESCE(x, 0)` |
| `x ILIKE '%abc%'` | `LOWER(x) LIKE '%abc%'` (SQLite's LIKE is already case-insensitive for ASCII) |
| `DATE_TRUNC('month', d)` | `date(d, 'start of month')` → `'2025-03-01'` |
| `DATEADD(day, 30, d)` | `date(d, '+30 day')` |
| `DATEDIFF(day, a, b)` | `CAST(julianday(b) - julianday(a) AS INTEGER)` |
| `x::DATE`, `x::NUMBER(12,2)` | `CAST(x AS ...)`, `ROUND(x, 2)` |
| `TRY_TO_NUMBER(x)`, `TRY_TO_DATE(x)` | `CASE WHEN x GLOB '[0-9]*' THEN CAST(x AS INTEGER) END`, `date(x)` (returns NULL if unparseable) |

3. **Watch semantics, not just spelling.** `IFF(NULL >= 100, a, b)` returns `b` (a NULL condition is not true) —
   exactly like `CASE`. `DATEDIFF('month', '2025-01-31', '2025-02-01')` is **1** in Snowflake (it counts
   boundaries crossed), not "0 full months".
4. **Keep the WHERE/QUALIFY split straight.** `WHERE` filters rows *before* windows are computed; `QUALIFY`
   filters *after*. The portable version therefore always needs a subquery/CTE.
5. **Re-run and compare** row counts and totals between the two versions before you trust either.

```sql
-- Snowflake                                   -- Portable
SELECT customer_id, order_id                   WITH ranked AS (
FROM orders                                      SELECT customer_id, order_id,
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (                             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
  PARTITION BY customer_id                                ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;  FROM orders)
                                               SELECT customer_id, order_id FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
```
lessons.snowflake_notes:
**The Snowflake features you'll meet in every code review**

```sql
-- QUALIFY: filter on a window function without a subquery
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;

-- IFF / NVL / NVL2 / ZEROIFNULL / NULLIFZERO
SELECT IFF(list_price >= 100, 'premium', 'standard')  AS price_band,
       NVL(category, 'Uncategorized')                  AS category,
       NVL2(email, 'has email', 'missing')             AS email_flag,   -- NVL2(x, if_not_null, if_null)
       ZEROIFNULL(list_price)                          AS list_price_0,
       NULLIFZERO(quantity)                            AS qty_or_null
FROM products;

-- Dates: DATE_TRUNC returns a DATE/TIMESTAMP (not text); DATEADD/DATEDIFF take a unit first
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)              AS order_month,   -- 2025-03-01
       DATEADD(day, 30, order_date)                 AS plus_30,
       DATEDIFF(day, order_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS age_days,
       LAST_DAY(order_date)                         AS month_end,
       YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), DAYOFWEEK(order_date)
FROM orders;

-- Case-insensitive matching
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%johnson%';      -- Snowflake LIKE is case-SENSITIVE!
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE ANY ('%smith%', '%lee%');

-- Casts: :: is shorthand for CAST; TRY_ variants return NULL instead of failing the query
SELECT '2025-12-31'::DATE, 42.129::NUMBER(10,2), order_id::VARCHAR,
       TRY_TO_NUMBER('S001'), TRY_TO_DATE('31/12/2025'), TRY_CAST('abc' AS INT);
```

**Identifier case folding.** Unquoted identifiers are folded to UPPER case: `select customer_id from orders`
really reads `ORDERS.CUSTOMER_ID`. Quoted identifiers are case-sensitive: a table created by a tool as
`"order_items"` (lower case, quoted) must then *always* be referenced as `"order_items"`. Rule of thumb:
never quote identifiers in DDL, and you'll never need to quote them in queries. String comparisons
(`'Gold' = 'gold'`) are case-sensitive in Snowflake unless a collation says otherwise — unlike SQLite's LIKE.

**Other everyday differences:** `LISTAGG(x, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)` (≈ SQLite `group_concat`),
`ARRAY_AGG`, `SPLIT_PART(s, '-', 1)`, `BOOLEAN` is a real type (`WHERE is_active`), integer division
`7/2` returns `3.5` (SQLite returns `3`!), `TOP n` / `LIMIT n` both work, and `SELECT ... EXCLUDE (col)`
/ `RENAME` let you trim `SELECT *`.

worked_example.question: A Snowflake analyst sent: `SELECT order_id, order_date, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month, DATEADD(day, 14, order_date) AS return_window_ends, IFF(order_status = 'cancelled', 0, 1) AS is_live FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2025-11-01'`. Reproduce it in SQLite.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       date(order_date, 'start of month')                         AS order_month,
       date(order_date, '+14 day')                                AS return_window_ends,
       CASE WHEN order_status = 'cancelled' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END     AS is_live
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-11-01';
worked_example.explanation: Each Snowflake function has a one-line SQLite twin: DATE_TRUNC → `date(d, 'start of month')`, DATEADD → `date(d, '+14 day')`, IFF → `CASE`. Because dates are stored as ISO text ('YYYY-MM-DD'), the string comparison `order_date >= '2025-11-01'` is a correct date comparison — in Snowflake the column would be a real DATE and the literal is cast implicitly.

common_mistakes: Assuming LIKE is case-insensitive everywhere: it is in SQLite (ASCII), it is NOT in Snowflake — use ILIKE.
Swapping DATEDIFF arguments: Snowflake is DATEDIFF(unit, start, end) and returns end − start.
Expecting DATEDIFF('month', ...) to count complete months — it counts boundaries crossed.
Translating QUALIFY by moving the window function into WHERE — window functions are not allowed in WHERE; use a CTE.
Quoting lower-case identifiers in Snowflake DDL ("order_items") and then fighting case-sensitive names forever.
Relying on SQLite's integer division (7/2 = 3); Snowflake returns 3.5.
recall: Portable equivalent of QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1?
Compute ROW_NUMBER() AS rn in a CTE/subquery, then WHERE rn = 1 in the outer query.
What do NVL(x, y) and ZEROIFNULL(x) correspond to?
COALESCE(x, y) and COALESCE(x, 0).
How does Snowflake treat an unquoted identifier like order_items?
It folds it to upper case (ORDER_ITEMS); quoted identifiers keep their exact case.
What do TRY_TO_NUMBER / TRY_CAST do differently from CAST?
They return NULL instead of raising an error when the value can't be converted.
lessons.review_next: Next, Lesson 42 opens the raw_order_events JSON payloads — Snowflake's `payload:customer.id::INT` path syntax and its SQLite twin `payload ->> '$.customer.id'`. Re-read the QUALIFY ↔ CTE table above first.

exercises.title: ILIKE → case-insensitive LIKE
exercises.question: Snowflake query from the CRM team: `SELECT customer_id, name, email FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%johnson%'`. Reproduce it — they suspect a duplicate account.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, email for every customer whose name contains 'johnson' in any letter case. The match must work regardless of the database's default LIKE case sensitivity (so normalise the case yourself).
hints: ILIKE = case-insensitive LIKE. Make both sides the same case.
LOWER(name) LIKE '%johnson%' is portable to every database.
SELECT customer_id, name, email FROM customers WHERE LOWER(name) LIKE '%johnson%';
exercises.why: SQLite's LIKE happens to be case-insensitive, Snowflake's LIKE is case-sensitive. A query that finds 2 rows in the prototype finds 1 in Snowflake unless you use ILIKE or LOWER().

recall.q: Is LIKE case-sensitive in Snowflake?
recall.a: Yes. Use ILIKE (or LOWER(col) LIKE 'pattern') for case-insensitive matching.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT customer_id, name, email FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE '%johnson%';
exercises.sf_note: SQLite's LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII, Snowflake's LIKE is case-sensitive. LOWER(name) LIKE '%johnson%' works in both; in Snowflake you can also write name ILIKE '%johnson%'.

exercises.title: IFF, NVL and ZEROIFNULL on the price sheet
exercises.question: Snowflake query: `SELECT product_id, NVL(category, 'Uncategorized') AS category, ZEROIFNULL(list_price) AS list_price, IFF(list_price >= 100, 'premium', 'standard') AS price_band FROM products`. Reproduce it exactly.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, category (NULL replaced by 'Uncategorized'), list_price (NULL replaced by 0) and price_band = 'premium' when the ORIGINAL list_price >= 100, otherwise 'standard' (note: a NULL list_price makes the condition not-true, so it lands in 'standard' — exactly what IFF does). All 25 products.
hints: NVL and ZEROIFNULL are both COALESCE in disguise.
IFF(cond, a, b) = CASE WHEN cond THEN a ELSE b END. Test the original column, not the COALESCEd one.
COALESCE(category,'Uncategorized') AS category, COALESCE(list_price,0) AS list_price, CASE WHEN list_price >= 100 THEN 'premium' ELSE 'standard' END AS price_band
exercises.why: Most dialect differences are just spelling. Knowing the portable spelling lets you read any warehouse's SQL — and IFF/CASE treat NULL conditions identically (product 19 → 'standard').

recall.q: What does IFF(NULL > 5, 'a', 'b') return?
recall.a: 'b' — a NULL condition is not TRUE, so the ELSE branch is taken (same as CASE).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT product_id, NVL(category, 'Uncategorized') AS category, ZEROIFNULL(list_price) AS list_price, IFF(list_price >= 100, 'premium', 'standard') AS price_band FROM products;

exercises.title: DATEADD and DATEDIFF for 2025 sign-ups
exercises.question: Growth sent: `SELECT customer_id, signup_date, DATEADD(day, 30, signup_date) AS trial_end, DATEDIFF(day, signup_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_signup FROM customers WHERE signup_date >= '2025-01-01'`.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, signup_date, trial_end (signup_date + 30 days, as 'YYYY-MM-DD') and days_since_signup (whole days from signup_date to the as-of date '2025-12-31', an integer) for customers who signed up on or after '2025-01-01'.
hints: DATEADD(day, n, d) → date(d, '+n day').
DATEDIFF(day, a, b) → julianday(b) - julianday(a), cast to INTEGER.
date(signup_date,'+30 day') AS trial_end, CAST(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(signup_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_signup
exercises.why: Tenure, recency and SLA windows are all DATEADD/DATEDIFF. Mind the argument order: Snowflake DATEDIFF(unit, start, end) is end − start.

recall.q: In Snowflake, what does DATEDIFF('month', '2025-01-31', '2025-02-01') return?
recall.a: 1 — DATEDIFF counts unit boundaries crossed, not complete units.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT customer_id, signup_date, DATEADD(day, 30, signup_date) AS trial_end, DATEDIFF(day, signup_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_signup FROM customers WHERE signup_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE;
exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       signup_date,
       date(signup_date, '+30 day')                                       AS trial_end,
       CAST(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(signup_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_signup
FROM customers
WHERE signup_date >= '2025-01-01';

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT customer_id, signup_date, DATEADD(day, 30, signup_date) AS trial_end,
DATEDIFF(day, signup_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_signup FROM customers
WHERE signup_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE;
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT customer_id,
       signup_date,
       DATEADD(day, 30, signup_date)                    AS trial_end,
       DATEDIFF(day, signup_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE)   AS days_since_signup
FROM customers
WHERE signup_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use DATEADD(day, 30, signup_date) instead of date(signup_date, '+30 day') and DATEDIFF(day, signup_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) instead of the julianday() difference; DATEDIFF already returns an integer.

exercises.title: DATE_TRUNC and :: casts in a monthly revenue query
exercises.question: Finance's Snowflake query: `SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)::DATE AS order_month, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)::NUMBER(12,2) AS gross_revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE GROUP BY 1`.
exercises.prompt: Return order_month (first day of the month, 'YYYY-MM-01'), valid_orders (distinct orders) and gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) per month for orders dated on or after '2025-01-01'. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: DATE_TRUNC('month', d) → date(d, 'start of month').
::NUMBER(12,2) on a sum is a rounding/typing step → ROUND(..., 2). GROUP BY 1 → group by the expression.

SELECT date(o.order_date,'start of month') AS order_month, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price),2) AS gross_revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ... GROUP BY 1;
exercises.why: Monthly bucketing is the single most common transformation in reporting; in Snowflake it's always DATE_TRUNC, in SQLite strftime/date modifiers.

recall.q: What does `x::NUMBER(12,2)` mean in Snowflake?
recall.a: CAST(x AS NUMBER(12,2)) — a fixed-point number with 2 decimals (the value is rounded).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)::DATE AS order_month, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS valid_orders, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)::NUMBER(12,2) AS gross_revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE GROUP BY 1;
exercises.solution:
SELECT date(o.order_date, 'start of month')       AS order_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)                  AS valid_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2)  AS gross_revenue
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
  AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY date(o.order_date, 'start of month');

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)::DATE AS order_month, COUNT(DISTINCT
o.order_id) AS valid_orders, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)::NUMBER(12,2) AS
gross_revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE
o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND o.order_date >=
'2025-01-01'::DATE GROUP BY 1;
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)::DATE       AS order_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)                      AS valid_orders,
       SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)::NUMBER(12,2)  AS gross_revenue
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
  AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'::DATE
GROUP BY 1;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) instead of date(order_date, 'start of month'); GROUP BY 1 and ::NUMBER(12,2) casts work as shown in the question.

exercises.title: QUALIFY → ROW_NUMBER in a CTE
exercises.question: Customer success: `SELECT customer_id, order_id AS latest_order_id, order_date AS latest_order_date FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1`.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, latest_order_id and latest_order_date: each customer_id's most recent valid order (valid = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); break date ties by the higher order_id. Include every customer_id that appears on a valid order (also the orphan id 99).
hints: SQLite has no QUALIFY. Compute ROW_NUMBER() first, filter second.
Put the window in a CTE (WITH ranked AS (...)) and filter WHERE rn = 1 outside.

WITH ranked AS (SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders WHERE ...) SELECT ... FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
exercises.why: Deduplicating to 'latest record per key' is everywhere in Snowflake (QUALIFY on CDC tables). You must be able to write it both ways.

recall.q: Does QUALIFY run before or after WHERE?
recall.a: After — WHERE filters rows, window functions are computed, then QUALIFY filters on them.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT customer_id, order_id AS latest_order_id, order_date AS latest_order_date FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;
exercises.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                              ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
)
SELECT customer_id,
       order_id   AS latest_order_id,
       order_date AS latest_order_date
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT customer_id, order_id AS latest_order_id, order_date AS latest_order_date FROM
orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER()
OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;
*/
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake has QUALIFY, so the CTE is optional: ... FROM orders WHERE <valid> QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1.

exercises.title: Recency status: QUALIFY + DATEDIFF + IFF together
exercises.question: The retention team's Snowflake query: `SELECT customer_id, order_date AS last_order_date, DATEDIFF(day, order_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_last_order, IFF(DATEDIFF(day, order_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) > 180, 'lapsed', 'active') AS recency_status FROM orders o WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id) QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1`.
exercises.prompt: For every existing customer (customer_id present in customers) with at least one valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), return customer_id, last_order_date (date of their most recent valid order), days_since_last_order (integer days from that date to '2025-12-31') and recency_status = 'lapsed' if days_since_last_order > 180, else 'active'.
hints: Only the date of the latest order is needed, so MAX(order_date) per customer is an alternative to ROW_NUMBER.
Compute days_since_last_order once in a CTE, then derive the status from it (no repetition).

WITH last_valid AS (SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date) AS last_order_date FROM orders WHERE <valid> AND EXISTS(...) GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT ..., CAST(julianday('2025-12-31')-julianday(last_order_date) AS INTEGER) ...
exercises.why: Real Snowflake queries stack several dialect features at once. Translating them step by step (and spotting that QUALIFY here is just a MAX) is the skill.

recall.q: When can a QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() = 1 be replaced by a plain GROUP BY + MAX?
recall.a: When you only need the ordering column itself (e.g. the latest date), not other columns from that row.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT customer_id, order_date AS last_order_date, DATEDIFF(day, order_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_last_order, IFF(days_since_last_order > 180, 'lapsed', 'active') AS recency_status FROM orders o WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id) QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1;  -- Snowflake lets you reuse a column alias (days_since_last_order) later in the same SELECT list.
exercises.solution:
WITH last_valid AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order_date
    FROM orders AS o
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
      AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
    GROUP BY o.customer_id
), aged AS (
    SELECT customer_id, last_order_date,
           CAST(julianday('2025-12-31') - julianday(last_order_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_last_order
    FROM last_valid
)
SELECT customer_id,
       last_order_date,
       days_since_last_order,
       CASE WHEN days_since_last_order > 180 THEN 'lapsed' ELSE 'active' END AS recency_status
FROM aged;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT customer_id, order_date AS last_order_date, DATEDIFF(day, order_date,
'2025-12-31'::DATE) AS days_since_last_order, IFF(days_since_last_order > 180,
'lapsed', 'active') AS recency_status FROM orders o WHERE order_status IN
('completed','shipped','returned') AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE
c.customer_id = o.customer_id) QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1;  -- Snowflake lets you reuse a column alias
(days_since_last_order) later in the same SELECT list.
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT customer_id,
       order_date                                      AS last_order_date,
       DATEDIFF(day, order_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE)   AS days_since_last_order,
       IFF(days_since_last_order > 180, 'lapsed', 'active') AS recency_status
FROM orders AS o
WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id)
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use DATEDIFF(day, last_order_date, '2025-12-31'::DATE) instead of the julianday() difference. QUALIFY replaces the CTE, and Snowflake lets a later SELECT item reuse an alias (days_since_last_order) defined earlier in the same list.

lessons.title: Querying semi-structured JSON-like data
lessons.objective: Extract top-level and nested fields from JSON payloads with path expressions, cast them to proper types, and understand why missing keys (and JSON nulls) come back as SQL NULL.
lessons.context: The e-commerce platform streams every order as a JSON event into raw_order_events before it lands in the clean orders tables. When the pipeline breaks, or a new field appears (customer tier, tags) that the clean tables don't have yet, the analyst who can query the raw JSON directly gets the answer first.
lessons.recipe:
**Recipe: pull fields out of a JSON column in 4 moves**

1. **Look at one payload** (`SELECT payload FROM raw_order_events LIMIT 1`) and sketch the shape:
   `{"order_id", "placed_at", "customer": {"id","region","tier"?}, "items": [{...}], "shipping": {"method","address":{"city","country"}}, "tags"?: [...]}`
2. **Write the path.** `$` is the document root, `.key` steps into an object, `[0]` into an array:
   `'$.customer.id'`, `'$.shipping.address.city'`, `'$.items[0].price'`.
3. **Extract as a SQL value** with `payload ->> '$.path'` (or `json_extract(payload, '$.path')`).
   `->>` returns TEXT/INTEGER/REAL; `->` returns a JSON fragment (keeps quotes, objects stay JSON).
4. **Handle absence:** a missing key and a JSON `null` both extract as SQL NULL. Use `COALESCE` for defaults
   and `json_type(payload, '$.path')` when you must tell them apart (`NULL` = key absent, `'null'` = present but null).

```sql
SELECT event_id,
       payload ->> '$.order_id'                 AS order_id,
       payload ->> '$.customer.id'              AS customer_id,
       COALESCE(payload ->> '$.customer.tier', 'none') AS tier
FROM raw_order_events;
```
lessons.snowflake_notes:
In Snowflake the payload would be a **VARIANT** column and you navigate it with `:` and `.` / `[ ]`:

```sql
SELECT event_id,
       payload:order_id::INT                        AS order_id,
       payload:placed_at::TIMESTAMP_NTZ             AS placed_at,
       payload:customer.id::INT                     AS customer_id,
       payload:customer:tier::STRING                AS tier,          -- ':' and '.' both step in
       payload['shipping']['address']['city']::STRING AS city,        -- bracket notation (needed for odd keys)
       payload:items[0]:price::NUMBER(10,2)         AS first_price,
       GET_PATH(payload, 'shipping.method')::STRING AS shipping_method
FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload:shipping.address.country::STRING = 'Canada';
```

- **Always cast** (`::STRING`, `::INT`). Without it you get a VARIANT: `payload:customer.tier` displays as `"gold"`
  *with quotes*, and comparing VARIANT to a string can surprise you.
- **Missing key → SQL NULL**, but a JSON `null` → a *VARIANT null* (displays `null`, `IS NULL` is FALSE!).
  `IS_NULL_VALUE(payload:customer.region)` detects it; casting with `::STRING` turns it into SQL NULL.
  (SQLite's `->>` collapses both to SQL NULL; `json_type` returns `'null'` vs NULL to tell them apart.)
- `TYPEOF(payload:customer.tier)` ≈ `json_type` → `'VARCHAR'`, `'INTEGER'`, `'OBJECT'`, `'ARRAY'`, `'NULL_VALUE'`.
- Field names in paths are **case-sensitive** (`payload:Customer` ≠ `payload:customer`), unlike column names.
- Loading: `PARSE_JSON(text)` turns a string into VARIANT; `TRY_PARSE_JSON` returns NULL for bad JSON.

worked_example.question: Show the order id, shipping method and destination city of the first 5 events.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT event_id,
       payload ->> '$.order_id'                AS order_id,
       payload ->> '$.shipping.method'         AS shipping_method,
       payload ->> '$.shipping.address.city'   AS city,
       payload ->  '$.shipping.address'        AS address_json
FROM raw_order_events
ORDER BY event_id
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: `->>` returns plain SQL values you can filter, group and join on. `->` returns the JSON fragment itself — handy for eyeballing a nested object, useless for arithmetic. In Snowflake the same query reads `payload:shipping.address.city::STRING`.

common_mistakes: Using -> (returns JSON text, with quotes) where you meant ->> (returns a SQL value).
Expecting an error for a misspelled key — you silently get NULL. Check a few rows by eye.
Forgetting ::STRING / ::INT in Snowflake and comparing VARIANTs ('"gold"' with quotes vs 'gold').
Treating a Snowflake VARIANT null as SQL NULL — IS NULL is false for it until you cast.
Assuming arrays are 1-based: items[1] is the SECOND line.
recall: Difference between -> and ->> in SQLite?
-> returns a JSON fragment; ->> returns a plain SQL value (text/number/NULL).
Snowflake spelling of payload ->> '$.shipping.address.city'?
payload:shipping.address.city::STRING
What does json_type return for a key that is absent?
SQL NULL (vs the text 'null' for a JSON null).
lessons.review_next: Lesson 43 looks at whole values — objects vs arrays, array lengths, optional keys — and builds JSON with json_object / json_group_array (Snowflake OBJECT_CONSTRUCT / ARRAY_AGG).

exercises.title: Flatten the top-level scalars
exercises.question: Data engineering wants a typed view of the raw events' key fields.
exercises.prompt: For all 60 events return event_id, order_id (payload $.order_id), placed_at (payload $.placed_at, as the raw text) and customer_id (payload $.customer.id).
hints: The ->> operator extracts a SQL value: payload ->> '$.key'.
Nested objects are reached with dots: '$.customer.id'.
SELECT event_id, payload ->> '$.order_id' AS order_id, payload ->> '$.placed_at' AS placed_at, payload ->> '$.customer.id' AS customer_id FROM raw_order_events;
exercises.why: This is literally the first staging model you'd build on a raw VARIANT table in Snowflake.

recall.q: What does the $ mean in '$.customer.id'?
recall.a: The root of the JSON document.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT event_id, payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, payload:placed_at::STRING AS placed_at, payload:customer.id::INT AS customer_id FROM raw_order_events;
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT event_id,
       payload:order_id::INT        AS order_id,
       payload:placed_at::STRING    AS placed_at,
       payload:customer:id::INT     AS customer_id
FROM raw_order_events;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake, payload is a VARIANT: read fields with path notation and cast them, e.g. payload:customer:id::INT or payload:items[0]:price::NUMBER(10,2), instead of payload ->> '$.customer.id' / json_extract. A missing key gives SQL NULL.

exercises.title: Filter on a deeply nested field
exercises.question: Logistics: which orders were shipped to Canada, and how?
exercises.prompt: Return event_id, order_id, shipping_method ($.shipping.method) and city ($.shipping.address.city) for events whose $.shipping.address.country is 'Canada'.
hints: You can use a JSON path in WHERE exactly like in SELECT.
Two levels of nesting: '$.shipping.address.country'.
... WHERE payload ->> '$.shipping.address.country' = 'Canada';
exercises.why: Filtering on nested attributes without first building a clean table is what makes semi-structured data useful for fast investigations.

recall.q: Why must you cast payload:shipping.address.country::STRING in Snowflake before comparing?
recall.a: Without the cast it's a VARIANT (a JSON string with quotes); the cast gives a plain SQL string.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT event_id, payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, payload:shipping.method::STRING AS shipping_method, payload:shipping.address.city::STRING AS city FROM raw_order_events WHERE payload:shipping.address.country::STRING = 'Canada';
exercises.solution:
SELECT event_id,
       payload ->> '$.order_id'              AS order_id,
       payload ->> '$.shipping.method'       AS shipping_method,
       payload ->> '$.shipping.address.city' AS city
FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload ->> '$.shipping.address.country' = 'Canada';

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT event_id, payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, payload:shipping.method::STRING AS
shipping_method, payload:shipping.address.city::STRING AS city FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload:shipping.address.country::STRING = 'Canada';
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT event_id,
       payload:order_id::INT                     AS order_id,
       payload:shipping:method::STRING           AS shipping_method,
       payload:shipping:address:city::STRING     AS city
FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload:shipping:address:country::STRING = 'Canada';
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake, payload is a VARIANT: read fields with path notation and cast them, e.g. payload:customer:id::INT or payload:items[0]:price::NUMBER(10,2), instead of payload ->> '$.customer.id' / json_extract. A missing key gives SQL NULL. Filter the same way: WHERE payload:shipping:address:country::STRING = 'Canada'.

exercises.title: Missing keys become NULL: tier breakdown
exercises.question: Marketing added an optional customer tier to the event feed. How many events carry it?
exercises.prompt: Return tier and events: the number of events per value of $.customer.tier, where events without a tier key are labelled 'none'.
hints: A missing key does not raise an error — it extracts as NULL.
COALESCE(payload ->> '$.customer.tier', 'none') gives you the label.
SELECT COALESCE(payload ->> '$.customer.tier','none') AS tier, COUNT(*) AS events FROM raw_order_events GROUP BY 1;
exercises.why: Optional fields are the norm in event data. If you GROUP BY the raw path you get a NULL group that dashboards often hide — label it explicitly.

recall.q: What does payload ->> '$.no_such_key' return?
recall.a: NULL — missing keys are not errors.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT NVL(payload:customer.tier::STRING, 'none') AS tier, COUNT(*) AS events FROM raw_order_events GROUP BY 1;
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT NVL(payload:customer:tier::STRING, 'none') AS tier,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS events
FROM raw_order_events
GROUP BY 1;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake use NVL(payload:customer:tier::STRING, 'none') instead of COALESCE(payload ->> '$.customer.tier', 'none'); a missing key also extracts as NULL.

exercises.title: Absent key vs JSON null
exercises.question: Some events have no region. Is the region key missing, or present with a null value? The answer decides whether the bug is in the producer or in the CRM.
exercises.prompt: For events whose $.customer.region does not extract as a text value, return event_id, customer_id ($.customer.id), region_type = json_type of $.customer.region and tier_type = json_type of $.customer.tier (json_type returns NULL when the key is absent and the text 'null' when the key holds a JSON null).
hints: Filter with payload ->> '$.customer.region' IS NULL — that catches both absent and JSON null.
json_type(payload, '$.path') returns 'text', 'integer', 'real', 'object', 'array', 'null' — or SQL NULL if the path doesn't exist.

SELECT event_id, payload ->> '$.customer.id' AS customer_id, json_type(payload,'$.customer.region') AS region_type, json_type(payload,'$.customer.tier') AS tier_type FROM raw_order_events WHERE payload ->> '$.customer.region' IS NULL;
exercises.why: region_type = 'null' tells you the producer sent the key with no value (these are customers 9, 16 and the orphan 99 — they have no region upstream either); tier_type NULL means the key was never sent.

recall.q: How do you distinguish an absent key from a JSON null in SQLite?
recall.a: json_type(doc, path): SQL NULL = absent key, the text 'null' = key present with JSON null.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT event_id, payload:customer.id::INT AS customer_id, TYPEOF(payload:customer.region) AS region_type, TYPEOF(payload:customer.tier) AS tier_type FROM raw_order_events WHERE payload:customer.region::STRING IS NULL;  -- TYPEOF gives 'NULL_VALUE' for JSON null, NULL for absent
exercises.solution:
SELECT event_id,
       payload ->> '$.customer.id'               AS customer_id,
       json_type(payload, '$.customer.region')  AS region_type,
       json_type(payload, '$.customer.tier')    AS tier_type
FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload ->> '$.customer.region' IS NULL;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT event_id, payload:customer.id::INT AS customer_id,
TYPEOF(payload:customer.region) AS region_type, TYPEOF(payload:customer.tier) AS
tier_type FROM raw_order_events WHERE payload:customer.region::STRING IS NULL;  --
TYPEOF gives 'NULL_VALUE' for JSON null, NULL for absent
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT event_id,
       payload:customer:id::INT AS customer_id,
       CASE TYPEOF(payload:customer:region)
            WHEN 'NULL_VALUE' THEN 'null'   WHEN 'VARCHAR' THEN 'text'
            WHEN 'INTEGER'    THEN 'integer' WHEN 'DECIMAL' THEN 'real' WHEN 'DOUBLE' THEN 'real'
            WHEN 'OBJECT'     THEN 'object'  WHEN 'ARRAY'   THEN 'array'
       END AS region_type,
       CASE TYPEOF(payload:customer:tier)
            WHEN 'NULL_VALUE' THEN 'null'   WHEN 'VARCHAR' THEN 'text'
            WHEN 'INTEGER'    THEN 'integer' WHEN 'DECIMAL' THEN 'real' WHEN 'DOUBLE' THEN 'real'
            WHEN 'OBJECT'     THEN 'object'  WHEN 'ARRAY'   THEN 'array'
       END AS tier_type
FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload:customer:region::STRING IS NULL;
exercises.sf_note: Snowflake's TYPEOF(payload:path) is the counterpart of json_type, but it returns upper-case Snowflake type names: 'VARCHAR' (SQLite 'text'), 'INTEGER' ('integer'), 'DECIMAL'/'DOUBLE' ('real'), 'OBJECT', 'ARRAY', 'BOOLEAN' ('true'/'false') and 'NULL_VALUE' for a JSON null (SQLite 'null'). An absent key gives SQL NULL in both. The solution maps the names with a CASE so the output matches the course's expected values. To test for a JSON null directly, use IS_NULL_VALUE(payload:customer:region).

exercises.title: Join JSON to the clean tables
exercises.question: Operations wants valid orders by shipping method — the method only exists in the raw feed, the status only in orders.
exercises.prompt: Join raw_order_events to orders on the payload's $.order_id = orders.order_id and return shipping_method ($.shipping.method) and valid_orders = number of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) per method.
hints: An extracted JSON value can be used as a join key like any column.
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload ->> '$.order_id', then filter on o.order_status.

SELECT e.payload ->> '$.shipping.method' AS shipping_method, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders FROM raw_order_events e JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload ->> '$.order_id' WHERE o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY 1;
exercises.why: Enriching clean facts with a raw attribute that hasn't been modelled yet is a weekly task. In Snowflake, forgetting ::INT on the key can turn the join into a slow VARIANT comparison.

recall.q: Why cast payload:order_id::INT before joining in Snowflake?
recall.a: So both sides are the same SQL type — VARIANT-to-NUMBER comparisons are implicit and can be slow or surprising.

exercises.snowflake: SELECT e.payload:shipping.method::STRING AS shipping_method, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders FROM raw_order_events e JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload:order_id::INT WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1;
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.payload ->> '$.shipping.method' AS shipping_method,
       COUNT(*)                              AS valid_orders
FROM raw_order_events AS e
JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = e.payload ->> '$.order_id'
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY e.payload ->> '$.shipping.method';

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT e.payload:shipping.method::STRING AS shipping_method, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders
FROM raw_order_events e JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = e.payload:order_id::INT WHERE
o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1;
*/
exercises.solution_sf:
SELECT e.payload:shipping:method::STRING AS shipping_method,
       COUNT(*)                             AS valid_orders
FROM raw_order_events AS e
JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = e.payload:order_id::INT
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY 1;
exercises.sf_note: In Snowflake, payload is a VARIANT: read fields with path notation and cast them, e.g. payload:customer:id::INT or payload:items[0]:price::NUMBER(10,2), instead of payload ->> '$.customer.id' / json_extract. A missing key gives SQL NULL. Cast the join key: ON o.order_id = e.payload:order_id::INT.

exercises.title: Index into an array: the first order line
exercises.question: Merchandising asks: which orders started with a big-ticket item (first line priced at 100 or more)?

'$.items[0].price' = price of the first element of items.
... WHERE payload ->> '$.items[0].price' >= 100;

recall.q: Is JSON array indexing 0-based or 1-based?

exercises.snowflake: SELECT event_id, payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, payload:items[0].product_id::INT AS first_product_id, payload:items[0].qty::INT AS first_qty, payload:items[0].price::NUMBER(10,2) AS first_price FROM raw_order_events WHERE first_price >= 100;

       payload ->> '$.items[0].price'      AS first_price
FROM raw_order_events
WHERE payload ->> '$.items[0].price' >= 100;

/* Snowflake notes:
SELECT event_id, payload:order_id::INT AS order_id, payload:items[0].product_id::INT
AS first_product_id, payload:items[0].qty::INT AS first_qty,
payload:items[0].price::NUMBER(10,2) AS first_price FROM raw_order_events WHERE
first_price >= 100;
*/

SELECT event_id,
       payload:order_id::INT                 AS order_id,

       payload:items[0]:qty::INT             AS first_qty,
